title: Tom Cruise's praise of Kate Middleton highlights her 'untouched by scandal' reputation: expert
summary: Tom Cruise's glowing praise of Kate Middleton at the London "Digger" premiere reflects her unique standing in the royal family, experts say.
story: Simon Vigar, author of "The Four Wives of Windsor," praises Kate Middleton’s intelligence and says Prince William trusts the Princess of Wales "absolutely implicitly" for impartial advice.
Tom Cruise's recent effusive praise for Kate Middleton was not just Hollywood flattery, according to royal experts.

The Prince and Princess of Wales, both 44, joined Cruise at the world premiere of the 64-year-old actor's new movie "Digger" in London on Sept. 22. During an interview with "Extra" at the film's Los Angeles premiere on Monday, Cruise raved over the royal couple and shared a particularly glowing assessment of Middleton.

"It was just so fun sitting there watching them watch it and for them to be part of it," Cruise said, via People magazine. "I have so much respect for them, you know, they’re amazing people and how dedicated they are to their country and also… what they give to the world. They’re just beautiful people and fun, very funny."
KATE MIDDLETON’S CAREFULLY PLANNED PATH TO THE THRONE REVEALED AS EXPERT SAYS SHE ‘PLAYED THE LONG GAME’
"She’s got a great sense, incredible sense of humor," Cruise said of Middleton. "I mean, obviously very intelligent and fun."
Tom Cruise recently gushed over Kate Middleton after she and Prince William attended the London premiere of the actor's movie "Digger." (Getty Images for Warner Bros.)
"They’re so charismatic and so elegant," he gushed. "That dress that she was wearing? Stunning."
PRINCE WILLIAM, KATE MIDDLETON FINALLY FEEL FREE TO SHOW AFFECTION IN PUBLIC: EXPERTS
"William did well," Cruise added with a smile. "Way to go, smart choice. Yeah, I gotta give it to William. Way to go. Smart choice."
Cruise's comments quickly made headlines, with royal experts arguing they reflected Middleton's unique standing within the monarchy rather than simply offering another celebrity compliment.
KATE MIDDLETON HAILED AS THE MONARCHY'S 'SAVING GRACE' AFTER CANCER BATTLE TRANSFORMED HER ROYAL ROLE: EXPERTS
Cruise said that William and Kate are "so charismatic and so elegant." (Getty Images for Warner Bros.)

While speaking to Fox News Digital, royal expert Christopher Andersen said that the Hollywood icon's admiration underscores why Middleton has become one of the royal family's greatest assets, pointing to her enduring appeal and scandal-free reputation.

"Do not underestimate the importance of her immense popularity," he said. "Kate Middleton is universally adored, and, unlike most celebrities, is virtually untouched by scandal. Like everybody else on the planet, Tom Cruise certainly wouldn't mind having some of that fairy dust rub off on him."
PRINCE WILLIAM FACES 'WORK-SHY' CRITICISM BUT IS SECRETLY RUNNING MONARCHY LIKE A CEO, EXPERT SAYS
Andersen, who authored the 2026 biography "Kate!: The Courage, Grace, and Power of the Woman Who Will Be Queen," noted that Cruise was also likely drawn to Middleton's beauty and style.
"If she wasn't movie-star gorgeous and stunningly fashionable, I don't think Tom Cruise would be drooling all over her," he said.
Fox News may be compensated for or earn a commission if you buy through our referral links.
"Kate!: The Courage, Grace, and Power of the Woman Who Will Be Queen" by Christopher Andersen is available now. (Gallery Books)
Royal commentator Amanda Matta echoed Andersen's opinion, arguing that Cruise's praise speaks to Kate's central role within the monarchy.

"While this was definitely an easy sound-bite for Cruise to pull out, it also happens to be true," she told Fox News Digital. "I think what Cruise is picking up on with this remark is that Kate is the entire reason the Wales brand works."
PRINCE WILLIAM AND KATE MIDDLETON’S ‘GENUINE LOVE STORY' IS BUILT ON BEING A 'VERY NORMAL FAMILY': AUTHOR
Cruise said that "William did well" by marrying Middleton. (WireImage)

"She wasn’t born into nobility, but that worked in her favor to help the Palace connect with the modern public," Matta continued. "Kate’s grounded humor and elegance are both central to William's public image now, and the public’s warmth toward her is one of the monarchy’s most valuable assets."
Royal commentator Richard Fitzwilliams told Fox News Digital that Cruise's remarks simply reflect the majority of the public's perception of Middleton.
KATE MIDDLETON SCALES UK'S THREE HIGHEST PEAKS IN 24 HOURS WITH A DEEPLY PERSONAL MESSAGE FOR CANCER SURVIVORS

"He’s just saying what most people think," Fitzwilliams said. "She is exquisite, her intelligence, humor and dress sense are part of her personality, which has given them both a worldwide aura as a couple. This is of enormous help to Britain, as soft power is so significant and also to the charities they both do so much for."
Cruise, Middleton, William and David Beckham are pictured at the "Digger" premiere. (Getty Images for Warner Bros.)
Royal experts also told Fox News Digital that Cruise's remarks about Middleton carried extra weight given the action star's decades-long relationship with the British royal family.
KING CHARLES RESPONDS TO CHARLES SPENCER'S CLAIMS ABOUT PRINCESS DIANA IN A RARE STATEMENT

The actor met the late Princess Diana at the 1992 London premiere of "Far and Away" alongside his co-star and then-wife Nicole Kidman. Andersen recalled that he had previously written about their first encounter and the "schoolgirl crush Diana had on Cruise" in his 1998 best-selling book "The Day Diana Died."

"Diana joked that she wouldn't mind if Kidman were out of the way. ‘Nicole kept giving me dagger eyes,’ Diana told a friend, ‘as if to say keep your hands off my handsome husband!’" Andersen remembered.

After their first meeting, Cruise and Diana went on to develop a friendship. In 1995, Cruise invited the princess and her sons, William and Prince Harry, to visit the set of the original "Mission: Impossible" movie at Pinewood Studios outside London.
In 2022, royal expert Neil Sean wrote that Cruise was "devastated" when Diana died in a car accident at the age of 36 in August 1997.
"She was a magical person and really engulfed you with her personality," Cruise told Sean.

Cruise has been linked to the royal family since the early days of his career when he and then-wife Nicole Kidman met Princess Diana at the London premiere of their 1992 movie "Far and Away." (Tim Graham)
KATE MIDDLETON WEARS PRINCESS DIANA'S PEARL BRACELET AT TROOPING THE COLOUR AS CHARLOTTE MIRRORS HER MOTHER
Cruise and Kidman were among the celebrity guests who paid tribute to the late princess at her funeral on Sept. 6, 1997.

William would later forge his own friendship with Cruise, who held a special screening of his 2022 sequel "Top Gun: Maverick" for the prince and Middleton ahead of the movie's release. Cruise invited the royal couple after learning that William, who previously served as a pilot with the Royal Air Force, was a huge fan of the original film. The Prince and Princess of Wales later attended the London premiere of "Top Gun: Maverick" at the invitation of Cruise.
At the time, Cruise told PA News Agency that he and William had "a lot in common," explaining, "We both love England, and we're both aviators. We both love flying."
The actor later appeared in King Charles III's 2023 coronation concert and previously took part in Queen Elizabeth II's Platinum Jubilee celebrations.
"Cruise, perhaps more than most Hollywood stars, has had a fairly up close and personal relationship with the royal family," Andersen noted.
Middleton and William previously joined Cruise at the premiere of "Top Gun: Maverick." (Photo by Dan Kitwood/Getty Images)
Having witnessed both Diana's extraordinary popularity and Middleton's rise within the royal family, Andersen explained he believes Cruise's admiration is well-founded.

"Obviously Kate is meeting, if not transcending, the public's inevitable expectations based on her Diana-like approachability," he said.
Royal expert Hilary Fordwich told Fox News Digital that Cruise's comments captured the qualities that have made Middleton one of the world's most admired royals.

"His remark managed to sum up what is so immensely universally appealing about her, that she is dignified, discreet, elegant, intelligent and poised all whilst being wonderfully warm as well as interested in others, so authentically," she said.
Fordwich said that Cruise's remarks captured Middleton's universal appeal. (Chris Jackson)

title: Sylvester Stallone's advice to those who are struggling 50 years after 'Rocky' changed his life
summary: Sylvester Stallone, now 80, shares the motto he lives by and why he wrote "The Steps" so his children could understand his journey from obscurity.
story: Actor and filmmaker Sylvester Stallone discusses his unlikely rise to stardom and reflects on the experiences that shaped his career. He also shares some of his biggest filmmaking influences and looks back on the lessons he learned from movies on ‘Special Report.’
Fifty years after "Rocky" made Sylvester Stallone a household name, the 80-year-old says his advice to people who are struggling is "you have nothing to lose" if you try.

"Rocky," a story about a low-level boxer who got the unexpected chance to become a champion, parallels the actor’s own life from being so broke he had to sell his dog to winning the Oscar for the 1976 classic.

"What would you tell the kid who’s sleeping on the bench at Port Authority with $80 in his pocket?" Fox News’ Bret Baier asked Stallone on "Special Report" on Tuesday while discussing his new memoir "The Steps."
'I PLAY ROCKY' REVIVES THE GAMBLE THAT MADE SYLVESTER STALLONE A SUPERSTAR
Sylvester Stallone said his own motto is "I tried." (Getty Images)

"You have nothing to lose. Seriously, you have nothing to lose. With failure you don’t get shot. There’s no firing squad," Stallone said. "The only thing you have to lose is your peace of mind if you don’t try. At least try. You may quit halfway through, but at least say, ‘I tried.’"
Stallone said his own motto is "I tried."
SYLVESTER STALLONE SAYS HE'D BE IN 'BIG TROUBLE' TRYING TO MAKE HIS CAREER IN TODAY'S HOLLYWOOD
As a broke 23-year-old backpacking through the Pyrenees in Europe in 1969, Stallone wrote in the book that a fortune-teller predicted he would find fortune by 1976, the same year "Rocky" came out.
"And she said also, ‘A woman will bring you into the circle of attention, and that was my manager, Jane Oliver, who’s the only one like who plucked me from obscurity," he said.
SYLVESTER STALLONE REVEALS SURPRISING HEALTH STRUGGLE BEHIND HIS FAMOUSLY RIPPED PHYSIQUE
Actors Sylvester Stallone and Carl Weathers perform a boxing scene in the 1976 movie "Rocky." (Getty Images)
Early in his career, Stallone went by the name Mike, but decided to go back to Sylvester.
Stallone felt pre-"Rocky" that he was drifting off into "total obscurity" and thought if Humphrey Bogart could make a career with his name, then "Sylvester’s not so bad."
SYLVESTER STALLONE'S 'TULSA KING' SEASON 4 TEASER SPARKS FAN FRENZY: 'THE KING IS BACK!'
Sylvester Stallone as boxer Rocky Balboa trains with a punchbag in the 1976 film "Rocky." (Getty Images)
"I thought, that’s memorable because I’ve never met another Sylvester. So at least it was just another hook that maybe people would remember as opposed to Mike."
Stallone told Baier that he decided to write his book now because he wanted his children to "understand the journey" it took to get him where he is now.
MATT DAMON SAYS HOLLYWOOD'S 'RUTHLESS' NATURE HAS TAKEN HIM AWAY FROM FATHERHOOD MORE THAN HE'D LIKE
The "Tulsa King" actor called ushering at a theater his "film school," explaining that he would watch three showings a night on his shift and would take notes from films like "M*A*S*H."
"I thought, where do you learn more about a film than in a theater where you actually see a reaction?"
HOLLYWOOD PRODUCER BEHIND 'APOLLO 13' REJECTS POLITICS IN HIS MOVIES, SEEKS TO UNITE AUDIENCES

He said college is "very cloistered," whereas in a theater it’s "instant enjoyment or repulsion or they leave. So, I learned a great, great deal. It’s like with a waiter – you want to learn the restaurant business? Be a waiter."
"I learned more in a movie theater than I would imagine in college," he said.
Stallone, with fellow winner Beatrice Straight, holding his Oscar after winning in 1977. (Getty Images)
TOM CRUISE ADMITS RUMORS ABOUT HIS 'INTENSE' BEHAVIOR ON MOVIE SETS ARE TRUE
Stallone also wrote that the "go the distance" speech in "Rocky" almost didn’t happen because the producers wanted to cut it.

title: Ella Langley addresses criticism in emotional concert speech as 'Choosin' Texas' dominates charts
summary: Ella Langley addressed critics in a viral video from her Columbus, Ohio, concert, revealing how harsh opinions nearly made her question her career.
story: Ella Langley speaks about her deep appreciation for supporters and how their connection transformed her path during an interview tied to the 2026 iHeartRadio Music Awards held March 26, 2026, in Los Angeles.
Ella Langley shared an inspiring message with her fans during her latest concert.

During one of her recent performances in Columbus, Ohio, the 27-year-old singer opened up about the amount of criticism she's received since her breakthrough in the industry, saying, "I don’t think I’ve ever had more opinions on myself in my life than I have in this last year."

"The way I look. The way I speak. The way I dress. The way I move. The way I sing. The way I write," she explained per a TikTok video. "At first it bothered me. I won’t even lie. At first I was like, what am I going to do about this? I don’t know, if this is what I’m signing up to do, I don’t know about this."
She went on to say that what she "signed up" for was to make music, but if this was going to continue for her entire career, she thought, "I don’t know if I’m strong enough for this, Lord."
Langley shared how she is able to handle the criticism that comes with being in the public eye. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)
ELLA LANGLEY TELLS FANS TO STOP MEASURING THEMSELVES AGAINST SOCIAL MEDIA IN VIRAL CONCERT VIDEO

While it bothered her at first, Langley explained she began imagining that the critiques were being aimed at her younger self who put in the hard work to get her to where she is today, which put into perspective how strong she actually has had to be.

"That’s the girl that rode in the 15-passenger van night after night after night. She rode in a Honda Accord night after night after night, chasing her dream, living on bar food, living on tip jar money. She didn’t have anything but a dream and the ability to get up and do it every single day. So I’m going to tell you right now, I am proud of that girl that everybody seems to be picking on a little bit," she said.
The singer recently went viral when a video of her turning down a fan who asked her out on a date following her concert in Knoxville, Tennessee.

In the video, TikTok user Tiki is heard taking his chance to ask the singer out on a date, shouting through a fence in the parking lot, "Ella, how many likes to take you on a date?" She replied, "Not enough in the world," as she frowned and looked away.

Along with the online criticism comes career highs and record-breaking songs, as Langley's hit song, "Choosin' Texas," has stayed at the top of the Billboard Hot 100 list for a historical 24 consecutive weeks.

The "St. Elmo's Fire" star advised his son, John Owen Lowe, to stay alert before heading out for a night in New York City – advice he brushed aside before returning home hours later with a black eye.

"The first time my sons were old enough to go to the nightclubs, they were here [in New York], and you know they're country rubes, my kids," Lowe said during an appearance on the "Chicks in the Office" podcast. "They grew up in Santa Barbara. They're not street smart."

Despite their impressive academic credentials, Lowe said his sons still had a few lessons to learn outside the classroom.

"So, my son was like, 'Yeah, I'm meeting my friends' … and I go, 'Where is it?' And he goes, 'It's down in the Bowery' and this and that and the other. I was like, 'All right, well, listen. You know, just keep your head on a swivel,'" Lowe shared. "He goes, 'Dad, Dad, I'm fine. I'm going to be fine.' I'm like, 'John Owen, it's New York. I'm just saying.' He goes, 'Dad, stop it!'"
"He was home by midnight with a black eye," Lowe recalled. "And had gotten mugged by a guy with a knife because he was on his phone not paying attention."

"But that's the thing is like, you know, it's like all kids are clueless experts," he explained.

title: Lady A's Charles Kelley diagnosed with rare blood cancer after painful health scare

title: ‘Saved by the Bell’ star Dennis Haskins dead at 75
summary: Dennis Haskins first portrayed Mr. Belding on "Good Morning, Miss Bliss" before the role became iconic across the "Saved by the Bell" franchise.
story: "Saved by the Bell" star Dennis Haskins, best known as beloved Bayside High Principal Richard Belding, has died at 75. His former co-stars are paying tribute to the actor on social media. (This video contains AI-assisted content.)
Dennis Haskins, the actor best known for playing Bayside High School Principal Richard Belding on the hit sitcom "Saved by the Bell," has died. He was 75.

Haskins' representative confirmed his death to Fox News Digital, saying, "It’s a tragic loss. Everyone loved Mr. Belding and those of us who got to know Dennis loved him even more. He was a great person, and he loved, I mean absolutely LOVED his fans. He always had time for them, no matter what. He was my client and dear friend for over 20 years, and I will miss him terribly. I’m heartbroken."
His cause of death is currently unknown.
HOLLYWOOD STARS WHO DIED IN 2026: PHOTOS
Dennis Haskins portrayed Principal Belding throughout "Saved by the Bell," earning a place in pop culture as the strict but caring school administrator. (Getty Images)
Haskins' former "Saved by the Bell" co-stars are remembering the actor following his death.

Mario Lopez, who played A.C. Slater, was among those to pay tribute to Haskins, remembering his former co-star as someone who brought a playful energy to the set despite portraying Bayside High's principal.

"Heartbroken to hear about my old friend Dennis Haskins. He played the principal, but Dennis was the biggest kid on the SBTB set. If you knew him, you loved him—and if there was karaoke, you knew Dennis was getting on that mic! I’m grateful for the laughs, the memories, and the friendship we shared all these years. Rest easy, my friend. You’ll always be part of our Bayside family," he wrote in a heartfelt social media post.

The cast of "Saved by the Bell," including Lark Voorhies, Ed Alonzo, Tiffani Thiessen, Mark-Paul Gosselaar, Dennis Haskins, Elizabeth Berkley, Dustin Diamond and Mario Lopez, is pictured together. (NBCU Photo Bank/NBCUniversal/Getty Images)
Tiffani Thiessen, who played Kelly Kapowski, also shared memories of Haskins, on Instagram.

"Dennis Haskins was a steady presence in my teenage years, the kind of figure who kept us in line while making sure we knew he was in our corner. I will always remember his kindness and be grateful for the memories we as a cast got to share with him. RIP Mr. B"
Lark Voorhies, who played Lisa Turtle on the hit sitcom, shared an emotional tribute on Instagram, reflecting on her nearly 40-year friendship with Haskins.
Voorhies called him a "fabulous person, a loyal friend, and someone with such a kind, gentle heart," and said she would miss his warmth and laughter.
Her tribute highlighted the longtime bond between the cast members, who remained connected decades after the original series ended.

title: Judge Judy passed the torch to son Adam Levy with one blunt piece of advice
summary: Adam Levy reveals the blunt advice his mother Judge Judy Sheindlin gave him before he took the bench on "Adam's Law" and how he confronts nepo-baby pressure.
story: Judge Adam Levy’s new courtroom show Adam’s Law premieres this month.

Judge Judy Sheindlin's son Adam Levy recalled how his famous mother displayed her trademark bluntness while encouraging him before he took the bench for his new syndicated reality court series "Adam's Law."

Levy, 58, is the presiding judge on the show, which was created by Sheindlin, 83, who also serves as an executive producer through her company Queen Bee Productions. "Adam's Law" is also produced and distributed in national syndication by CBS Media Ventures.
During a recent interview with Fox News Digital, Levy shared the advice that Sheindlin gave him before the television icon handed off the gavel to her son.
JUDGE JUDY'S SON ADAM LEVY SAYS HE COULD FIX LOS ANGELES ‘IN A MONTH’

"She said, 'You've got this. I know you've got this. Have fun, do what you do, don't let people lead you to places where you don't feel comfortable, be true to yourself, and don't screw this up,'" Levy said with a laugh. "That's what she said."
Judge Judy's son Adam Levy shared the blunt piece of advice that his mother gave him before he launched his new show "Adam's Law." (Paramount)
Prior to her TV fame, Sheindlin was a New York Family Court judge known for her no-nonsense courtroom style. She was appointed to The Family Court in 1982 by then Mayor Ed Koch.

Sheindlin skyrocketed to fame after she was featured in a 1993 "60 Minutes" segment that introduced viewers to her tough, outspoken courtroom demeanor. She went on to star in the syndicated courtroom hit "Judge Judy" for 25 seasons from 1996 to 2021.

During its run, "Judge Judy" was the highest-rated courtroom show on television, regularly drawing millions of viewers and at one point attracting an audience of 10 million. It became one of the most successful syndicated programs in TV history. After wrapping "Judge Judy" in July 2021, Sheindlin returned to the courtroom that November with the Amazon streaming series "Judy Justice."
HAYDEN PANETTIERE AND THE CHILD STARS WHOSE RELATIONSHIPS WITH THEIR MOMAGERS TURNED COMPLICATED
Earlier this month, Sheindlin announced that the October finale of "Judy Justice" would mark her retirement from appearing on TV, and she was passing the torch to Levy.
Sheindlin starred in the hit courtroom reality series "Judge Judy" for 25 years. (Bob Riha Jr./Getty Images)

Levy is the son of Sheindlin and her ex-husband Ronald Levy, who also share daughter Jamie. He has practiced law for 25 years and previously served two terms as the Putnam County District Attorney in New York.
JUDGE ADAM LEVY PREVIEWS HIS ‘NITTY-GRITTY’ NEW SHOW – AND HOW HIS STYLE COMPARES TO HIS MOM JUDGE JUDY
Before launching "Adam's Law" on Sept. 14, Levy appeared as a presiding judge on Prime Video's "Tribunal Justice" and "Justice on Trial," two courtroom series created by Sheindlin.

While speaking with Fox News Digital, Levy confessed that he was worried about how his mother would judge his performance when he made his TV debut on "Tribunal Justice." He admitted to feeling pressure to live up to her legacy, and he was anxious over being labeled a "nepo baby."
KAIA GERBER OWNS 'NEPO BABY' STATUS WHILE QUESTIONING OTHER CELEBRITY KIDS: 'SHOW ME WHY YOU DESERVE THIS JOB'

"I was nervous," he recalled. "Not doing what I was doing, that was in my wheelhouse. I didn't want to disappoint her. And I knew that there were a lot of other people, a lot of other lawyers and judges that were just as qualified, if not more so, to be in the seat I was in."

"And, but for my DNA, I would still be trying cases someplace else," he continued. "So there was a lot of pressure to prove that, and it wasn't even to myself — because I knew that, again, it was in my wheelhouse — but to show everyone, ‘Listen, I get it. I get this whole nepo baby stuff. I do.’ And I can understand why people sometimes are disappointed and angry and upset and at the offspring of famous people."
"But at the same time, I just wanted people to give me a fair shot, a chance," Levy added.
"Adam's Law" premiered on Sept. 14. (Paramount)
Levy recalled feeling relieved when Sheindlin told him that he was "a natural" after watching him on "Tribunal Justice."
"When she saw me for the first time, she said, 'There, now you know. Now you've got nothing to worry about.' And that was nice to hear," he said.

Levy told Fox News Digital that while Sheindlin has never criticized the rulings that he makes on his shows, she has sometimes shared how she would have handled the cases differently. He explained that the two regularly discuss his cases and Sheindlin is continuing to actively mentor him.
JUDGE JUDY PREPARING TO END DECADES-LONG RUN AS TV'S TOUGHEST JUDGE
"She's hands-on," he said. "She's not retired. She is rewired. So, while she may not be in front of the camera anymore, that does not mean that she has removed herself from the courtroom genre."

"She and I discussed many of the cases before they are tried and when they are taped," Levy continued. "We will go over the facts of the case. We will go all over the legal issues, the moral issues, we will go over the background information that I have uncovered and how, if at all, to use it during the trial."
Levy said that his discussions with Sheindlin were in keeping with a tradition that his family members, many of whom include prosecutors and defense attorneys, carried on for 30 years.
Sheindlin is pictured with Levy and her husband, ex-Bronx State Supreme Court Justice Gerald Sheindlin. (Howard Earl Simmons/NY Daily News Archive via Getty Images)
"Whenever we had cases, we would go out to dinner as a family," he recalled. "And we would — whoever was on trial, we would bring our case file, and we would throw it in the middle of the table."

"Everyone would take a piece, and we'd review it," Levy continued. "We would find the strengths and the weaknesses and how to go about arguing the issues before — whether it was a bench trial with a judge or a jury. I mean, that's what we did."
JUDGE JUDY WARNS OF 'DANGER' IF PROSECUTORS DON'T RETRY LINDSAY CLANCY AFTER MURDER TRIAL ENDS IN MISTRIAL
"And that's what I do now with Judy," he added. "So I think it's seamless. The process is seamless. That's what we do."
Levy explained that his judicial style is "a bit different" than that of his mother, though viewers will also recognize certain similarities.

"It is still about taking personal responsibility for yourself, doing the right thing, telling the truth when you're in court — all of those things are the same," he said. "The way that I go about it though is my own style. It's a little more understanding at times, I think, but when someone comes in to court and misrepresents their case or lies, that's when you'll see the DNA come out."

Levy also shared that his approach to the litigants who appear before him in court was influenced by his upbringing under Sheindlin's watchful eye. He told Fox News Digital that he and his sister Jamie could "never" get away with anything while they were growing up.
Levy served two terms as district attorney in Putnam County. (Robert Sabo/NY Daily News Archive via Getty Images)
JUDGE JUDY SAYS THOSE WHO DON'T LIKE AMERICA SHOULD 'GO SOMEWHERE ELSE'

"I kid around, and I say, hundreds of millions of people have watched her over the last 30 years. And they see a tough lady, a tough judge, cutting through the nonsense, and they see it every day," he said. "I, when I saw her on TV, would say, 'Yeah, that's exactly who I grew up with. Exactly.'"

"And when the litigants would say something that offended her sense of common sense, or said something that was demonstrably false, I could sympathize with that litigant because I, as a kid, would try to do the same thing," Levy continued. "And when they would say it, I would just close my eyes and wince because I knew what was coming. And she never disappointed me while watching her on the show."

"But in all fairness, at the same time, I also remember when things would happen, and I would tell the truth as a child, as a teenager, and she did not believe something I said that was the truth," he shared. "And I remembered how that felt. And so with that in mind, as I'm doing the show now, as part of my own style, is not to so quickly reject something someone says if it sounds or if it would seem to be inconsistent with common sense."

"Sometimes, things happen that are inconsistent with commonsense," Levy noted. "Everyday life, things just — you get a curveball. And just because you get a curveball, and you respond to that curveball in a certain way doesn't mean that — and you tell about it — doesn't mean that you're lying."
Levy said his judicial style was shaped by his mother's tough-love upbringing. (Donaldson Collection/Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)
Levy explained that his childhood experiences led him to make a major format change to "Adam's Law" that differentiated the series from his mother's courtroom shows.

On "Judge Judy," Sheindlin generally questioned litigants and reviewed the case file as the proceedings unfolded on camera. She would receive the case materials at the start of each hearing, summarize the dispute, and then question the parties, with much of the evidence being introduced during the televised proceeding.
However, Levy said that he built more time into his process so he could thoroughly vet each case before litigants stepped into his courtroom.

"I insisted on changing the format to requiring the litigant to provide their evidence before they come to the show so that I could review it," he said. "And if something did seem off, I was able to examine it, do a background check on it."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Levy is pictured with law clerk Jessica Ramirez and bailiff Rodney Young on his show. (CBS Media Ventures)

"I was able to spend a little more time or no — I could spend a lot more time," Levy continued. "Sometimes it would take me a day, one full day, to review one case that would end up 17 minutes on TV."

"It would take me 48 hours sometimes to go through it to make sure that, at least to me, I got it right. Because I didn't want to accuse someone of being a liar, where they were really telling the truth."
When asked who between himself and his mother would be more likely to show mercy if they heard the exact same case separately, Levy had a definitive answer.

"I would," Levy said. "Because she has never been on the other end of her takedown. I have."

"I needed mercy from her, so I'm probably more likely to give it than she is," he added with a laugh.

title: Royal family unclear of Harry and Meghan’s motives as ‘frustration’ lingers: expert
summary: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle's return to the U.K. has the royal family questioning their motives as experts debate a half-in half-out role.
story: Royal commentator Richard Fitzwilliams says the Duke and Duchess of Sussex are unlikely to return as working royals despite questions over their UK role and security.
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle have been back in the U.K. for a month, and senior members of the royal family still don't know what their agenda is.
On Sept. 16, People reported that a palace source said, "The royal family still don’t know what their motives are," just weeks after Harry and Markle officially moved overseas.

Royal commentators told Fox News Digital they are divided over Harry and Meghan’s return to the U.K., with some accusing the palace of undermining the couple while others said the intervention was necessary to reaffirm that they remain private citizens and will not resume a "half-in, half-out" royal role.
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle have returned to the U.K. after living in California. (Chris Jackson)

A little over a week after Harry and Markle made their plans to relocate back to the U.K. public, King Charles issued a letter via the Lord Chamberlain, Lord Benyon, stating that they would be classified as non-working royals.
MEGHAN MARKLE’S UK RETURN POSES PALACE CONTROL ‘NIGHTMARE,’ EXPERT WARNS
Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital that the palace is undermining Harry and Meghan’s return while preventing them from creating royal-style events.
"Harry and Meghan claim to want a private family life in Britain with access to Harry’s roots, while they repeatedly invade their own privacy."

"Harry and Meghan simply want to be left in peace, allowing themselves privacy to protect their children and to cover some charity activities. The palace, I feel, are being driven by officials and maybe William to constantly undermine this return. Officially, they are making sure Harry and Meghan are not seen to be creating royal-style events," he said.
According to Turner, the letter on behalf of the king was unnecessary.
PRINCE WILLIAM AND KATE MIDDLETON 'PLAYING IT COOL' AS PRINCE HARRY AND MEGHAN MARKLE RETURN TO THE UK: EXPERT
Meghan Markle and Prince Harry were deemed "private citizens" by King Charles upon their return to Britain. (Wiktor Szymanowicz/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images)

"In my mind, the act of clarification was not necessary, creating humiliation for the couple and a cowardly act by those behind the letter," he began. "William may see the return as a distraction from his popularity and, as it seems already, Harry has received some favorable accolades from people he is meeting at events -- this could be an annoyance to William’s ego."

Hilary Fordwich, British royal expert, told Fox News Digital that the letter on behalf of the king was just clarification on what they already agreed upon when Harry and Markle stepped away as senior royals in 2020.

"Harry and Meghan claim to want a private family life in Britain with access to Harry’s roots, while they repeatedly invade their own privacy. They are retaining their independent charitable and commercial careers while also posturing themselves as working royals, which is directly thwarting the Sandringham agreement to refrain from monetizing their titles. The palace’s public intervention demonstrates the concerns surrounding their posturing with official royal type activities."
Prince William and Prince Harry are seen together in 2021. (Getty Images)
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
"The public clarification from King Charles III was another line in the sand, restating what was already agreed regarding the Sussexes' departure for the U.S. in 2020," Fordwich said.

"The Lord Chamberlain’s letter not only stated that the Sussexes were actually not undertaking royal engagements, it reiterated no change in their status, clarified that they are no longer working royals and that their HRH styles remain in abeyance,' Fordwich noted.

Fordwich added, "The unusually explicit institutional language clearly indicated the degree of royal frustration regarding the Sussexes. It certainly didn’t state anything regarding the couple leaving Britain. It was more of an attempt to mitigate the ambiguity and blurred roles the couple keep creating, which is reputationally damaging to the royal brand, particularly due to the commercial aspects, as monetizing the monarchy is so distasteful."
Richard Fitzwilliams, royal commentator, touched on the "half-in, half-out" royal role that Harry and Markle allegedly want now that they're back in the U.K.
"My feeling is that Harry and Meghan will not get the opportunity to become a half-in, half-out, which is what basically they've wanted, not officially," Fitzwilliams began.
Prince William, Prince Harry, Meghan Markle and Kate Middleton in 2018. (Getty Images)

He continued, "They won't be working members of the royal family. Harry is, of course, fifth in line [to] the throne still. And there's no question that I think they would like the option. After all, they have come to the United Kingdom in August without any warning by three days to the king. That is absolutely extraordinary. We still don't know the main reason they are here, and their children have been taken to another school."
Fordwich also discussed the "half-in, half-out" mentality.

"This certainly further strains H’s relationship with Prince William since he is deliberately disregarding the explicit wishes of their much-loved grandmother Queen Elizabeth II, who was adamant there could be no ‘half-in-half-out’ scenario," she said.

Fordwich continued, "Most wisely, Prince William is remaining dedicated to duty and his disciplined approach to the monarchy centered on the king, the Wales family and a limited number of working royals is appreciated by the public, as reflected in YouGov polling. His continuing to avoid all the Sussex 'drama,' will no doubt serve him most well."
WATCH: Prince Harry, Meghan Markle unlikely to get 'half in, half out' royal role: expert
Earlier this month, a source close to Harry and Markle told People magazine that they are "public figures."
"Members of the public know who they are. The idea that they can live a normal, ‘private’ life is sadly not realistic," the source said at the time, while also raising concerns over their security.
Fitzwilliams touched on the security issue with Fox News Digital and weighed different scenarios where it would be difficult to grant Harry and Markle "VIP automatic security."
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"But what would it mean if the security, for example, which is being looked at again, as Harry has requested, if they get VIP automatic security, and it certainly seems likely there's going to be some compromise. Would that, for example, involve looking after Meghan in the United States? I mean, I would think it unlikely, but, of course, the point is not for the popularity rating. I think people don't want it. It's a question of the nature of the threat. And if they did get it, then the feeling is perhaps they should do a certain amount to justify it," he said.
Meghan Markle, Prince Harry and King Charles in 2018. (Getty Images)

"Could they hope to get through to do royal duties or some royal duties of some sort in that way? Harry, after all, is thoroughly likable, and they regard themselves as public figures, and they would've liked an opportunity to clarify what was in the letter that the king said round," Fitzwilliams continued. "We know Prince William is adamantly opposed to them doing anything, and indeed there's a deep, deep rift there. He believes he's been betrayed. And when you look at the situation since Megxit, you can see why they're mistrusted. But there's questions to whether or not in some form they will be performing some type of royal activity somewhere, probably Britain, even despite opinion polls, which are low. [It] won't go away for quite a long time."

title: Reality star claims daughter, 20, 'had fentanyl in her system' in airport bodycam
summary: Teresa Giudice claimed Milania Giudice "had fentanyl in her system," according to airport bodycam footage. And Milania responded saying she was "laced."
story: Teresa Giudice claimed her daughter Milania had fentanyl in her system as bodycam video showed the 20-year-old's tense encounter with police at Tampa International Airport. (This video contains AI-assisted content.)
Milania Giudice allegedly had fentanyl in her system, Teresa Giudice claimed in bodycam video.

The "Real Housewives of New Jersey" star made the claim while attempting to explain her daughter's behavior during an encounter with officers at Tampa International Airport, according to bodycam footage obtained by Page Six.
Milania, 20, fired back, as seen in the bodycam footage, saying, "Cause I was laced ... I go to college," before her sister Gia told her, "You're reckless."

title: What to know about pentobarbital after death row inmate survives 2 lethal injection doses
summary: A look at pentobarbital reveals why the barbiturate used in Christa Gail Pike's failed lethal injection may not have reached fatal concentrations.
story: A Tennessee execution fails after multiple botched lethal injection attempts on an inmate who survives the ordeal. Steve Harrigan reports on the failed attempts and the governor's decision to halt future executions.

A high-profile execution attempt in Nashville ended in chaos and raised urgent medical questions after Tennessee death row inmate Christa Gail Pike survived two separate doses of lethal pentobarbital, the Associated Press reported.
Pentobarbital is a short-acting barbiturate, according to medical authorities at the National Institutes of Health (NIH).

Historically prescribed as a sedative, anti-seizure medication or sleep aid, pentobarbital enhances the activity of GABA, the brain's primary inhibitory neurotransmitter, slowing activity throughout the central nervous system.
TENNESSEE DEATH ROW INMATE SURVIVES 2 LETHAL INJECTION DOSES IN FAILED EXECUTION ATTEMPT
In clinical medicine, pentobarbital has been used for several purposes, including:

Controlling certain severe or acute seizuresInducing medically managed comas in some patients with severe traumatic brain injury and dangerously elevated intracranial pressureSedating patients before anesthesia or surgery
Controlling certain severe or acute seizures
Inducing medically managed comas in some patients with severe traumatic brain injury and dangerously elevated intracranial pressure
Sedating patients before anesthesia or surgery
Christa Gail Pike is seen during her trial for the murder of Colleen A. Slemmer on March 18, 1996, in Knox County Criminal Court. (USA Today Network via Reuters Connect)
Because newer, safer drugs with lower risks of overdose have largely replaced barbiturates in hospital settings, pentobarbital is now rarely used in routine patient care.

However, it remains a primary agent in veterinary euthanasia and lethal injection protocols across several U.S. states, according to the National Library of Medicine, FDA-approved veterinary drug labeling and the Death Penalty Information Center.
How pentobarbital is used in lethal injections
In a high-dose lethal injection protocol, pentobarbital is administered intravenously in large, ultra-lethal quantities — typically 2.5 to 5 grams (far exceeding clinical therapeutic doses).
JUDGE BLOCKS ALABAMA'S NITROGEN GAS EXECUTION METHOD, RULES IT IS UNCONSTITUTIONALLY CRUEL
When injected directly into a vein, the progression follows three stages, according to medical sources.

Rapid unconsciousness: Within seconds to a few minutes, the drug crosses the blood-brain barrier, inducing surgical anesthesia and loss of consciousness.Respiratory depression: As brainstem activity slows to a halt, the body's ability to breathe automatically is suppressed, causing rapid respiratory arrest.Cardiac arrest: As breathing stops and oxygen levels fall, combined with the drug's depressant effects, the heart eventually stops beating.
Rapid unconsciousness: Within seconds to a few minutes, the drug crosses the blood-brain barrier, inducing surgical anesthesia and loss of consciousness.
Respiratory depression: As brainstem activity slows to a halt, the body's ability to breathe automatically is suppressed, causing rapid respiratory arrest.
Cardiac arrest: As breathing stops and oxygen levels fall, combined with the drug's depressant effects, the heart eventually stops beating.
What happened in the Christa Pike execution?
Pike, 50, who was convicted in the 1995 murder of classmate Colleen Slemmer, was slated to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.

Media witnesses and defense filings reported that Pike remained conscious and vocal, experienced breathing difficulties, and snored loudly for over 40 minutes after receiving the drug. (Tennessee Department of Correction via AP)
Media witnesses observed her asking if her arm was supposed to feel that way (burning), breathing raggedly, and audibly snoring behind closed curtains over an hour-long span.
The incident prompted Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to halt all remaining executions in the state pending an independent investigation.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

According to statements from the Tennessee Department of Correction (TDOC), officials administered two doses of pentobarbital, in accordance with the state's established single-drug execution protocol.
State officials maintained that they strictly adhered to the protocol and that the chemical supply was verified.

According to the NIH and Cleveland Clinic, pentobarbital is a short-acting barbiturate used medically as a central nervous system depressant to treat severe seizures and induce medically managed comas. (iStock)
Media witnesses and defense court filings described several problems during the procedure.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Difficulty establishing IV access: Defense filings noted that execution staff struggled to establish clear IV lines, a potential point of failure in lethal injections.Failure of the execution: Despite receiving two doses of pentobarbital, Pike continued breathing, occasionally lifting her head and audibly snoring for more than 40 minutes after the second dose.Transfer to a hospital: At 8:53 p.m., prison staff ended the procedure and transferred Pike to an off-site hospital.

Transfer to a hospital: At 8:53 p.m., prison staff ended the procedure and transferred Pike to an off-site hospital.

Why do pentobarbital injections fail?
Several possible explanations have been raised in court filings and medical literature, although no cause has been confirmed in Pike’s case.
Medical experts point out that if an IV line slips out of the vein, pentobarbital leaks into surrounding muscle and fat, absorbing too slowly to reach the brain at a lethal concentration. (iStock)

IV infiltration: If an IV line slips out of the vein, the drug can leak into surrounding tissue instead of entering the bloodstream. Absorption is slower, which may delay or prevent the drug from reaching the brain at a concentration sufficient to cause unconsciousness and death.Individual metabolism or tolerance: Differences in liver function, drug metabolism or prior exposure to barbiturates could affect how the body responds to pentobarbital.Drug quality or potency: Because major pharmaceutical manufacturers restrict the use of their drugs in executions, states may obtain pentobarbital from compounding pharmacies, raising questions about its potency, consistency or storage.

title: Surprising culprit tied to 1 in 8 cancer cases worldwide, major study reveals
summary: A new IARC analysis links 2.3 million cancer cases worldwide to 12 infections, with H. pylori, HPV and hepatitis B leading the global burden.
story: Dr. Joshua Cohen, medical director of the Gynecologic Cancer Program of City of Hope Orange County in Irvine, California, told Fox News Digital that it’s important to seek treatment or preventive mechanisms for certain infections linked to cancer.
About one in eight new cancer cases worldwide in 2024 — 2.3 million cases — have been linked to infections, according to a new analysis from the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC).

The researchers identified 12 specific infections that were linked to human cancer cases, including Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori), human papillomavirus (HPV), hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), Epstein–Barr virus (EBV), Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus, Schistosoma haematobium, HTLV-1, Opisthorchis viverrini, Clonorchis sinensis, Merkel cell polyomavirus and HIV.
The following five infections contributed to nearly all the global cases.
POPULAR DAILY DRINKING HABIT COULD NEARLY TRIPLE RISK OF DEADLY CANCER, MAJOR STUDY FINDS
H. pylori : ~760,000 casesHPV: ~750,000 casesHBV: ~360,000 casesEBV: ~260,000 casesHCV: ~160,000 cases
H. pylori : ~760,000 cases
HPV: ~750,000 cases
HBV: ~360,000 cases
EBV: ~260,000 cases
HCV: ~160,000 cases
About one in eight new cancer cases worldwide in 2024, 2.3 million cases, were linked to infections, according to a new analysis from the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC). (iStock)

"The findings underscore the major role that infection control can play in reducing the global cancer burden," said study co-author Dr. Harriet Rumgay, a scientist in the Cancer Surveillance Branch at IARC, in a press release.

"Despite progress in vaccination and screening, infection-related cancers remain a major global challenge, with the burden falling disproportionately on populations in low- and middle-income countries."
CANCER DOCTOR REVEALS 5 HABITS THAT MAY REDUCE DISEASE RISK AND IMPROVE OUTCOMES
The researchers say many of these cancers could have been prevented through vaccination, treatment or screenings.
The study, conducted in France, analyzed cancer data from 2024. The findings were published in The Lancet Oncology on Sept. 28.
Study limitations
The study had several limitations, the researchers acknowledged.
Because the study used population-level estimates rather than tracking individual patients over time, the results depended on the quality of available cancer data in each country.
Additionally, it only included infections already proven to cause cancer, so the total impact could be underestimated.
The researchers identified 12 specific infections that were linked to human cancer cases, including Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) and human papillomavirus (HPV). (iStock)

"We know that there are certain infections that we are exposed to over our lifetime that may result in an increased risk of certain cancers," Dr. Joshua Cohen, medical director of the Gynecologic Cancer Program of City of Hope Orange County in Irvine, California, told Fox News Digital.
"However, most cancers are not caused by infection."
DOCTORS PUSH NEW BLOOD TESTS FOR COLON CANCER AS CASES SURGE IN YOUNGER ADULTS
HPV is one of the most common drivers of cancers that arise along the rectum, vagina or cervix, as well as the oropharynx (back of the throat), according to Cohen, who was not involved in the study.
"Eighty percent of the population has been exposed to certain types of HPV strains," he said. "About 40,000 people in the U.S. are diagnosed with these cancers each year."
"Most cancers are not caused by infection."
For most people who are exposed to HPV, the body will clear the virus on its own, Cohen said.
"We don't know why some patients' immune systems allow them to clear the HPV infection and some don't."
Another very common cancer, although less so in the U.S., is gastric cancer, he noted, which is linked to H. Pylori, an infection in the stomach.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"We don't screen everybody for H. pylori in the U.S. — it's more common in other parts of the world, like Southeast Asia."
However, those who have peptic ulcer disease or significant epigastric pain should talk with a gastroenterologist about getting screened and treated for H. pylori, the doctor advised.
Prevention strategies
There are things people can do to reduce the risk of infection-related cancers, according to Cohen.
"As a patient, the most important thing is to think about your health, what you can do to prevent yourself from developing these infections or your family," he said.
The researchers say many of these cancers could have been prevented through vaccination, treatment or screenings. (iStock)
"And if you do have one of these infections, what can you do to reduce your risk of developing a subsequent cancer?"
Cohen emphasized that Americans have access to an HPV vaccination that can help prevent many of these infections.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"If you’re under the age of 45 and you've not had an HPV vaccination, there is various good safety data that you should get vaccinated," he said. "That will cover, at least in the U.S., most risks regarding oropharyngeal cancers, vaginal cancers, cervical cancers, penile cancers and anal cancers."
"There are steps we can take as doctors to keep you safe and hopefully reduce the risk of developing cancer for those that have had an infection," an oncologist said. (iStock)
The doctor reiterated that developing one of the listed infections doesn’t necessarily mean someone will develop cancer.
"The vast majority of patients who have an HPV infection or H. Pylori, or even hepatitis B or C, are not going to develop cancer," he said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
But because these infections have been associated with certain cancers, it’s important to seek treatment for them.

Symptoms such as epigastric pain (pain or discomfort in the upper middle part of your abdomen), acid reflux, abnormal vaginal bleeding or pain with swallowing could be related to medical conditions that may be associated with certain infections or cancer, the doctor warned.
"There are steps we can take as doctors to keep you safe and hopefully reduce the risk of developing cancer for those that have had an infection," Cohen added.

title: Rapid weight loss on popular drugs could ‘starve’ the brain, expert warns
summary: Dr. Tommy Wood warns GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy can shrink brain tissue when caloric restriction cuts off vital energy the brain needs.
story: Dr. Tommy Wood, a professor of pediatrics and neuroscience at the University of Washington, shares how GLP-1 weight-loss drugs like Ozempic can affect brain reserve, and why resistance training is critical to protect it.

As GLP-1 weight-loss medications like Ozempic and Wegovy continue to surge in popularity, experts warn that rapid weight loss and severe caloric restriction could deprive the brain of vital energy and nutrients.

Dr. Tommy Wood, a professor of pediatrics and neuroscience at the University of Washington, said the drugs' effects on the brain may depend on whether the body is getting enough energy and nutrients during weight loss.

"The best way to think about this is the spectrum of what we call energy availability," Wood told Fox News Digital at Strong NY, New York City's largest annual fitness and wellness festival. "The brain is your most energy-hungry organ in the body."
POPULAR GLP-1 WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS LINKED TO POTENTIALLY DEADLY BRAIN DISORDER
According to Wood, brain reserve — the physical amount and integrity of brain tissue — follows a bell-shaped curve relative to the body's energy availability.
Excess energy caused by obesity, high blood sugar and metabolic disease can lower the brain's resilience by damaging blood vessels and contributing to insulin resistance.

As GLP-1 weight-loss medications like Ozempic and Wegovy continue to surge in popularity, experts warn that rapid weight loss and severe caloric restriction could deprive the brain of vital energy and nutrients. (iStock)
In these cases, GLP-1 medications can provide cognitive benefits by lowering blood pressure and improving blood sugar control.

However, Wood noted that the lower end of the energy spectrum poses its own structural risks to the brain. Because the brain relies heavily on continuous fuel, extreme caloric deficits can force the organ to consume its own tissue.
POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS CAN BECOME AN ‘ATOMIC BOMB’ AT HIGH DOSES, DOCTOR WARNS

"There was a study that looked at the brains of people who ran a marathon ... because the marathon is so energy-intensive, the white matter in the brain actually shrank during a marathon because the brain didn't have enough energy … so it was eating its own white matter," Wood said, noting that the participants' brains recovered after resting and refueling.
"It just shows that the brain is really energy-hungry, and it will decrease its size if it's not getting enough energy."
If people aren't eating enough, they're not getting the nutrients that are critical for brain health, according to Wood. (iStock)
Muscle quality
Concerns about lean muscle loss when taking GLP-1 medications are often nuanced, Wood said. Some of the early "lean mass" that's lost is actually fat that had built up inside the muscles.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"So technically, your muscles get smaller, but you don't get weaker," he told Fox News Digital. "And the quality and functioning of your muscles actually gets better."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

However, risks arise when individuals taking GLP-1 medications drastically reduce their food intake for extended periods. Chronic under-eating can deprive the central nervous system of essential structural nutrients, Wood warned.
Ensuring adequate intake of core neuro-nutrients — including B vitamins (B12, folate, B6), vitamin D, iron and omega-3 fatty acids — prevents long-term cognitive impairment. (iStock)

"It is possible that you can end up going too far," he said. "If you're not eating enough, you're not getting the nutrients that are critical for the brain. So you're not getting in enough omega-3 fats, which we know are really important. You're not getting enough iron and protein and all those kinds of things."
Protecting the brain during weight loss

To safeguard brain health while losing weight, Wood recommends pairing weight-loss regimens with resistance training twice a week to maintain functional muscle mass and to stimulate brain growth factors.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Additionally, ensuring adequate intake of core "neuro-nutrients" — including B vitamins (B12, folate, B6), vitamin D, iron and omega-3 fatty acids — prevents long-term cognitive impairment, according to Wood.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"For most people, I think it's going to be beneficial to start, but you just need to make sure that you don't push it too far, that you're now getting enough of everything that the brain needs," he advised.

title: Heavy drinking surges among Americans in one age group as other generations cut back
summary: Adults ages 50 to 64 saw heavy drinking surge more than 36% since 2018, even as overall U.S. alcohol use finally began to decline post-pandemic.
story: Dr. Chris Tuell, clinical director of addiction services at the University of Cincinnati College of Medicine, discusses why alcohol poses higher risks to people as they age, and shares tips for moderating intake.

New research shows that U.S. alcohol use has declined for the first time since the COVID-19 pandemic, but drinking remains above pre-pandemic levels — with one particular group showing a sharp increase in heavy intake.

A study led by the University of Southern California/Keck Medicine found that among adults ages 50 to 64, alcohol use increased by nearly 4% from 2018 to 2024, while heavy drinking increased by more than 36%.
Across all age groups, alcohol use declined by nearly 2%, and heavy drinking declined by more than 8% from 2022 to 2024. However, overall alcohol use remained above pre-pandemic levels.
BEER, WINE OR LIQUOR? MASSIVE STUDY REVEALS WHICH WAS LINKED TO LOWER DEATH RISK
Among Gen Z adults, alcohol use declined by more than 5%. Millennials drank approximately 17% less from 2022 to 2024.

The findings, which were published on Sept. 21 in Annals of Internal Medicine, were based on self-reported data from the National Health Interview Survey, which included 114,352 U.S. adults from 2018 to 2024.

A study led by the University of Southern California/Keck Medicine found that among adults ages 50 to 64, alcohol use increased by nearly 4% from 2018 to 2024, while heavy drinking increased by more than 36%. (iStock)
Heavy drinking was defined as five or more drinks per day or 15 or more drinks per week for men within the preceding 12 months and at least four daily drinks or eight weekly drinks for women.
Men were found to have a larger alcohol decline than women (2.4% vs. 1.1%), but women had a larger reduction in heavy drinking (9%) compared to men (7.7%).
ALCOHOL TIED TO SURPRISING CANCER DEATH PATTERN IN ADULTS UNDER 55, RESEARCHERS FIND

"Women’s heavy drinking rose more than men's during the pandemic and is still about 13% above where it was in 2018," lead study author Brian P. Lee, M.D., associate professor of medicine at the Keck School of Medicine of USC, told Fox News Digital. "Women develop liver damage at lower levels of drinking than men, so that number carries more weight than it looks."
The study was funded in part by the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism and the National Institutes of Health.
Men were found to have a larger alcohol decline than women (2.4% vs. 1.1%), but women had a larger reduction in heavy drinking (9%) compared to men (7.7%). (iStock)
Study limitations
The chief limitation of the study is that people reported their own levels of drinking, which tend to run low, according to Lee.

"It also can't tell us why drinking changed, only that it did," he told Fox News Digital. "And we have two years of decline after four years of increases, so I'd describe this as a promising turn rather than an established trend."
The researchers also did not investigate the reasons younger adults reduced alcohol consumption.
"Women develop liver damage at lower levels of drinking than men, so that number carries more weight than it looks."
Potential reasons older adults are drinking more
Dr. Chris Tuell, clinical director of addiction services at the University of Cincinnati College of Medicine, said many factors may contribute to the increased rate of drinking among older adults.
"As we approach our 50s and 60s, we start reflecting on our lives, and changes start to happen," Tuell, who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital.
The loneliness epidemic in the U.S., and the fact that people are more "polarized" and "disconnected," may also come into play, according to an addiction expert. (iStock)
The loneliness epidemic in the U.S., and the fact that people are more "polarized" and "disconnected," may also come into play, according to Tuell.
Grief and loss may also lead to increased drinking as people seek a way to escape or cope with the loss of friends and family members.

"One out of four people will experience some mental health issue … depression, anxiety, loss, grief — these are real things that are impacting people," Tuell said. "And it's at a time where a person might feel very vulnerable."
BRAD PITT SAYS HE CAN DRINK IN ‘RESTRAINED MANNER’ AFTER 7 SOBER YEARS, BUT EXPERT RAISES RED FLAG
As people age, there may also be increased issues related to chronic pain and medical issues, resulting in reduced function.
"Now I have these aches and pains, or maybe I'm diagnosed with something more serious," Tuell said as an example. "So that becomes a problem that I now have to deal with."
Grief and loss may also lead to increased drinking as people seek a way to escape or cope with the loss of friends and family members. (iStock)
Many aging adults are also approaching retirement age, which can result in a loss of structure and change the identity they’ve had for decades, the expert noted.

"I wake up and something I've done every day for many, many years is no longer happening. So I'm more bored. What do I do with my time? This is unfortunately a perfect storm for things like substance use."
Risks of alcohol for older adults
As older adults experience body changes, they don't metabolize alcohol the same way they once did, Tuell noted.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"What I used to drink maybe five years ago … that same amount now can affect me differently, because I'm not metabolizing it like I used to," he said.
Women are especially impacted by alcohol, Tuell said, likely because they may have less body fat and don't have as much water in their bodies.
For those who are over 50 and drinking more than they did before 2020, the lead researcher recommends asking a doctor about liver health, "even if nothing feels wrong." (iStock)
Lee noted that while alcohol doesn't harm everyone equally, the risk starts at low levels and goes up with every additional drink.
"There isn't a level the evidence shows to be safe."
Red flags
To determine whether someone has a problem with alcohol, Tuell recommends using the "three Cs."

Control: "Is there a loss of control? I can't manage this behavior any longer."Compulsive: "I can’t stop doing it. I continue to do it despite the negative consequences. Knowing that I could lose my job, I could lose my marriage, I could lose lots of things in my life, I do it anyway."Continued use despite adverse consequences: "I can't stop thinking about it — it might be the first thing I think about when I wake up in the morning or the last thing I think about when I go to bed."
Control: "Is there a loss of control? I can't manage this behavior any longer."

Compulsive: "I can’t stop doing it. I continue to do it despite the negative consequences. Knowing that I could lose my job, I could lose my marriage, I could lose lots of things in my life, I do it anyway."

Continued use despite adverse consequences: "I can't stop thinking about it — it might be the first thing I think about when I wake up in the morning or the last thing I think about when I go to bed."
Alcohol can still be problematic even if someone doesn’t have an addiction, Tuell noted.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
For example, they might drink more than they should, to the point where they get a hangover or put themselves at risk.
"Maybe it's impacting my interactions with other people, interpersonal relationships, hobbies, interests," he said. "Maybe it's affecting my sleep."
In a normal sleep pattern, people go through a cycle four to five times per night, but when they drink, it's more like two to three times, the expert said. (iStock)

In a normal sleep pattern, people go through a cycle four to five times per night, but when they drink, it's more like two to three times, Tuell said. "So, we're not getting good rest during that period."
It’s never too late to seek help with alcohol dependency, he pointed out.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"I've treated people in their 80s who still have a lot of life left," Tuell said, pointing out that Americans are living longer. "So we're aging, we're getting older, and there are a lot of life changes happening … physically, emotionally, psychologically."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
For those who are over 50 and drinking more than they did before 2020, Lee recommends asking a doctor about liver health, "even if nothing feels wrong."

"There are clear increases in cancer and liver risk with alcohol, even at low levels," he warned. "Even advanced liver disease might have no symptoms, and the earlier alcohol-related liver damage is caught, the more of it can be undone."

title: Dengue fever outbreak triggers states of emergency in 3 southern counties
summary: Three Florida counties declared emergencies as 190 locally acquired dengue fever cases were confirmed, with Hillsborough County reporting 170 infections.
story: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine Professor Dr. Marty Makary weighs in on whether Americans should be concerned about the rise in both COVID cases and Dengue fever in the U.S. and discusses Potassium Chloride meds being recalled for heart risks.
Three Florida counties have declared states of emergency amid the spread of dengue fever in the state.
As of Sept. 23, Pasco County, Hillsborough County and Pinellas County have made the declarations due to a spread of the mosquito-borne disease, according to each county’s news release.

The local emergency declarations allow county officials to expedite mosquito-control operations, make emergency purchases, coordinate response efforts and, where applicable, seek state or federal assistance or reimbursement, the releases state.
TROPICAL DISEASE SPREAD BY MOSQUITOES CLAIMS FIRST RECORDED DEATH IN SOUTHERN US STATE
Under Florida law, local emergency declarations expire after seven days unless they are renewed.

A total of 190 locally acquired dengue cases have been confirmed across six Florida counties, according to the latest Florida Department of Health surveillance report, which covered cases with onset through Sept. 19.
Three Florida counties have declared states of emergency amid the spread of dengue fever in the state. (Getty Images)
Of the 190 locally acquired cases, 170 were reported in Hillsborough County, seven each in Miami-Dade and Pinellas counties, three in Orange County, two in Pasco County and one in Palm Beach County.
The 190 locally acquired infections are separate from travel-associated dengue cases reported in Florida this year.
TICK-BORNE 'RABBIT FEVER' SPREADS WITH CASES REPORTED NEAR MAJOR METRO AREA

Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral illness that can cause fever, severe aches, nausea, rash and, in rare cases, life-threatening complications, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
"The Aedes mosquitoes that can transmit dengue are active during the day and thrive in warm, humid environments like those found in Florida."

Dengue is endemic in many tropical and subtropical regions, including Southeast Asia, the Western Pacific islands, Latin America and Africa. Though less common in the continental U.S., locally acquired cases have been recorded in Florida, California and Texas.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"The Aedes mosquitoes that can transmit dengue are active during the day and thrive in warm, humid environments like those found in Florida," an entomologist spokesperson at the SC Johnson Center for Insect Science and Family Health, makers of OFF!, said in a statement sent to Fox News Digital.

"As dengue cases continue to be reported in the Tampa area, taking steps to help prevent mosquito bites is especially important," the expert went on. "Staying aware of local mosquito activity and consistently protecting against bites are important steps people can take to help reduce their risk."
Stopping the spread

The Florida Mosquito Control Association (FMCA) previously said crews are increasing aerial and ground treatments in areas showing dengue virus activity, while also inspecting private properties for potential mosquito breeding sites, according to reports.

The local emergency declarations allow county officials to expedite mosquito-control operations, make emergency purchases, coordinate response efforts and, where applicable, seek state or federal assistance or reimbursement. (iStock)

FMCA has urged residents to empty or cover standing water around their homes. The mosquito that spreads dengue is a container breeder, meaning it lays eggs in buckets, planters, plant saucers, tires, discarded toys and other objects that collect small amounts of water, experts say.

The SC Johnson Center for Insect Science and Family Health entomologist shared the following recommendations to prevent the spread of mosquito-borne disease.

Use an EPA-registered insect repellent: Review, follow and apply repellent label directions to help prevent mosquito bites.Eliminate sources of standing water nearby: Where there’s standing water, there can be mosquitoes. Mosquitoes need only one tablespoon of water to breed, so areas like rain gutters, birdbaths or buckets with stagnant water are all possible breeding sites.Layer repellent and sunscreen correctly: When using both sunscreen and mosquito repellent, apply sunscreen first, followed by insect repellent. Be sure to follow the label directions for both products and reapply as directed.Protect throughout the day: Don’t limit mosquito precautions to dawn and dusk. The Aedes mosquitoes that can spread dengue are active throughout the day, so use protection whenever mosquito exposure is possible.

Eliminate sources of standing water nearby: Where there’s standing water, there can be mosquitoes. Mosquitoes need only one tablespoon of water to breed, so areas like rain gutters, birdbaths or buckets with stagnant water are all possible breeding sites.

Layer repellent and sunscreen correctly: When using both sunscreen and mosquito repellent, apply sunscreen first, followed by insect repellent. Be sure to follow the label directions for both products and reapply as directed.

Protect throughout the day: Don’t limit mosquito precautions to dawn and dusk. The Aedes mosquitoes that can spread dengue are active throughout the day, so use protection whenever mosquito exposure is possible.
The FMCA also advises people to dress in long sleeves, light colors and closed-toed shoes outdoors.
Dengue is endemic in many tropical and subtropical regions, including Southeast Asia, the Western Pacific islands, Latin America and Africa. (iStock)
Symptoms and treatment
Many people infected with dengue have no symptoms, and most people who do become sick recover within a week or two, according to Mayo Clinic.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
In some cases, however, the illness can progress to severe dengue, a potentially life-threatening condition.
Symptoms typically begin four to 10 days after the bite of an infected mosquito.

Warning signs can develop quickly, often within a day or two after the fever subsides. Those may include severe stomach pain, repeated vomiting, unusual bleeding or bruising, difficulty breathing, extreme tiredness and irritability, or restlessness.
People experiencing warning signs of severe dengue should seek immediate medical care.

title: ‘Superman’ star Christopher Reeve’s son reveals 'shock' cancer diagnosis at age 34
summary: Will Reeve, son of Christopher Reeve, revealed his embryonal carcinoma diagnosis and orchiectomy on air, drawing parallels to his parents' battles.
story: "Super/Man: The Christopher Reeve Story" co-director Peter Ettedgui told Fox News Digital that Reeve’s wife, children and friend Robin Williams made the actor realize he wanted to live after becoming paralyzed.
Will Reeve, son of the late famed "Superman" actor Christopher Reeve, announced that he recently battled cancer.
The "Good Morning America" correspondent, 34, shared during Tuesday’s show that he was diagnosed with testicular cancer earlier this year, assuring viewers that he is "OK."

"The diagnosis was a shock and the treatments were a slog," he said. "Today, though, I am relieved to announce that we arrived at our destination and this cancer is in the rearview mirror. But what a journey."
WILLIAM SHATNER SAYS DOCTOR DISMISSED KEY WARNING SIGN BEFORE STAGE 4 CANCER DIAGNOSIS
Reeve said he found a "hard, tender lump in [his] left testicle" just a few months after his wedding to luxury event planner Amanda Dubin.
Will Reeve (left), son of the late famed "Superman" star Christopher Reeve (right), announced he recently battled cancer. (Getty Images)
An ultrasound revealed that he had "a mass that had to come out." After undergoing surgery to remove the testicle (an orchiectomy), Reeve discovered the mass was embryonal carcinoma.
The aggressive subtype of testicular cancer can spread more quickly than some other forms, according to the American Cancer Society.
POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY PLAY SURPRISING ROLE IN CANCER OUTCOMES
Reeve later underwent a second surgery to remove lymph nodes from his abdomen after some cancer cells had spread there.
The surgery took place at Memorial Sloan Kettering, which is where his mother, Dana Reeve, died from lung cancer in 2006 at age 44. His father died in 2004 at the age of 52.
Actor Robin Williams, right, poses with actor Christopher Reeve, wife Dana Reeve and son Will, left, at the 2004 Tribeca Film Festival in May 2004. (Evan Agostini/Getty Images)

Reeve shared that he also underwent two rounds of chemotherapy to lower the risk that the cancer would return. He said he experienced several side effects from the medication, including ringing in the ears, bone pain, night sweats, blood clots and constant headaches.

He did not lose his hair because he used a method called "cold capping," which is used during certain chemotherapy treatments to help reduce hair loss by cooling the scalp and constricting blood vessels.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
After finishing his second round of chemotherapy on July 31, Reeve said he received "clean scans" on Sept. 8.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
In an interview with People, Reeve said he is "going to be fine," although it has been "one heck of a chapter."

"I’m fortunate that I caught this early," he said. "Yes, I had to jump through some flaming hoops to get to the other side, but it could have been much worse had I ignored it or delayed going to the doctor."

Actor Christopher Reeve gets a kiss from his son Will during a "20/20" special interview Sept. 29, 1995, in New Jersey. The show was Reeve's first appearance since his horseback riding accident. (Getty Images)
Reeve also praised his wife for serving as his "caregiver," similar to how his mother helped care for his father after a 1995 horseback-riding accident left him paralyzed.
"I learn[ed] more about what it was like to be my dad in the final nine years of his life, where he had my mom and our family taking care of him," Reeve said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
He added that the experience taught him how to "repurpose [adversity] into something hopeful."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Testicular cancer is among the most treatable cancers, particularly when detected early, according to the American Cancer Society. Experts recommend seeing a doctor promptly for any lump, swelling, pain or change in a testicle.
Fox News Digital reached out to Reeve’s representatives requesting comment.
