title: 4 simple habits can help slow muscle loss as you age, fitness expert says
summary: A fitness coach reveals four key strategies to slow age-related muscle loss, from daily protein intake to strength training and sleep habits.
story: Jacob Zemer, a New York-based fitness coach who primarily trains clients ranging from 35 to 55 years old, said there are several reasons that adults start losing muscle as they get older.

As Americans increasingly turn to GLP-1 medications — which have been linked to a loss of lean muscle, especially during rapid weight loss — experts say preserving strength and mobility should be a priority as people age.

Jacob Zemer, a New York-based fitness coach who primarily trains clients ranging from 35 to 55 years old, said that beyond GLP-1s, there are several other reasons that adults start losing muscle as they get older.
"The biggest change is lifestyle," he told Fox News Digital. "When you're in your teen years or your 20s, you're running around, you're doing activities that lend themselves to building muscle."
FITNESS EXPERT REVEALS 6 THINGS PEOPLE OVER 35 SHOULD DO AFTER WORKOUTS TO STAY STRONG
That tends to change as people shift focus to career and family, the expert said.
"You simply become more sedentary, which lowers your metabolism and your level of activity, so you're going to have less muscle."
The expert said he believes that everyone should be "very mindful" about building muscle, starting from a young age. (iStock)
As people approach their 40s, hormone levels begin to change for both men and women, Zemer noted.
"That means we partition the calories we're using less and less for protein and building muscle, and more and more for simply storing as fat," he said.
THIS EXERCISE HABIT MAY SLASH DEMENTIA RISK AND HELP YOU LIVE LONGER, STUDY FINDS
"We see this all the time … people start to store fat in their tummies, and they start have less muscle."
Zemer said he believes that everyone should be "very mindful" about building muscle, starting from a young age.

For general health, the U.S. Physical Activity Guidelines recommend that adults strength train at least two days per week, working all major muscle groups (legs, hips, back, abdomen, chest, shoulders and arms). (iStock)
"All the way up into your 50s, your goal should be to build muscle so that when you enter your golden years — your 60s, 70s, 80s — it's kind of like your 401K," he said.

"You're going to be depleting from it as you go through life. So in your 30s and 40s, you just have to be more strategic about it, because your lifestyle has changed. You need to go to the gym and train in order to have that muscle later in life."
Zemer shared the following strategies that can help people slow down muscle loss as they age.
No. 1: Get adequate protein
Protein helps to stimulate muscle protein synthesis, the body's process of repairing and building muscle, according to Zemer.
EATING TOO MUCH PROTEIN COULD BACKFIRE, EXPERTS WARN AFTER LONGEVITY REVIEW
Including enough protein in your daily diet can help reduce the risk of sarcopenia, which is the age-related loss of muscle mass and strength.
While people’s protein needs will vary based on age, activity level and fitness goals, Zemer said people who regularly strength-train generally benefit from higher intake.
Including enough protein in your daily diet can help reduce the risk of sarcopenia, the age-related loss of muscle mass and strength. (iStock)

"If you're a sedentary person, you don't need to be obsessed with protein," he told Fox News Digital. "Very few people aren't getting enough protein in terms of macronutrients. But if you're training and going to the gym, you want to be getting somewhere between 0.8 to 1 gram of protein per pound of body weight."
No. 2: Strength-train regularly

For general health, the U.S. Physical Activity Guidelines recommend that adults strength train at least two days per week, working all major muscle groups (legs, hips, back, abdomen, chest, shoulders and arms).
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention advises using moderate or greater intensity until it's difficult to complete another repetition with good form.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
The guidelines also recommend pairing the strength training with 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity (or 75–150 minutes of vigorous activity) each week.
Lifting weights isn’t just about building muscle, but also preserving muscle, according to Zemer.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"Even if you have a busy week, and you went to the gym and you lifted weights 30 minutes twice a week, that may not be enough to build new muscle, but that is certainly enough to maintain muscle," he said.
"So it's very important that you lift weights a couple of times a week as you age."
For beginners, the trainer recommends focusing on a few basic functional movements. (iStock)

For beginners, Zemer recommends focusing on a few basic functional movements. Body-weight exercises like squats, lunges, push-ups and pulling movements help build strength for everyday activities, while carrying weighted objects — known as a farmer's carry, Zemer said — can improve grip, balance and overall stability.
For people who feel intimidated by the gym, working with a qualified trainer for a few sessions can help boost confidence and refine technique, according to Zemer.
No. 3: Get sufficient sleep
Perhaps the most difficult strategy for maintaining muscle is to get enough quality sleep — seven to nine hours, Zemer emphasized.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Now, if you don't get that every night, you're not going to lose muscle," he noted. "But when you start to look at actual serious sleep deficiency, like we're talking five hours consistently, that is when you see rapid muscle loss."
No. 4: Find alternatives if necessary
"The worst thing you can do, even if you're injured, is to stop doing anything," Zemer said.

Even without structured workouts, regular movement can help slow age-related muscle loss, while being sedentary is associated with rapid declines in muscle mass and strength, the expert cautioned. (iStock)
"Find things you can do. Even if something hurts you, even if your knees aren't like what they used to be."
Even without structured workouts, regular movement can help slow age-related muscle loss, while being sedentary is associated with rapid declines in muscle mass and strength, the expert cautioned.
GLP-1s and muscle loss

The above strategies are especially important for people who are taking GLP-1 medications for weight loss, Zemer noted, as these drugs can lead to muscle loss in the absence of strength training or adequate protein.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"If you are on a GLP-1, just remember you're accelerating the rate of fat loss, but you're also accelerating the rate of lean muscle," he said.
"You want to make sure you're getting that protein and training, so that you are not losing muscle on top of the fat loss."

title: Sylvester Stallone reveals surprising health struggle behind his famously ripped physique
summary: Sylvester Stallone revealed he became bulimic while prepping for "Rambo" and reached 2.6% body fat during "Rocky III" in a stunning new interview.
story: Brian Pollack, a licensed clinical social worker and certified eating disorders specialist in Summit, New Jersey, said it was "incredibly admirable" for Stallone to share his experience.
Sylvester Stallone is sharing some health obstacles he has faced while playing physically demanding roles over the decades.
The Academy Award-nominated actor, 80, revealed during an interview with The New York Times that he has suffered from an eating disorder.

While prepping for his role in the 1982 movie "Rambo," Stallone — who has authored a new memoir, titled "The Steps" — said he took pains to appear more "animalistic," drawing inspiration from jaguars and cats.
MEN FACE NEW PRESSURE TO STAY ‘HOT’ AS THEY AGE — AND IT’S NOT JUST ABOUT LIVING LONGER
"Then it became an obsession. Really bad. It got to the point where I became bulimic," he said during the interview.
Actor Sylvester Stallone, as Rocky Balboa, shows off his muscles in the boxing ring on the set of Rocky III in May 1982 in Los Angeles, California. (James Drake/Getty Images)

Bulimia nervosa is an eating disorder marked by episodes of binge eating — consuming a large amount of food while feeling a loss of control — followed by purging behaviors such as vomiting, excessive use of laxatives or diuretics, fasting or excessive exercise, according to the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH).

"I couldn’t hold anything down. Or I didn’t want to keep it down because I became so obsessed with staying at that point of fitness, literally an obsessive body-worship kind of thing," Stallone shared.
CONTROVERSIAL STREAMER CLAVICULAR EXPLAINS VIRAL 'LOOKSMAXXING' TREND AS GEN Z ADOPTS EXTREME REGIMEN

The actor said that while filming "Rocky III," he reached his lowest body fat of 2.6%. The National Academy of Sports Medicine classifies body fat as "dangerously low" if it falls below 8% for men ages 20–69 and below 14% for women ages 20–69.

Sylvester Stallone strikes at a punching bag in a boxing ring while his coach, Burgess Meredith, watches during training at a gymnasium in a still from the film, "Rocky," directed by John G. Avildsen, 1976. (Getty Images)
Stallone also admitted that he took steroids during some time periods. "You have to," he said. "But you do it in a sensitive way — six weeks on, six weeks off … that also took a terrible toll."

Years of injuries sustained while doing his own stunts — something he described as "very masochistic" — have also taken a toll on Stallone’s body, he said, leading to multiple surgeries on his back, shoulder and neck.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"I’ve abused my body," he said. "Everything is held together with baling wire, but I still want to stay in good shape."
Stallone also revealed that he has dealt with anxiety over the decades, recounting the first incident while watching footage from one of his films when he was 36 years old.
"I’ve abused my body," Stallone said in the New York Times interview. "Everything is held together with baling wire, but I still want to stay in good shape." (Getty Images)
"All of a sudden, I stood up and the hair on my neck went up and I started getting hot and I go, ‘I’m dying, this is it, I’m on my way out,’" he said in the interview.

The actor said the panic attacks happened "again and again and again," often resurfacing before high-profile television appearances. As he aged, Stallone continued to experience anxiety and sometimes felt compelled to leave crowded rooms.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Brian Pollack, a licensed clinical social worker and certified eating disorders specialist at Hilltop Behavioral Health in Summit, New Jersey, said it was "incredibly admirable" for Stallone to share his experience.

"There are so many examples of what can take place in Sylvester Stallone's life that have led him to moments of objectivity and body awareness," Pollack, who has not treated Stallone, told Fox News Digital.
Rocky Balboa (Sylvester Stallone) skips rope under the watchful eye of his manager, Mickey (Burgess Meredith), and trainer Johnny (Stuart K. Robinson) in Rocky II. (Getty Images)

The expert suggested that a desire to maintain his success may have fueled Stallone’s rigid routines, steroid use, intense performance expectations, fear of failure, and the pressures associated with the entertainment industry.
"The idea that a man enhances his appearance to remain consistent with his own public image and internal comfort goes back decades — [Stallone] isn’t the first, and he isn’t the last," Pollack said.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"He has to almost keep himself in this homeostatic state where people expect Sylvestor Stallone to be Rocky, which is his quintessential role," he went on.

"And through his career, one could surmise the need to be able to put all of that together and keep it consistent as he goes through the development and life cycles of maturation, not only in his brain, but also in his body."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Giulia Suro, a licensed clinical psychologist and certified eating disorder expert at Monte Nido in Washington, D.C., added that the Sylvester Stallone revelation was a "game-changer."
"Eating disorders continue to be misconstrued as primarily female illnesses," she told Fox News Digital.
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Popular weight-loss drugs can become an ‘atomic bomb’ at high doses, doctor warns
summary: Dr. Will Cole warns that macro-dosing GLP-1s isn't the answer to metabolic health, advocating for micro-dosing peptides paired with lifestyle changes.
story: Dr. Will Cole discusses peptide therapy, arguing that medications affecting appetite should be used carefully alongside nutrition, exercise and other lifestyle interventions.
As interest in peptides continues to grow, experts are increasingly looking beyond weight loss to their potential role in healthy aging.
Functional medicine expert Dr. Will Cole told Fox News Digital that peptides are "intimately connected" with longevity, cellular healing and metabolic health.

"[Peptides] help with cellular communication," said Cole, co-author of the upcoming book "Heal Your Cells." The recommendations for peptides depend on the context in which they're used, he said, noting that the answer often falls "somewhere in the middle."
THINKING ABOUT PEPTIDES? DOCTORS REVEAL KEY DOS AND DON’TS AS ‘WILD WEST’ MARKET GROWS

Citing previous research, Cole noted that an estimated 93% of U.S. adults are metabolically unhealthy, leaving only about 7% who meet the criteria for optimal metabolic health — a figure he described as "wild."
Peptides have surged in popularity for weight loss, muscle building, performance enhancement, chronic disease management and even wound repair. (iStock)
"That's common, but not normal," Cole said. He added that while GLP-1 medications can be beneficial, improving metabolic health also requires addressing lifestyle and other underlying factors.
FDA TO REVIEW 7 POPULAR PEPTIDES TOUTED FOR WEIGHT LOSS, HEALING AND LONGEVITY
Cole shared that he does not believe "macro-dosing" GLP-1s "forever and ever in perpetuity" is the solution to improving metabolic health.

While GLP-1s can reduce food cravings — often referred to as "food noise" — and promote weight loss, Cole said he’d like to see more research on how decreasing the desire for food could also decrease cravings for love, relationships and other mood-boosting factors.

The semaglutide weight-loss drug Wegovy, made by pharmaceutical company Novo Nordisk, is designed to treat type 2 diabetes, but is widely known for its weight-loss effect. (James Manning/PA Images via Getty Images)
Cole questioned whether suppressing food cravings could have unintended effects on other reward-related behaviors, including social relationships.
"So, are we circumventing pathways and pathologizing things that don't have to be pathologized?"

Cole argued that some degree of hunger signaling is healthy. "Food noise is actually a decent thing in balance, so shutting down your hunger cues with an 'atomic bomb' peptide dose is not the solution."
He added that he believes overreliance on GLP-1 medications may contribute to disordered eating patterns and a growing fear of hunger.
The expert said he believes that overreliance on GLP-1 medications may contribute to disordered eating patterns and a growing fear of hunger. (iStock)
Cole attributed the trend to a culture that favors simple, fast solutions over sustained lifestyle changes. "We want a magic pill," he said.
"And the truth is somewhere in the middle: Can we micro-dose? Can we do it cyclically? And can we pair it with lifestyle?"

The expert questioned why there has been an "epidemic rise" of metabolic problems, pointing to factors such as diets high in ultraprocessed foods, nutrient deficiencies, environmental toxins and the presence of stress and trauma.
"That is why we're seeing a rise of chronic health problems, not a pharmaceutical deficiency," he said.
Pairing peptides with lifestyle is a good balance to improve metabolic health, experts agree. (iStock)
Cole said he supports wider access to peptides, but emphasized the importance of transparency, product purity and clear labeling so healthcare professionals and consumers can make informed decisions.

Despite those concerns, Cole said he believes GLP-1s also hold significant therapeutic promise, citing their potential to reduce inflammation, help manage autoimmune conditions and improve gut health.

"But again, what's the lowest dose that yields a beneficial result paired with lifestyle? I think that's where peptides can really shine," he said.

title: Pope Leo visits site of miracle cures, meets people whose unexplained healings stunned doctors

Pope Leo XIV arrived in Lourdes from Paris on Saturday evening for his first-ever visit to the renowned place of miracle cures.

JUST 5 MINUTES OF PRAYER COULD HAVE SURPRISING HEALTH BENEFITS, STUDY FINDS

Priests sit before a Mass celebrated by Pope Leo XIV at the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes, France, on Sunday, Sept. 27, 2026. (AP Images)

title: Forgetting names and losing keys may signal something other than dementia
summary: Dr. Tommy Wood breaks down memory's three neurological stages and why noticing your own forgetfulness is actually a good sign, not an Alzheimer's flag.
story: Dr. Tommy Wood, a professor of pediatrics and neuroscience at the University of Washington, said minor forgetfulness is often caused by fatigue or stress rather than the beginnings of a neurodegenerative disease.

Everyday memory lapses, like misplaced keys or forgotten names, are often overinterpreted as early signs of dementia, but neuroscience experts say actual early cognitive changes may be reversible if addressed promptly.

Dr. Tommy Wood, a professor of pediatrics and neuroscience at the University of Washington, said minor forgetfulness is often caused by fatigue or stress rather than the beginnings of a neurodegenerative disease.

"For most people, it's just because you're stressed or you're tired and weren't paying attention," Wood told Fox News Digital at Strong New York, the city's largest annual fitness and wellness festival.
DOCTOR REVEALS '10-YEAR RULE' FOR EVALUATING BRAIN FOG AND DEMENTIA SYMPTOMS
"If you want to remember something ... you need to actually be focused, be paying attention. You need to tell your brain it's important to remember it."
Understanding memory loss
Wood said memory formation works in three stages: encoding (forming a memory), consolidation (storing it) and retrieval (accessing it).
Cognitive changes during aging are not inevitable, and taking proactive lifestyle steps early can help maintain or even restore brain function. (iStock)
When someone is stressed or sleep-deprived, the issue is typically retrieval, he said — the memory exists in the brain, but the individual struggles to access it in the moment.
In contrast, people experiencing a neurodegenerative disease often fail to encode the memory in the first place.
‘MIRACLE ON THE HUDSON’ HERO SULLY SULLENBERGER REVEALS ALZHEIMER’S WARNING SIGNS HE MISSED YEARS AGO
"They don't even remember or notice that there's something going on," Wood said. "If you're noticing something's not quite right, that's usually a good sign."
Preventable risk factors and reversibility

Dementia is clinically defined as the loss of cognitive function that's severe enough to impair an individual's ability to manage daily life independently. Alzheimer's disease and vascular dementia account for 70% to 90% of cases, with many individuals showing signs of both.
Research indicates that at least 50% of dementia cases can be prevented by modifying lifestyle and health risk factors.
True memory problems stem from a failure to encode new memories in the brain, whereas stress-related forgetfulness is merely an issue with retrieving existing memories. (iStock)
Key preventable risk factors include heart and metabolic health problems, as well as hearing and vision loss.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Wood emphasized that addressing physical health issues — such as obtaining hearing aids or undergoing cataract surgery — directly lessens cognitive decline risk.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"If you expect decline, you won't do the things that will prevent decline from happening," Wood told Fox News Digital. "Believing that it's possible means you'll actually engage in these processes, and then through that, you can prevent a lot of this decline."
Minor memory lapses, like forgetting keys or names, are usually caused by stress or fatigue rather than early dementia, the expert said. (iStock)

Wood's focus on reversible causes of cognitive symptoms aligns with guidance from Mayo Clinic and Cleveland Clinic, which note that several treatable medical conditions can mimic early dementia symptoms or contribute to subjective cognitive decline.

Common reversible causes include the following.

Vitamin deficiencies: Low levels of vitamin B12 or B1, which are essential for nerve and brain functionEndocrine disruption: Thyroid problems, particularly hypothyroidism, which slows brain metabolismMedication side effects: Interactions from sedative drugs, anticholinergics or polypharmacy in older adultsMental health conditions: Depression and severe anxiety, which can cause "pseudodementia," a state of cognitive slowing and memory lapse that resolves with mental health treatmentMetabolic and kidney issues: Chronic kidney or liver failure, as well as electrolyte imbalances, which alter levels of brain chemicals

Managing physical health issues — such as controlling high blood pressure, treating vision or hearing loss and staying physically active — directly reduces cognitive decline risks. (iStock)
Cleveland Clinic highlights that early clinical intervention is critical when individuals notice changes in "brain fog" or executive function.

"How your brain functions on a day-to-day basis is kind of the output of everything your brain is dealing with," said Wood. "But if you start to notice something, there's still time to make some changes if you need to."

title: 81-year-old refuses to stop working as wife battles cancer, then strangers try to help
summary: Don Johnson, 81, of Texas delivered lost luggage to cover his wife's cancer costs until a viral fundraiser begun by his daughter raised $700,000. Now, the GoFundMe campaign has been pulled.
story: Doorbell video shows 81-year-old Donald Johnson struggling to haul heavy suitcases up a steep staircase during a Texas delivery before his story spread widely online.
An encounter with an elderly delivery driver in Texas has captured attention after the reason he was still working came to light.

Donald Johnson, 81, was delivering lost luggage to a home when Erin Howell, a resident at The Colony, saw him struggling to carry a heavy bag up a steep set of stairs — a moment captured by her doorbell camera, according to reports.

Howell went outside to help and learned that Johnson had been making luggage deliveries as an independent contractor for the past three years to help cover medical expenses for his wife, Josephine Johnson, who is battling cancer, FOX 4 Dallas-Fort Worth reported.
MILITARY VETERAN’S PAINFUL WALK ACROSS AIRPORT TARMAC SPARKS STRANGERS TO RAISE OVER $135K
The couple has been married for 57 years. Donald Johnson continued to work during his wife's medical treatment.
He was continuing to make deliveries because he had struggled to find other work, he told Howell during their encounter.
Donald Johnson, pictured here, was delivering lost luggage to a home in Texas when a doorbell camera captured him struggling to lug heavy bags up a steep set of stairs. (TIKTOK/HelpDonRetire)
"It's the only job that will hire me," Johnson told her, according to the outlet.
Howell shared the elderly man's story online and even started a fundraiser to help with medical expenses and give him the chance to stop working and care for his wife.

As his story spread, thousands of strangers responded with donations and messages of support.
"I think I'm going to be able to stop working, and that's amazing," Johnson told FOX 4. "So we're not quite totally over the hump yet, but we're getting there very quickly."
Johnson was caught on video delivering luggage, pictured above, as an independent contractor to help cover the medical expenses of his wife. (TIKTOK/HelpDonRetire)
The outpouring of support and prayers had given her encouragement as she continued her cancer battle, Josephine Johnson told FOX 4.
"I can face it. I think that's the big difference," she said. "Some have made comments and they're praying for us. And it's just — it's a joyful feeling."

The family's circumstances, however, took another turn after the fundraiser was eventually removed from GoFundMe.

In a recent TikTok video, the couple's daughter, Amy Johnson, said the campaign had collected more than $700,000 — but that her parents would not receive the money because the donations were being refunded due to "a technicality."
The outpouring of support and numerous prayers from strangers had been encouraging the family in its battle.  (iStock)

Sitting alongside her parents in the TikTok, the daughter said the money that was raised was intended to help cover her mother's medical expenses as she battles pancreatic cancer and would also give her 81-year-old father the opportunity to stop working.

GoFundMe told FOX 4, however, that its trust and safety team determined the organizer account and fundraiser violated its terms of service. The company did not specify the exact reason for the decision.

title: One simple lifestyle choice could help you live longer, says longevity expert
summary: Dan Buettner, founder of Blue Zones, says dog ownership may be the best longevity strategy, citing research linking it to fewer heart attacks and reduced loneliness.
story: Dog ownership is linked to a lower risk of early death, better heart health, more daily movement and less loneliness. Longevity expert Dan Buettner says a four-legged companion may naturally reinforce key Blue Zones habits.
The most effective strategy for prolonging life might be at the end of a leash.

Dan Buettner, longevity expert and founder of the organization Blue Zones in Minneapolis, Minnesota, highlighted a growing body of scientific evidence showing that owning a dog is strongly associated with a reduced risk of early death, particularly from cardiovascular disease.

"The best thing you can do to add years to your life may surprise you. Get a dog!" Buettner advised during a recent episode of "The Dan Buettner Podcast." "Research shows that dog owners live longer, suffer fewer heart attacks and experience less loneliness. Why? Because a dog forces you to walk every day, gives you a purpose and provides unconditional love."
LEADING ONCOLOGIST REVEALS 6 HABITS THAT COULD PROMOTE LONGEVITY AND REDUCE YOUR RISK OF CHRONIC ILLNESS

Dog ownership is associated with a 24% reduction in all-cause mortality for the general population compared to non-owners, according to research published by the American Heart Association in its journal Circulation.
For individuals who have already suffered a major cardiac event, such as a heart attack or stroke, living with a dog reduced the risk of death by up to 33%.
"The best thing you can do to add years to your life may surprise you. Get a dog!" a longevity expert advised. (iStock)
Epidemiologists and psychologists point to three reasons why canine companions may extend human lifespans.

No. 1: Daily physical activity

Studies published in BMC Public Health indicate that dog owners walk an average of 22 more minutes per day than non-owners, making them significantly more likely to meet standard weekly physical activity guidelines.
Dog owners average an extra 22 minutes of daily walking compared to non-owners, making them more likely to meet standard recommended exercise benchmarks. (iStock)
No. 2: Stress reduction

Interacting with a pet lowers levels of cortisol — the body’s primary stress hormone —while boosting oxytocin, dopamine and serotonin. A 12-year Swedish study analyzing 3.4 million participants found that dog owners had lower blood pressure and reduced rates of cardiovascular disease.

No. 3: Reduced isolation
The U.S. Surgeon General has declared chronic loneliness a national public health epidemic, comparing its health risks to smoking 15 cigarettes a day.
Dogs act as natural "social catalysts," fostering community interaction and providing emotional attachment that combats isolation, particularly in single-person households, experts say.
Dogs act as social catalysts that mitigate chronic loneliness, addressing a health hazard that the U.S. Surgeon General equates to smoking 15 cigarettes a day. (iStock)
The links between human longevity and caring for a pet aligns with principles found in the "blue zones" — regions of the world with the highest concentration of centenarians.
These key principles include natural daily movement, a strong sense of purpose, stress reduction and deep social connections, according to Buettner.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
By incorporating a dog into a daily routine, owners can incorporate these habits without having to engineer complex health regimens.

"So if you want to live longer," Buettner advised, "go adopt a dog!"

title: Scientists reveal surprisingly easy exercise that may boost your mood in just 10 minutes
summary: A University of Tsukuba study found that a slow 10-minute jog boosted attention, self-control and mood in young adults by activating the prefrontal cortex.
story: A University of Tsukuba study indicates that running at very slow speed can enhance mood and cognitive function. Dr. Jessica Gray, a family medicine physician, joins 'Fox & Friends First' to discuss the details.
It might not take an all-out sprint or long trail run to lift your mood and sharpen focus, according to a new study.
A new study from the University of Tsukuba in Japan looked at 24 healthy young adults who completed a slow, 10-minute run on a treadmill in one session and rested in another.

After the easy jog, participants performed faster on a test of attention and self-control and reported feeling more alert and pleasant than they did after the resting phase, according to the small study published in the journal Imaging Neuroscience in August.
'PERFECT' WORKOUT FORMULA CAN TAKE JUST 10 MINUTES A DAY, HILARIA BALDWIN SAYS
Brain monitoring after the jog also showed more activity in parts of the prefrontal cortex, the area of the brain responsible for focus and decision-making.
The jog was purposely kept easy, with participants going at speeds from 1.9 to 3.7 mph on the treadmill. Their average heart rates clocked in at 105 to 107 beats per minute.
A small study suggests even a brief, easy jog may offer a short-term boost in mood and focus. (iStock)
"A single bout of running, even at very slow speed, elicits a pleasant mood and improved executive function," the researchers found.
SIMPLE BODY MOVEMENT COULD HELP THE BRAIN 'CLEAN ITSELF,' RESEARCHERS FIND
The finding "sheds light on the slow running benefits to brain health," they added.
Even gentle movement can provide a mental reset, though the study’s findings were limited to one short session. (iStock)
The benefits, they noted, stuck around even after participants' heart rates returned to baseline.
JUST 10 MINUTES OF DAILY FLOOR EXERCISES MAY IMPROVE BALANCE AND AGILITY, STUDY FINDS
The greater the up-and-down head movement during the jog, the more positive the participants' mood was afterward, though that finding was exploratory and does not necessarily prove cause and effect.
5 COMMON WALKING MISTAKES THAT COULD HURT YOUR PROGRESS, ACCORDING TO AN EXPERT

"Easy movement triggers the norepinephrine and dopamine pathways that wake up the part of the brain that is in charge of focus and self-control," said Dr. John La Puma, a California-based internist and author of "Indoor Epidemic," who was not involved in the study.
Brain monitoring during the post-jog attention test showed greater activity in prefrontal regions involved in focus and decision-making. (iStock)
Experts agree, however, that it does not mean one brief workout could be a cure-all.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"A brief jog should help someone get some energy in their system, which may make them feel better about themselves mentally and help them focus," said Dr. Scott Nass, a California-based family medicine physician at SwiftCareMD.
But Nass, who also wasn't involved in the research, said the effect is likely temporary.
Participants completed a test measuring attention and self-control after a 10-minute easy jog and after a resting session. (iStock)
For people living with depression or anxiety, a jog may briefly clear the mind but is "no substitute for medical care," he told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
The study was also limited in that it included just 24 healthy, young adults and measured outcomes immediately after just one exercise session.
The findings cannot be assumed to apply to older adults, novice runners or people with health conditions, and larger studies are necessary to confirm the results, Nass said.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
For a practical approach, La Puma suggested taking a 10-minute walk outside before the most mentally demanding part of the day.
Add 30-second jogging intervals, keeping the pace easy enough to speak in full sentences without becoming breathless, he said.
After the slow jog, participants reported feeling more alert and pleasant than they did after the resting session. (iStock)
People with heart disease, high blood pressure, Type 1 diabetes, recent surgery or joint pain should check with a clinician before starting a new routine, La Puma advised.

Deirdre Bardolf is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital.

title: Doctor reveals '10-year rule' for evaluating brain fog and dementia symptoms
summary: A UCLA neurology professor's 10-year self-assessment helps women determine if memory loss stems from estrogen changes during perimenopause or dementia.
story: Dr. Rhonda Voskuhl discusses how declining estrogen may affect cognitive function and why healthy lifestyle habits may not address every menopause-related change.

Losing a train of thought, struggling to recall once-familiar words or forgetting the reason for walking into a room can leave older adults wondering if they are experiencing early signs of Alzheimer’s disease or dementia.

However, these brain blips can often be tied to hormone shifts later in life, medical experts note, and women who experience a loss of estrogen during perimenopause and menopause are particularly affected.

According to Dr. Rhonda Voskuhl, a professor of neurology at UCLA and co-founder of Cleopatra RX in Los Angeles, women experiencing memory struggles in midlife should compare their cognitive function to their own past performance before assuming something is seriously wrong.
WOMEN WHO START COMMON HORMONE THERAPY IN THEIR 50S MAY HAVE 23% LOWER DEMENTIA RISK
"I think they should listen to themselves," Voskuhl told Fox News Digital at the Livelong Women’s Health Summit in New York City Friday. "They know. Just ask yourself."
For women, sudden memory lapses in midlife are often driven by estrogen loss during perimenopause and menopause rather than early-onset dementia. (iStock)
The 10-year assessment
To help women gauge whether their memory lapses are tied to hormonal shifts, Voskuhl recommends using a quick benchmark of comparing a current mental state to where it was a decade ago.
"The first question is, are you worse than you were 10 years ago?" she said, referencing the Voskuhl Brain Fog Menopause Assessment used at UCLA's Comprehensive Menopausal Program.
KATIE COURIC COULDN'T REMEMBER THE YEAR OR THE PRESIDENT DURING FRIGHTENING BRAIN EPISODE

"Ten years is a pretty good spot. And they think, ‘What was I doing 10 years ago? What was I like? Was I having problems finding the words? Was I at the point where I couldn’t multitask anymore? Was I slow in my processing?’ And they’ll remember."
This comparison can help reveal whether a woman’s cognitive changes may be linked to menopause, while giving patients and physicians a baseline for tracking symptoms over time.
CDC data shows that about one in nine adults report subjective cognitive decline, but less than half ever discuss these memory concerns with a healthcare professional. (iStock)
The NFL analogy

Standard memory tests don’t always catch subtle shifts in everyday cognitive function. In the medical community, this is known as subjective cognitive decline, when patients notice changes even though neurological testing remains normal.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reports that roughly one in nine adults report subjective cognitive decline, yet less than half discuss these memory concerns with a healthcare professional.
To illustrate why routine tests can miss early menopausal brain fog, Voskuhl compared it to a high-performing athlete.
"They know if they're not like they used to be."
"If somebody is an NFL football player, and he says, 'I'm weaker than I used to be,' and I go and do my neurological test, I say, 'Oh no, you're still strong,'" Voskuhl said.
What the player is feeling still matters, even if a standard test shows no obvious decline, she noted.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Women, too, can often recognize when their cognitive abilities have changed from their own baseline and should trust those observations, according to Voskuhl.

Standard neurological tests frequently miss menopausal brain fog because patients experience "subjective cognitive decline," noticing subtle personal drops in performance that clinical tests register as normal. (iStock)
Understanding the difference between hormonal brain fog and neurodegenerative disease comes down to how memory loss impacts daily function, experts agree.

Menopausal brain fog typically involves temporary, inconsistent lapses like misplacing items or experiencing slower processing speed, but overall reasoning skills and independence remain intact, according to the Mayo Clinic. Symptoms often fluctuate and can be exacerbated by stress or poor sleep.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

By contrast, early dementia causes persistent, progressive memory loss that interferes with basic daily tasks like managing finances, following familiar routes while driving or exercising sound judgment.
If cognitive concerns arise, experts advise getting a thorough medical evaluation to rule out other issues and finding a new doctor if symptoms are being dismissed. (iStock)
Amid cognitive concerns, experts advise seeking a full medical evaluation, including brain MRIs or vascular screenings, to rule out underlying issues like blood vessel disease or thyroid imbalances.

For women who feel their concerns are being dismissed, Voskuhl offered this advice: "When they have doctors who don't listen to them, they need to find another doctor."

title: Never smoked a cigarette? You could still be at higher risk for lung cancer
summary: Never-smokers carrying the rare EGFR T790M gene variant face 62 times the odds of lung cancer, a major study of 3.3 million people suggests.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel discusses a new study revealing a historic decline in adult cigarette smoking rates in the U.S. to under 10%.
A rare genetic mutation could put people at a dramatically higher risk of developing lung cancer even if they’ve never smoked.

A rare mutation in the gene EGFR T790M was found to increase lung cancer risk by 25 times compared with people who did not have the mutation, according to a new study published in the journal Science.
Among people who had never smoked, carriers of the mutation had about 62 times the odds of lung cancer compared with never-smokers who did not have it.
PANCREATIC CANCER VACCINE SHOWS PROMISE IN FIRST HUMAN TRIAL, PREVENTING DISEASE IN HIGH-RISK PATIENTS
The study, led by investigators at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and 23andMe Research Institute, analyzed data from more than 3.3 million people.
The gene variant showed no increased risk across 17 other cancers studied.
A rare genetic mutation could put people at a dramatically higher risk of developing lung cancer even if they’ve never smoked. (iStock)

"Today, lung cancer screening is driven almost entirely by smoking history," study co-author Jaclyn LoPiccolo, attending physician and lung cancer researcher at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, said in a press release.
CANCER WARNING SIGNS MAY APPEAR IN DNA YEARS BEFORE BLOOD TESTS DETECT TROUBLE

"Our findings raise the possibility that, in the future, screening could also be dictated by inherited genetic risk. If further studies confirm the benefit, people with EGFR T790M could be identified through genetic testing and offered personalized CT screening to identify lung cancers when they are at their most curable stage."
Among people who had never smoked, carriers of the mutation had about 62 times the odds of lung cancer compared with never-smokers who did not have it. (iStock)
Most U.S. carriers of the mutation were traced to a shared ancestry linked to British and Irish settlers in Southern Appalachia about 200–225 years ago, the researchers found.

The mutation remains rare nationwide, affecting roughly one in 15,000–16,000 people. It is more common in some parts of Southern Appalachia, where researchers estimate as many as one in 2,000 people may carry it.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"We found that the vast majority of carriers inherited the mutation from the same ancestral lineage," said LoPiccolo. "We could trace that lineage to British and Irish settlers in the United States and show that the mutation became enriched after a founder event and genetic bottleneck in Southern Appalachia about 200 years ago.
"It's a fascinating example of how human migration and genealogy can shape disease risk, generations later."
While the study establishes a strong association with lung cancer risk, it does not demonstrate that genetic testing improves mortality or other health outcomes. (iStock)
One of the "remarkable" findings of the study was the fact that a single mutation could have such a strong effect, according to Alexander Gusev, a quantitative geneticist at Dana-Farber.
"To my knowledge, it's one of the strongest, if not the strongest, cancer risk-increasing mutations that has ever been found," he said in the release.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Smoking is bad for lung cancer. This mutation is bad for lung cancer. When you do both, your risk is the sum of those two risks," he added. "So, you definitely don't want to smoke."

The researchers suggest that people with a strong family history of lung cancer, multiple lung nodules or tumors or family roots in parts of the southeastern U.S. should consider speaking with a genetic counselor about whether genetic testing or lung cancer screening makes sense for them.
"It's a fascinating example of how human migration and genealogy can shape disease risk generations later."
There were some limitations to the study.
Because the mutation is so rare, researchers identified relatively few carriers even among the millions of participants, meaning the exact size of the increased risk remains uncertain.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
The analysis also relied heavily on 23andMe research participants, who may not represent the broader population.
Because the mutation is much more common in certain parts of the U.S., the risk estimates may not apply equally to everyone, the researchers noted.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
While the study establishes a strong association with lung cancer risk, it does not demonstrate that genetic testing improves mortality or other health outcomes.
The study was funded in part by the National Institutes of Health and the American Cancer Society.

title: Popular weight-loss drugs may play surprising role in cancer outcomes
summary: GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy may lower cancer risk by altering the body's immune response, but researchers say key clinical trials are needed.
story: Sai Yendamuri, M.D., a thoracic surgeon at Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center in Buffalo, New York, speaks to Fox News Digital about whether weight-loss drugs could reduce cancer risk.
As GLP-1 medications continue reshaping the treatment of obesity and diabetes, researchers are also investigating whether the drugs could influence cancer risk and outcomes.
The American Association for Cancer Research's 2026 Cancer Progress Report, released earlier this month, noted that obesity is a major risk factor for many cancers.

As glucagon-like peptide-1 medications – including semaglutides like Ozempic and Wegovy, and tirzepatides like Mounjaro and Zepbound – are known to cause substantial weight loss and improve metabolic health, they have attracted significant interest among cancer researchers.
POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY HELP PROTECT AGAINST A DEADLY DISEASE, DOCTOR SAYS
While the AACR report cited studies suggesting GLP-1 medications may reduce the risk of certain cancers, it emphasized that the overall evidence is mixed and more research is needed.
"Randomized clinical trials remain the gold standard ... however, such trials have not yet been conducted specifically to assess cancer outcomes associated with GLP-1 RA use," the report stated.
As GLP-1 medications continue reshaping the treatment of obesity and diabetes, researchers are also investigating whether the drugs could influence cancer risk and outcomes. (iStock)

Sai Yendamuri, M.D., a thoracic surgeon at Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center in Buffalo, New York, reiterated that obesity is a leading cause of cancer, second to smoking. Additional risk factors include alcohol and poor nutrition, he noted, "which are all layered into obesity."

"So if obesity is related to cancer – both in terms of causing it and increasing its progression – the logical question is, would a drug that decreases obesity have an impact?" the doctor, who was not associated with the AACR report, said in an interview with Fox News Digital.
OZEMPIC-STYLE DRUGS LINKED TO MAJOR SLOWDOWN IN CANCER SPREAD, NEW STUDY FINDS
There are "many lines of evidence" that suggest this would be the case, Yendamuri suggested.
"For example, when people studied patients who were having metabolic surgery to decrease obesity, for example, the incidence of cancer decreased in those patients."
While the AACR report cited studies suggesting GLP-1 medications may reduce the risk of certain cancers, it emphasized that the overall evidence is mixed and more research is needed. (iStock)
Researchers then started looking at patients who were on GLP-1 receptor agonists, such as Ozempic.

"And then they compared the incidence of cancer in those patients to patients who were not taking GLP-1 receptor agonists – and many of those studies found that the risk of cancer was lower and the survival was higher in the patients taking GLP-1s," the doctor said.
DR OZ LINKS OBESITY TO CHRONIC DISEASE SURGE, SAYS GLP-1S CAN 'JUMPSTART' BETTER HEALTH

Although the majority of studies showed this effect, Yendamuri noted that some did not identify a relationship – and a couple of studies even showed an increased risk of some specific cancers, such as thyroid cancer.

"The reason you find this disconnect … is because these are retrospective studies," he said. "That is, they look at existing data, and they're trying to derive associations from existing data … but there are many other variables that can impact the result."
The American Association for Cancer Research's 2026 Cancer Progress Report, released earlier this month, noted that obesity is a major risk factor for many cancers. (iStock)
Yendamuri and his team of researchers have conducted their own studies of the relationship between obesity and lung cancer.
"We have found in every investigation we've done that obesity does increase the risk of lung cancer," he shared.
CANCER TREATMENT DELAYS SURGE ACROSS US AS DOCTOR WARNS SYSTEM ‘NEEDS FIXING IMMEDIATELY’

Obesity also depends on how it's defined and measured, Yendamuri noted. While body mass index (BMI) has traditionally been the standard measure, many obesity researchers are moving away from relying on BMI alone and instead using more precise assessments of body fat composition.
Yendamuri shared two key findings from his research.
"If someone's having a resection, a lung cancer surgery, for patients who are on GLP-1 receptor agonists, the recurrence rate seems to be lower."
"What we think is happening is that it changes the body’s immune response to cancer cells, and thereby improves its ability to fight cancer cells."
Additionally, patients with advanced-stage cancers who are in immunotherapy and taking GLP-1s had lower recurrence rates, he noted.
Based on preclinical laboratory studies, Yendamuri said he believes GLP-1 medications have only a limited direct effect on cancer cells.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"What we think is happening is that it changes the body’s immune response to cancer cells, and thereby improves its ability to fight cancer cells," he told Fox News Digital.
The effect may differ depending on the type of cancer, Yendamuri said, because the immune response is more important in some cancers than others.
The effect may differ depending on the type of cancer, an expert said, because the immune response is more important in some cancers than others. (iStock)
"For example, in some cancers like melanoma, we know that the immune response is incredibly important," he said.
Yendamuri acknowledged that at least some of the cancer benefit likely stems from weight loss.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Not every patient who takes GLP-1 receptor agonists responds with a substantial weight loss, so in future trials, it would be interesting to see if the benefit for patients depends on the weight loss," he said.
"If those patients who have weight loss with GLP-1 receptor agonists have the same cancer benefit as patients who do not have weight loss, that will answer that question."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Depending on the outcomes of future trials, the doctor said he is hopeful that GLP-1 drugs could one day be regarded as a preventive mechanism for cancer.

"Not every patient who takes GLP-1 receptor agonists responds with a substantial weight loss, so in future trials, it would be interesting to see if the benefit for patients depends on the weight loss," the expert said. (iStock)

"More and more, we are realizing that apart from the treatment that you get for cancer, lifestyle modifications – exercise, decreasing weight and now GLP-1 receptor agonists – will all have a role in both enhancing the treatment of cancer as well as preventing second cancers," he said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Yendamuri emphasized the importance of continued funding for the National Cancer Institute, noting that it supports researchers working to advance cancer research and develop new discoveries.

title: Reporter's Notebook: Congress dodged a fall shutdown, but the real fight looms
summary: Congress avoided a government shutdown this fall, but midterm elections could spark a December spending battle or a new shutdown in early 2027.
story: Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram reports on Senate Democrats blocking data center legislation and a bill barring members from stock trading on ‘Special Report.’
"And all at once, summer collapsed into fall…" – Oscar Wilde

Congress certainly collapsed into fall this year. It lacked the usual mayhem of an imminent government shutdown for the first time in years. The government is usually only funded through September 30, the end of the federal fiscal year. Lawmakers solved that fiscal riddle early.

So the beginning of fall in Congress is usually anything but enjoyable. Others are devouring cobbler, enjoying spiced pumpkin lattes and viewing leaves of amber. When a government shutdown looms, the infernality of summer continues to stew on Capitol Hill. Imagine simmering political temperatures mixed with boiling urban concrete and a soupçon of petrichor. That epitomizes the customary fall tension in the halls of Congress when lawmakers are on the precipice of a shutdown.
But this year is different.
TRUMP SIGNS GOVERNMENT FUNDING BILL, AVOIDING A SHUTDOWN AHEAD OF MIDTERMS
The U.S. Capitol past traffic on North Capitol Street in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday, Dec. 23, 2025. (Kent Nishimura/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

No shutdown. That’s a good thing, considering last year’s 43-day shutdown odyssey which crawled from October 1 into mid-November. Everything is funded through December 11. So at least members and journalists can enjoy some of those autumnal fall trappings and dash to the pumpkin patch. That’s because we don’t know what’s going to await everyone for the next spending round in mid-December.

Lawmakers are recovering from the battle scars of last fall. So with the midterms approaching, no one wanted to return to the 2025 contretemps. The sides are willing to tussle over spending. But only after the midterms.
Does that mean a shutdown in December? Unclear.

If Democrats seize control of the House or Senate — or both — that could compel House and Senate Republicans to fund the government the way they want through the fall of 2027 right away. They won’t want an interim spending bill which punts things into early next year when Democrats may have power.

That said, if Democrats capture either the House or Senate, they will argue that the voters have spoken and it’s incumbent on them to decide how to spend taxpayer money next year. Under those scenarios, Democrats will push for a stopgap bill, hoping to tangle with President Trump in the early days of 2027.
The only thing which is known is that President Trump will in fact still be in office come January. This scenario could spark a shut down next year – if not December.

The reason? You still need 60 votes to clear a filibuster (and probably two) in the U.S. Senate. That means Republicans just can’t ram through whatever spending package they want. That may work in the House. And the GOP could even test the willingness of Reps. Jared Golden, D-Maine, and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, D-Wash., to buck their party and assist passing a GOP-favored spending measure in the lame duck.
FETTERMAN STRONGLY SUPPORTS THE FILIBUSTER AS TRUMP URGES SENATE REPUBLICANS TO SCRAP IT
Rep. Jared Golden, D-Maine, attends a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center in Washington, July 17, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

But in the Senate, Republicans will certainly need the cooperation of at least seven Democrats to help them hit the 60 vote threshold. Those Democrats won’t be anxious to assist unless they won the majority and think they can apply their stamp on federal spending in the first quarter of next year.
This is the same problem which vexed the Senate during the shutdown of 2025.

The House passed a partisan spending bill to re-up all current funding on an interim basis. But Senate Republicans could never break a filibuster to lug that spending package across the finish line. The same circumstances may be true in December.
So could the 120th Congress begin in January with a shutdown?
It’s happened before. In fact, under very similar circumstances.

Democrats flipped control of the House during the 2018 midterms – two years into President Trump’s first term. But the President and outgoing House Speaker Paul Ryan, R-Wis., balked at a bipartisan spending package the Senate cleared just before Christmas that year. So the government closed. There was no way to resuscitate the Senate-approved package. So the 116th Congress began with a shutdown. It ran a then-record 35 days.

A possible government shutdown over spending disputes frankly serves as a symptom for what could be ahead if voters flip either or both bodies of Congress. Democrats will convulse at spending plans made by Republicans and the President. Plus, House Democrats likely add several progressives and Democratic Socialists to their ranks in November in solidly blue districts. Granted, those left-wing politicians won’t take office until January. But House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., must court the support of candidates Melat Kiros in Colorado along with Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez in New York to win the Speaker’s gavel. Any missteps by the Democratic brain trust in the lame duck could ignite an internecine firestorm – before Democrats potentially seize the majority in January.
Republicans could face their own issues, too.
SCHUMER PREACHES AFFORDABILITY IN DEM MIDTERM PITCH WHILE SABOTAGING GOP FIXES FOR SOARING COSTS

Democratic congressional candidate Melat Kiros speaks after winning the Democratic nomination during a primary election night watch party at The Broadway, Tuesday, June 30, 2026, in Denver. (Rebecca Slezak/AP Photo)

Some rank-and-file Republicans are ready to move on from House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA). Granted, it is said that Johnson is Speaker as long as President Trump wants him in the job. But what’s not clear is what happens if Republicans lose control of the House. Will the President and others support Johnson for Minority Leader? Does Johnson want that job? What happens to House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-LA) and House Minority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn.?

There are signals that House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, is interested in moving into leadership. Especially if the GOP loses the majority. Jordan is tight with President Trump. He lost a bid to become Speaker three years ago after Republicans unceremoniously ousted former Speaker Kevin McCarthy, R-Calif.

If Republicans lose the majority, it’s not clear that some Republicans will back Johnson for the top GOP job in the House – regardless of what President Trump says. Some House Republicans will blame the President if the party loses the House. Especially since they believe he’s responsible for the toxic political climate they face right now. It’s unknown if a Republican party out of power might begin pushing back against President Trump, frustrated by the economy, tariffs, the price of gasoline and the war in Iran. Most GOPers have shown a reluctance to break with the President so far. But that could change if voters hand Congressional Republicans their head in the midterms.

We haven’t even raised the question about the future of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y. – although the New York Democrat insists he isn’t going anywhere. But questions would emerge if Democrats don’t flip the Senate, considering that progressives and younger activists want to move on from the 75-year-old Schumer.

The same with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D. President Trump and Thune have never been close. If Republicans lose the Senate, would the President use that as a reason to call for the removal of the South Dakota Republican?
All of this will color those questions about spending bills, maybe renewing FISA – or even getting the House to sync up with the Senate on the college sports bill during the lame duck Congress.
Summer collapsed into fall. Capitol Hill was bereft of the usual autumnal mayhem.
So go pick out some pumpkins. Sip a cinnamon spice latte. Prepare for trick or treating. Fall is here.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
But that autumn Congressional bedlam is only delayed. It will hit Capitol Hill after the election.
Chad Pergram currently serves as Chief Congressional Correspondent for FOX News Channel (FNC). He joined the network in September 2007 and is based out of Washington, D.C.

title: 10 Democrat-held House seats Republicans could flip to save their majority
summary: President Donald Trump's margins in redrawn districts fuel Republican hopes of flipping 10 Democratic House seats in the battle for Congress.
story: Rep. Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla., discusses growing concerns about Democratic socialist candidates after Florida's primary elections.

The battle for control of Congress is entering its final sprint, with Republicans and Democrats just over a month away from learning who will wield power for the final two years of President Donald Trump's presidency.

House Democrats lead House Republicans in the most recent Fox News Power Rankings, with the left projected to win 215 seats in the lower chamber compared to 201 for the GOP. But 19 seats are still ranked as toss-ups, meaning the final majority is still anyone's to claim.

One issue that's given Republicans a glimmer of hope in an otherwise bleak cycle is the far-left insurgency that's gripped the Democratic Party. Several key victories by socialist candidates could threaten to push the party further left than most Americans are, a warning that GOP candidates across the country have shared.
FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: DEMOCRATS LEAD IN THE HOUSE, BUT REDISTRICTING KEEPS THE GOP IN THE GAME
Below is a list of 10 House districts currently held by Democrats where Republicans could see key victories that help them retain control.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., speaks onstage at the 2026 National Association of Black Journalists Convention at the Atlanta Marriott Marquis in Atlanta on Aug. 13, 2026. (Getty Images)
Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Ala., is running for re-election in a congressional district that's been redrawn to significantly favor Republicans.
SUPREME COURT ALLOWS ALABAMA GOP-BACKED CONGRESSIONAL MAP FOR MIDTERMS

A 2023 Supreme Court decision ordered Alabama to create a second Black opportunity district ahead of the 2024 election, meaning Black voters there would have meaningful sway in the general election. The resulting boundaries helped Figures win his seat, which was previously held by Rep. Barry Moore, R-Ala., who ran in a neighboring district that cycle.

But the Supreme Court's ruling in Louisiana v. Callais earlier this year significantly curbed the Voting Rights Act's enforcement of racial considerations in congressional maps, paving the way for southern states to alter district boundaries that were drawn to give minorities more representation.
BLOCKBUSTER SUPREME COURT VOTING RIGHTS RULING IGNITES REDISTRICTING WAR ACROSS SOUTHERN STATES

That hit Figures particularly hard. The new district would have voted for President Donald Trump by roughly 14% in 2024, according to 270ToWin. Both Fox News Power Rankings and the nonpartisan Cook Political Report (CPR) rate it as "likely Republican."
Florida lawmakers also altered their state's map ahead of November, aimed at giving Republicans a slight edge in the already-red state.
Rep. Darren Soto, D-Fla., who is running for a sixth term representing his district, was one of the Democrats whose seat was hit the hardest.
His newly redrawn district voted for Trump by nearly 18%, 270ToWin's analysis states.
REDISTRICTING GIVES REPUBLICANS AN EDGE, BUT AFFORDABILITY WILL DECIDE THE MIDTERMS
Fox News Power Rankings rates it as "lean Republican" while CPR ranks the seat as a "likely" Republican pickup.

Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Ala., speaks at a press conference on healthcare with other members of the House Democratic caucus in front of the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 12, 2025. (Nathan Posner/Anadolu via Getty Images)
The Tampa-area House seat held by Rep. Kathy Castor, D-Fla., was also among the blue seats redrawn by the Sunshine State's government to make it more competitive for Republicans.
The longtime moderate Democrat has served in Congress since 2007 and represented her current district since 2013.
She's facing off against a former Florida state lawmaker, Republican Mike Beltran, who also has name recognition in the area.

Under its new lines, which remove more Democrat-leaning places around the city of St. Petersburg in favor of more rural and suburban areas in the south and east, Trump would have won the district by 10.5% in 2024, according to 270ToWin.
Both Fox News Power Rankings and CPR rate it a "toss-up," meaning it's anyone's game.

Republicans redrew Florida's 22nd Congressional District in a way that could have pitted incumbent Reps. Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla., and Debbie Wasserman Schultz, D-Fla., against each other in a likely expensive and bruising primary.
But both opted to run in other districts, leaving the seat currently occupied by retiring Rep. Lois Frankel, D-Fla., as a potential opportunity for both parties.
Under Florida's new map, 270ToWin projects Trump would have won the district by roughly 10% in 2024.
Democrat Pia Dandiya, a political newcomer, is running against Republican businessman and Marine Casey Askar.
Both Fox News and CPR rank the district a "toss-up."

Rep. Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla., is running in Florida's 25th Congressional District after the GOP's aforementioned redistricting play, a seat that on paper was amended to give Republicans a slight edge.
Redistricting shifted the seat from one that ex-Vice President Kamala Harris won by single digits to one that Trump would have won by nearly 10 points.

Moskowitz has long touted his bipartisan work in Congress and as Florida's emergency management director under Gov. Ron DeSantis, giving Democrats some confidence that he could overcome the political shift in Republicans' favor.
Fox News' latest projections have the seat leaning Democrat, while CPR ranks it a "toss-up."
Rep. Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla., speaks during a press conference on Dec. 13, 2023 in Washington, D.C. (Jemal Countess/Getty Images for Congressional Integrity Project)
Rep. Cleo Fields, D-La., is retiring at the end of this year, making his seat another open race.
But the same 2023 and 2026 Supreme Court decisions that affected Figures in Alabama are at play in the Bayou State this year.

After the most recent decision rolling back the Voting Rights Act, Republicans were able to redraw the 6th district in a way that diluted the Black population, who primarily voted Democrat in 2024, to factor in more red-leaning areas.
Because of the Supreme Court’s ruling earlier this year, Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry signed legislation delaying the state’s House primary races to Nov. 3 and the general election to Dec. 12.
Both Fox News’ and CPR’s rankings project the seat to fall into Republican hands.
The retirement of moderate Rep. Jared Golden, D-Maine, has opened up a rare opportunity for a GOP pickup in the American Northeast.
Golden, who is known for frequently breaking from his own party on key issues like immigration and tariffs, represents a district that Trump won by 9% in 2024, according to 270ToWin.
Republicans have a particularly strong candidate in that open race, former Gov. Paul LePage.
Fox News rates the district a "toss-up," while CPR projects it as a likely Republican victory.
Perennial battleground Rep. Don Davis, D-N.C., is facing one of his toughest re-election battles yet thanks to North Carolina also joining the nationwide redistricting fight ahead of November.
Like Golden, Davis also won a district that went to Trump over Harris in 2024.
But under the state’s new maps, Trump’s margin of victory in that state widened considerably — and with it, Republicans’ chances of winning.
Davis is facing Republican Laurie Buckhout, who he defeated in 2024 by less than 2%.
Fox News rates the district a "toss-up," while CPR’s rankings say it leans slightly for Republicans.

Rep. Don Davis, D-N.C., speaks at a campaign event for then-Democratic presidential nominee Vice President Kamala Harris at East Carolina University, Oct. 13, 2024, in Greenville, N.C. (David Yeazell, File via AP)
Lone Star State Republicans kicked off the nationwide redistricting fight ahead of the 2026 midterms with a map that was redrawn to win the GOP up to five more seats in November.
Among those is a district currently represented by Congressional Progressive Caucus Chair Greg Casar, D-Texas.
But Casar is now running in the nearby 37th Congressional District, leaving the 35th a wide-open race that both parties see opportunity in.
Under the new boundaries, Trump would have won the district by roughly 10%, according to 270ToWin.
A GOP victory there, however, will depend heavily on its considerable Hispanic population shifting to the right again this year.
Both Fox News and CPR project the district leaning slightly in favor of Republicans.
Rep. Marcy Kaptur, D-Ohio, is also running a tougher race this year thanks to her state’s new congressional map.
Kaptur’s battleground district was shifted slightly to include more Republican-leaning areas, making an already difficult re-election bid even more of an uphill battle.
Trump would have won the district by 10.5% under its new lines, according to 270ToWin.

But Kaptur has survived several attempts at redistricting by Republicans since her first victory in 1982. She is the longest-serving woman in congressional history and the longest currently-serving House member from Ohio.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Both Fox News and CPR rated the district a "toss-up" in November.
Fox News' Remy Numa contributed to this report.

title: Trump’s new high-tech government hub holds some bizarre surprises: ‘Enjoy finding them’
summary: America.gov developers planted Easter eggs across Trump's new AI-powered site, including a Minecraft "End Poem" parody and a hot dog search bar.
story: Fox News White House correspondent Aishah Hasnie and Rep. Darrell Issa, R-Calif., discuss President Donald Trump's meeting with top tech CEOs at the White House, the launch of the AI-powered America.gov platform and how the initiative aims to keep the United States ahead of China in the global AI race.

Users digging into President Donald Trump’s new AI-powered America.gov discovered a series of hidden features embedded across the federal platform, including a "Minecraft"-inspired response and a search bar that transforms into a hot dog.
The Trump administration unveiled the revamped America.gov on Tuesday, consolidating information from more than 29,000 government websites into a single AI- powered search platform.
Some of the site's more unusual features quickly began circulating on social media, with users posting screenshots of AI responses and hidden interactive elements.

Users who entered "Play Minecraft," for example, were met with a lengthy, surreal response appearing to be modeled by the video game’s "End Poem," swapping its original language for references to government bureaucracy, privacy and federal programs.
TRUMP TO USHER IN ‘GOLDEN AGE’ OF AMERICAN TECH WITH DC BASH SHOWCASING POWERFUL NEW TOOL

Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaks during an event to unveil the new America.gov website at the Andrew W. Mellon Auditorium in Washington, D.C., on Sept. 29, 2026. (Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images)
The "End Poem" is text written by Julian Gough that shows up as rolling credits when a user completes the video game.

"This constituent dreamed of sunlight and trees. Of fire and water. It dreamed it created a small business. And it dreamed it destroyed a password. It dreamed it hunted a job, and was hunted by a recertification. It dreamed of shelter that would take a voucher," the response read in part when tested by Fox News Digital Wednesday. "Hah, the original interface. A million years old, and it still works.
By Thursday, however, Fox News Digital could no longer trigger the response using the same prompt.

"America.gov will continue to be updated to provide Americans the most accurate and reliable federal information and resources," a White House official told Fox News Digital Wednesday when asked about the unusual responses.
National Design Studio (NDS) developers indicated that hidden surprises, such as a hot dog, were intentionally built into America.gov.
"We put Easter eggs all over https://America.gov Enjoy finding them," wrote NDS team member Adam Bhaloo.
STATE DEPARTMENT CONSIDERS SHARING PASSPORT RECORDS FOR VOTER CITIZENSHIP CHECKS
Typing "hotdog" transformed the chatbot’s input bar into a frankfurter when tested by Fox News Digital Thursday. (America.gov)
In another scenario, typing "hotdog" transformed the chatbot’s input bar into a frankfurter when tested by Fox News Digital Thursday.
"29,000 agencies. One glizzy," wrote one user who tested it out.

TRUMP ANNOUNCES NEW 'AI FORCE,' VOWS TO PROTECT INDUSTRY AS AI CZAR ANNOUNCEMENT NEARS
