He traveled Saturday night to Lourdes, one of the Catholic Church’s most visited pilgrimage sites.
Jasmine Baehr is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital, where she covers politics, the military, legal debates surrounding life and family policy, as well as faith and culture.

title: Christa Pike is in critical condition after a failed execution in Tennessee, her lawyers say
summary: As harrowing details emerge from Tennessee’s failed execution of Christa Pike, who survived despite her lawyers saying she was administered two doses of a lethal drug, scrutiny is falling on how the procedure was carried out.
story: As harrowing details emerge from Tennessee’s failed execution of Christa Pike, who survived despite her lawyers saying she was administered two doses of a lethal drug, scrutiny is falling on how the procedure was carried out.

Nearly 24 hours after Pike was set to be put to death for a murder she committed when she was 18, her lawyers said Thursday afternoon that she was still alive. Her prognosis was unclear, lawyer Randall Spivey said, but she remained in critical condition and was receiving “lifesaving medical care.” Neither he nor another lawyer, Stephen Ferrell, who spoke with reporters, said they had seen her in the hospital.
“I’m haunted by last night,” said Spivey, who was there during the execution attempt.
Spivey said he counted at least seven needles used in Pike’s left arm alone, “one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her arm after an unsuccessful attempt.”

He added that Pike’s right arm had turned purple after the second round of the drug pentobarbital, a sedative used in Tennessee’s execution protocol, was dispensed. Pike’s lawyers said they also learned of “blistering and burning around the sites of the injection.”

The description sheds additional light on what occurred inside of the execution chamber as the execution team attempted to put Pike, 50, to death. After the curtain to the chamber was opened at 7:26 p.m., a media witness said Pike complained that “my arm feels like it’s about to burst open.”
Other media witnesses said Pike moaned that one spot was “really throbbing” and was kicking so often she knocked a sheet that was laid on her.
She continued to make snoring sounds, groan and move after the drugs were presumed to have taken effect, the witnesses said.
Five minutes after the second dose, “it was clear that Miss Pike was still breathing,” Spivey said.

He said he did not see any lifesaving care provided to Pike when he was able to witness the events unfold, but there was a time before the witnesses were led out when no one could see what was happening. Medical care was administered in an ambulance that was called at 8:50 p.m. to the prison in Nashville where executions are held.
“Last night was not just inefficient; it was cruel and it was torturous,” Spivey said.

Medical experts told NBC News that Pike’s injuries could be consistent with the drug failing to go directly into her bloodstream but ending up in surrounding tissue because of incorrect insertion or leaking.

If that happened, it would mean less of the drug getting into her circulatory system, keeping her breathing and moving rather than becoming deeply comatose before death, said Dr. Jonathan Groner, an emeritus professor of clinical surgery at the Ohio State University College of Medicine.
Burning around the injection site could also be evidence of the drug not getting properly injected into a vein, he added.
“I’ve seen partial thickness burns look red or purple,” Groner said.

Ferrell said he thinks a “number of factors” could explain the execution failure, but said that based on what medical experts told their team about Pike’s difficult veins, it seems like the intravenous line may have infiltrated.

This occurs when a misplaced needle deposits the medication into the arm instead of the bloodstream. That, he said, would be consistent with Pike’s complaints that her arm was hurting during the process, and that it felt like it was “about to explode.”
Where is Christa Pike now?

Spivey described venous issues that Pike has had throughout her life, noting problems with typical blood draws. It’s part of the reason she feared this method of execution, and why she requested a different method, the lawyers said.
“I do know that that really was her biggest fear,” Ferrell said. “It was not a fear of dying. It was a fear of a prolonged, painful, traumatic death, and that’s what happened minus the death.”
Spivey said he was given an emergency number for the Tennessee Supreme Court to call if something went wrong with the execution, but that when he called it, it went to voicemail.
Pike’s attorneys have since appealed her execution. Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee has stayed Pike’s execution until a third-party investigation uncovers what happened Wednesday.
“This is a tragedy. There is no one that wanted what happened last night to happen. It shouldn’t have happened,” Lee said at a news conference Thursday morning.
He declined to give details on Pike’s condition and said he would be hiring a team to look into the circumstances surrounding the failure.
“I do hope he cares, because this is as a citizen of Tennessee, this is something that was done in all of our names,” Spivey said of Lee.

It’s the second time an execution did not go as planned in Tennessee this year. Tony Carruthers, convicted in three 1994 killings, was granted a one-year reprieve after executioners in May couldn’t find a vein for a backup IV.
Many questions remain in Pike’s case: Was she in pain when this was occurring? Will she remember what happened? Will there be long-term damage? Ferrell said he does not have the answers.

“We may never know what all she was suffering through, either because she can’t remember it, she can’t tell it, or it overwhelms her in such a way that, you know, sometimes pain and suffering affects people that way,” he added.

Pike’s conviction stems from a 1995 murder case. Pike, along with two other teenage accomplices, worked together to torture, slash and fatally beat Colleen Slemmer, Knoxville police said at the time. Pike was convicted in Slemmer’s death and sentenced to death; she was on death row for decades.
A number of last-minute efforts to stop the execution were unsuccessful. Pike was set to be the first woman Tennessee has executed in more than 200 years.

title: Supreme Court to decide lawfulness of Trump’s immigrant detention policy
summary: WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court said Thursday it will consider whether immigrants subject to deportation can be held in detention indefinitely while their cases are adjudicated.
story: WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court said Thursday it will consider whether immigrants subject to deportation can be held in detention indefinitely while their cases are adjudicated.
The eventual ruling could endorse or end a key feature of President Donald Trump’s hard-line immigration crackdown.
The case was among three the court took up ahead of the justices’ return to action Monday for a new nine-month term following a summer break. Rulings in all three are due by the end of June.

The focus in the first case is whether such immigrants should have a chance to argue at a bond hearing that they can be released while the deportation process moves forward, which was standard practice under previous presidents.
The justices will hear a Trump administration appeal in the case of Ricardo Aparecido Barbosa da Cunha, a man from Brazil who originally entered the United States in the mid-2000s.

He was detained following a traffic stop in Norwood, Massachusetts, in September 2025. He sued, and a federal district judge ordered that he be released. The New York-based 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals upheld that decision on appeal.

Lower courts have been divided on the issue, although the majority have sided with immigrants who have argued that the federal law the Trump administration cites to hold them without a bond hearing only applies to people detained near the border.

Since last summer, the Trump administration has sought to apply that federal law to anyone deemed to have entered the United States illegally, even if they are nowhere near the border and have lived in the country for years.
Several cases on the issue are pending at the Supreme Court.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

“Try as it might, the government cannot twist the law to detain immigrants for months or even years on end without a bond hearing. Not only is it cruel and inhumane; it is unlawful,” Michael Tan, a lawyer with the American Civil Liberties Union representing various detainees, said in a statement.

In court papers, Solicitor General D. John Sauer, representing the Trump administration, called the issue a “critically important question of immigration law.” The policy removes a “perverse incentive” whereby people who evade detention when they enter the United States get treated more leniently than those detained at the border, he added.
The litigation, Sauer said, is “disrupting the orderly administration of immigration law.”

Thousands of people have already been detained under the policy, which could apply to millions of immigrants if expanded, and many of them have contested it. The case does not concern immigrants who have been convicted of certain crimes. Under federal law, they can be detained until they are deported, although separate lawsuits have raised questions about whether they should be eligible for bond hearings, too.

ACLU lawyers said in court papers that the Trump administration policy is a “radical reinterpretation” of immigration law, pointing out that some of those being detained were young children when they crossed the border.
Those challenging their confinement are not a flight risk or a potential danger to the public, ACLU lawyers say.

title: Diddy placed in solitary following NBC News report on his VIP prison life
summary: Sean “Diddy” Combs has been placed in solitary confinement following an NBC News report on his VIP lifestyle inside prison.
story: Sean “Diddy” Combs has been placed in solitary confinement following an NBC News report on his VIP lifestyle inside prison, according to a source with knowledge of the matter.

The disgraced hip hop mogul arrived at the Fort Dix federal prison in New Jersey in October after he was sentenced to 50 months behind bars for transporting people across state lines for sexual encounters.

Since then, he has spent thousands of dollars a month to bring his high-end lifestyle to the low-security prison, NBC News reported Tuesday in a story based on interviews with four men who spent time in the same unit as Combs.

They said he had no trouble acquiring contraband items such as cellphones and premium liquor, including Hennessy. He also pays several inmates who cook special meals for him, clean the toilet and shower areas before he uses them, do his laundry, make his bed and even give him Chinese-style massages.
“This is not some normal s--- you see in jail. This is some rich s---,” one of the sources said. “It looks crazy, but again, it’s Diddy.”
NBC News also obtained photos and videos inside the prison, which includes footage of Combs appearing to use a contraband cellphone.
Diddy appears to use cellphone in prison
After the report was published, Combs was removed from his dormitory-style quarters and placed in a special housing unit, better known as solitary confinement or the SHU, according to the source.
A Bureau of Prisons spokesperson would neither confirm nor deny that Combs was moved.

“For privacy, safety, and security reasons, we do not comment on the conditions of confinement for any incarcerated individual, including quarters assignment or whether a particular individual is the subject of allegations, investigations, or sanctions,” the spokesperson said.
TMZ was first to report that the Bad Boy Records founder was moved to solitary.
Federal prisons often transfer inmates to the special housing unit when they are the subjects of an investigation, experts say.
“We’d put people in the SHU while we were gathering evidence,” said Vito Maraviglia, a retired special investigator for the Bureau of Prisons who worked at Fort Dix in the late 1990s.

Maraviglia said the New Jersey prison is known as one of the cushiest in the federal prison system. It has segmented housing areas that are more difficult to monitor than at other facilities, making it easier for inmates to hide and use contraband items like cellphones.
“A high-profile guy like that, with all that money, I’m surprised they put him at a place like Fort Dix,” Maraviglia said.

Inmates placed in the SHU are locked in a cell with one other person for at least 23 hours a day, according to two men who spent time at Fort Dix. Inmates are allowed a book or two and a wind-up radio, the sources said, and they must wear an orange jumpsuit instead of the regular khaki uniform or grey sweatpants and shirts.
Meals are delivered in trays but commissary access is restricted, and they are permitted to shower only a few days a week. The sources said they must otherwise wash up in a sink.
“It’s nasty down there,” one of the sources said.
It isn’t Combs’ first time in solitary confinement at Fort Dix. Last summer, he was placed in the special housing unit after he got into a fight with another inmate.
He was later kicked out of a drug treatment program at the prison but continued paying inmates to do a range of services for him, NBC News reported Tuesday.

The story prompted responses from people as varied as Combs’ longtime nemesis 50 Cent and the prominent attorney Gloria Allred, who represents a woman suing him for allegedly raping her more than 20 years ago. (Combs has denied the allegations, and the case is ongoing.)

“These serious allegations against Mr. Combs cry out for an immediate federal investigation and appropriate federal action including a prosecution if the allegations of having and using a cell phone while incarcerated can be proven beyond a reasonable doubt,” Allred said in a statement.
Other famous people have also received perks in prison, including Martha Stewart and Harvey Weinstein.

Combs’ trial last year centered on drug-fueled orgies he organized called “freak offs.” They involved male sex workers and his former girlfriends – including the singer Cassie – who filed a lawsuit against Combs alleging years of physical and sexual abuse. (The case was settled, with Combs denying any wrongdoing.)
The trial ended in a split verdict, with a New York jury finding him not guilty on the more serious charges of sex trafficking and racketeering charges that could have put him in prison for life.

title: What we know about the pilot hailed as a hero for averting crash of Israel-bound plane
summary: He is being hailed around the world as a hero for helping stop a passenger plane bound for Israel from plunging into the ground, despite his own severe injuries.
story: He is being hailed around the world as a hero for helping stop a passenger plane bound for Israel from plunging into the ground, despite his own severe injuries.

Images of Capt. Smit Machchhar covered in blood have gone viral after he fought his fellow pilot, who, according to Israeli officials, stabbed him and attempted to nose-dive the plane carrying 174 people from Dubai to Tel Aviv.

While bleeding profusely, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door, allowing other passengers and the Emirati crew to overpower the other pilot and take control of the aircraft. The flight was diverted to an airport in Saudi Arabia, where it landed safely.

The Mumbai native’s actions have “shown the world the highest form of courage” and “prevented another 9/11 like attack from happening,” Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said Thursday, after speaking with Machchhar’s family. “The whole world is proud of him,” he added.
Machchhar spoke previously of getting the “aviation bug” at 19 while pursuing a management course to grow his family’s textile business.
He worked for years at a low-cost Indian airline before joining Flydubai, and had nearly 10,000 hours of flying experience before Wednesday’s incident.

Machchhar is being treated in a hospital in Tabuk city in northwest Saudi Arabia, with his condition described as “stable” on Wednesday by the Indian Embassy in Riyadh. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Fox News he was “very badly wounded.”

Deepak Mittal, India’s ambassador to the United Arab Emirates, said on X he met with Machhar’s family on Thursday in Dubai and “conveyed full support of the Government of India in ensuring welfare and wellbeing of the Indian Hero.”
Netanyahu called Machchhar “a true hero.”

“Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker — preventing a catastrophic mid-air disaster,” he said.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Machchhar’s former employer, the Indian budget carrier SpiceJet, said on X that he flew for the airline for 10 years. According to his LinkedIn profile, Machchhar joined the Emirati low-cost carrier Flydubai in 2022 after flying for SpiceJet since 2011.

On Wednesday, the veteran captain was flying a Boeing 737 Max 8, the newer variant of the 737 plane that Machchhar had nearly 10,000 hours of experience flying, according to his profile and a YouTube podcast interview he gave last year.
“My first aircraft was a Boeing, and it’s always been that aircraft all my life,” he said.
Machchhar said he had flown challenging routes, dodged bad weather, and handled medical emergencies in the air before.
His mother was “scared” when he first told her of his plan to become a pilot, he said in the 2025 interview, but his supportive father agreed to cover the steep fees for aviation training.

Between 2008 and 2009, Machchhar trained for 18 months at an aviation college in New Zealand. It was the first time he had been outside India, he said, and he had only been on a “couple of flights” as a passenger before learning to fly.
He “stood out” among those training and did well with his studies, Mainland Air chief executive Philip Kean told New Zealand’s 1News, adding: “We’re all very proud of him here.”
In his early days as a qualified pilot, he took whatever flight routes he was assigned.
“When I started flying ... the only thing I wanted to do then was fly,” Machchhar told the podcast. “I didn’t want to sleep, I didn’t want to go anywhere, and they loved me for it.”
“For a pilot to gain that experience and to refine your skills is what a pilot is,” he added.
But his attitude changed when he got married and started a family, he said.
“Now I would say I try when I get out of the cockpit or the aircraft, I don’t want the other guy to know that I’m a pilot. I don’t want to discuss aviation,” he said.
“Now the kids are there,” he said. “They want to play with you.”
In the interview, Machchhar also spoke about the “rigorous training” that pilots and cabin crew undergo, which includes safety and emergency procedures.
“When we are up there and if something happens, who is going to save you? You’ll be lucky enough to have a doctor on board,” he said.
“They can save your life,” he said, referring to the cabin crew.

title: Screaming, panicking, blood: Passengers detail horrifying Israel-bound flight
summary: TEL AVIV — A stabbing, an emergency alert, a terrifying mid-air plunge.
story: TEL AVIV — A stabbing, an emergency alert, a terrifying mid-air plunge.

Details are still emerging after an Israel-bound flight carrying some 180 people emitted a distress signal Wednesday, raising fears of a possible hijacking when one pilot stabbed the other in the cockpit.
Aviatar Alevi, who was onboard the Flydubai flight Wednesday, described people “screaming, running, panicking, blood.”
“At the start I thought it was a plane malfunction, but then I started hearing screaming about the stabbings,” Alevi, 17, told NBC News. “Then I understood the weight of the actual situation.”
“We didn’t know what was going to happen,” he said, adding that the possibility of death “was definitely an option.”
The plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, one of its rudders damaged, apparently by the force of its descent.
The passengers, who had been flying from Dubai before the crisis, were mobbed by media and flag-waving fellow Israelis after finally arriving at Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion Airport.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
They said they had feared for their lives after the plane plunged more than 14,000 feet in the span of 29 seconds at one point, according to FlightRadar24.
“Imagine sitting on the plane, all scared after you fell down five kilometers. You don’t understand anything,” 16-year-old Peleg Itali told NBC News.

Captain Smit Machchhar, an Indian national, was recovering in a hospital in Saudi Arabia on Thursday as the other pilot, so far identified only as an Omani citizen, was being interrogated elsewhere in the country. Machchhar was widely praised for his efforts to prevent the plane from crashing, opening the cockpit door and allowing passengers and crew to rush in.

Both Machchhar and the pilot who initiated the attack were transferred to Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, on Thursday, according to a statement from the Saudi Arabian Ministry of Interior, citing an unnamed “official source” at the ministry.

“The source indicated that initial investigations conducted by the competent authorities in the Kingdom, with the participation of a security team from the sisterly United Arab Emirates, revealed an assault on the pilot by his co-pilot, resulting in both sustaining various injuries,” the ministry said in the statement. “The source confirmed that the pilot and his co-pilot, after their health improved and the medical team cleared them, departed the Kingdom for Abu Dhabi this morning.”
Few details had emerged about the pilot as of Thursday morning. Questions about a possible motive, including whether it was terrorism-related, hang over the attack.

“I don’t think it was a hijacking. It looks like a suicide attempt, simply because of what this hero, Yaniv, has described,” Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on “CBS Evening News,” as he praised Yaniv Hayun, who rushed into the cockpit and subdued the attacker.

Hayun, who was pictured with his shirt spattered with blood sitting next to Netanyahu, said that he had confronted the pilot who had initiated the attack, according to the Israeli government press office.
“I grabbed the attacker, and choked him, pulled him out first,” Hayun said. “I started pulling the controls.”
“Thank God, we pulled it off. We really put our heads together and worked as a team,” Hayun said, adding: “It was between fear and a sense of a do-or-die situation.”
“We had to win. We had to pull through and come out on top,” he said. Hayun told Netanyahu that he had acted based on what he’d seen on a TV show and helped stabilize the plane.
Flydubai said on-duty crew who were onboard the flight were able to land the plane.
Motive under investigation
Netanyahu said it was still too early to determine why the pilot apparently stabbed his colleague and appeared to try to take over the Flydubai flight, and whether there was any Iranian involvement.

“We’ve had signs that Iran, in particular through its proxies, was intending to heighten terrorist attacks against Israel and Israeli nationals abroad,” he said. “But I think it’s too early to say whether there was Iranian collusion here.”
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz, meanwhile, branded the incident a “jihadist terrorist attack attempt,” without expanding on how he reached that conclusion.
President Donald Trump also weighed in, calling it “an incredible story.”
“It seems as though the co-pilot was perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack job, and he stabbed the pilot,” Trump told reporters.
On Thursday, Trump told reporters at the White House that the pilot who initiated the attack could be linked to Iran.
“I would say the answer, based on what I’m hearing, is yes. But we’re working on it right now,” he said.
Asked if the pilot could have been radicalized or working with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, Trump replied, “Could have been, yeah.”
All the passengers were Israeli, according to Netanyahu’s office. Four were dual American-Israeli citizens, two U.S. officials told NBC News.

With few details on the suspect or on any potential motive surrounding the incident, Doron Spielman, a spokesperson for Netanyahu’s office said there was a “strong opinion” that the incident was a terror attack “but we can’t be sure until we debrief everybody.”
An investigation by Saudi authorities is ongoing, David Mencer, a spokesperson for the Israeli Prime Minister’s Office, separately said.
A senior U.S. official briefed on the Israeli investigation and a Saudi official also briefed on the probe said the stabbing increasingly looks like an act of terrorism based on early findings.
The United Arab Emirates’ Attorney-General, Dr. Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, separately ordered an investigation into the incident.

His office said the probe would seek to “gather information and evidence, establish the facts and circumstances of the incident, and determine the underlying motives,” in addition to examining “whether the incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose, or involved any prior planning or direction.”

Hessa Alyahya, spokesperson for the Saudi Embassy in the U.S., said authorities were waiting to determine whether the attack was a dispute between the pilots or whether it was an act sponsored by Iran or the Houthis.
Israel and Saudi Arabia do not have official diplomatic relations.

title: How 16 undecided voters are weighing their 2026 election options
summary: The voters, who participated in a recent NBC News poll and spoke to reporters afterward, are laser-focused on high prices and largely disappointed with both parties.
story: James Morton isn’t sure which party he’s going to support in November’s elections, and he doesn’t like his options.

Morton, a 67-year-old retired truck driver in Colorado, said Democrats have “gone too far to the left towards socialism,” while Republicans are “globalists” who “don’t care about the working-class people in this country.”

Morton, an independent who voted for Donald Trump in 2024, is leaning toward backing third-party candidates in races for the House and the Senate this year. But he said his decision will come down to the high cost of living.

“The No. 1 thing is getting the cost of things back down, inflation under control, and pretty much that’s it,” Morton said. He noted that he and his wife have been buying different groceries as they navigate high prices.

Morton is among the 5% of voters surveyed last month in a national NBC News poll who said they weren’t sure which party they wanted to see controlling Congress after this year’s elections. NBC News spoke with 16 of those undecided voters as they weigh their votes this fall, some of whom declined to share their full names discussing politics.

These voters feel little loyalty to either party — and many of them said that’s in part because they aren’t sure either party understands what’s important to them. Almost every one said high costs are top of mind.

In the NBC News poll, 50% of voters said they wanted Democrats to win control of Congress in the midterms, while 45% said they wanted Republicans to have control. How the undecided voters in between resolve their strong, sometimes conflicting feelings could ultimately decide what Congress looks like in 2027, from who controls the majority to how many seats that party holds.
Costs dominate

Voters’ focus on making ends meet has been standing out in recent polling. In the latest NBC News survey, voters ranked cost of living and inflation as the most important issues facing the country, followed by government corruption and threats to democracy.

“I don’t like how expensive things are, and I don’t think anyone does,” said Aidan Valenzuela, a 19-year-old security worker in Texas, who said he hasn’t decided whom to support in his state’s hotly contested races for governor and the Senate.
Joanne, a 72-year-old Vermont independent who works for a heating company, said she plans to sit out her state’s governor’s race, and she hasn’t decided whom she’ll support farther down the ballot.

“I just want somebody to bring some of these prices back down,” she said. Joanne said her husband relies on multiple medications, including insulin. “It’s pretty expensive and leaves nothing for anything else.”
Luke Melanson, 49, of Louisiana, who is retired from construction work, said the rising cost of groceries has changed how he shops.
“I’m not eating as much. I’m eating less food because I can only afford so much,” he said.

Melanson doesn’t identify with either political party, instead considering himself a libertarian, and he declined to say where he was leaning in the midterm election. But he is frustrated with both parties and wants to see new candidates emerge who can personally relate to his financial position.

“I want a plumber. I want someone that ran a smaller business, like a Kroger’s,” he said. “A teacher. I take anybody that isn’t a lawyer or someone so ultra-rich that the pay gap is so far they would never understand what I’m going through.”
Meanwhile, South Carolinian Darien Thompson, a 25-year-old unarmed security guard at a mall, sees gas as the biggest financial woe of the moment. The cost of his commute is only going up.
“It does take a mental load when it’s like, well, it’s going to cost this much to get to work and back, and I’m only making this much,” Thompson said.
It doesn’t bode well for his long-term hopes of owning a home, and he doesn’t see any current politicians stepping up to tackle the issues in a way that has earned his support.
“Politicians are getting into these petty squabbles,” he said. “But it’s, like, none of us can afford houses.”

Thompson doesn’t see himself voting for a Republican in November, but he’s still undecided. He has leaned Democratic before, voting for then-Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024, but his vote this year will depend entirely on the specific candidate Democrats run in his area.

Ibraham, a 42-year-old truck driver in Ohio who isn’t registered with either party, said he plans to back Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown in the Senate race in his state. Ibraham supported Harris in 2024 and said his vote this year is driven almost entirely by the surging price of diesel and a higher cost of living.

“I’ve been driving for nine years. I’ve never seen anything like it. Never. Never, ever. Even during Covid, it didn’t get that high,” Ibraham said, noting that his weekly diesel costs have jumped from $2,000 to $3,500 or $3,700.
“I’m spending an extra $1,500 on diesel every week. Just think about it — it’s a fortune,” he said.
Down on both parties and Trump
Ibraham described his support for Brown as more about opposing Republicans than endorsing Democrats, blaming the GOP-controlled White House and Congress for the current economic struggles.
“It’s not about Brown,” Ibraham said of his Senate vote. “It’s just voting against the Republicans for what they’re doing. That’s it.”

Other voters who were undecided but leaning toward Democrats expressed similar views, expressing caution and saying their potential support for Democrats was motivated more by reining in Trump and Republicans.
For Subscribers
Several voters — including those who backed Trump two years ago — specifically voiced concerns about Trump’s handling of the economy and the war in Iran.
For Subscribers

“I will probably support [a] Democrat this time around just so there’s some check and balances in place,” said Aaron L., a 30-year-old California independent who works in tech. He didn’t vote in 2024 while he was moving, but he said he most likely would have voted for Trump. But nearly two years into Trump’s second term, Aaron said, the economy is “a mess.”
“It seems like the party, the Republican Party, just follow whatever Donald Trump says,” Aaron said.
Like other undecided voters, Aaron said the economy and the war in Iran were among his top issues. Dissatisfaction with the war was high, including among Trump voters.

“One of his platforms was no more useless wars, and here we are — we’re back,” said Kevin, a 35-year-old civil engineer in Massachusetts. Kevin, a Democrat, voted for Trump in 2024 hoping he would boost the economy.

This year, he said, he is leaning toward supporting Republican Mike Minogue in the Massachusetts governor’s race, hoping he could shake up the state, and leaning toward backing Democratic Sen. Ed Markey for re-election.
“It goes back to the checks and balances,” Kevin said of the possibility that he could split his ticket, saying he wants to see a Democratic-controlled Congress end the war in Iran.

Kaleb Saracino, 21, of Nevada, doesn’t like how many resources are being poured into the Iran war or the idea that the U.S. is fighting there in behalf of Israel. He said he wants the government to cut off support for Israel, bring down costs and refocus on issues affecting everyday Americans.
“The cost of groceries, the cost of gas, the cost of living have all gone up because of these endless wars,” Saracino said.
Saracino knows he doesn’t want to support Trump, so he’s leaning toward the Democrats this year. But he doesn’t have warm feelings for either party.
“They’re looking out for themselves, their careers, because they’re career politicians, not so much the betterment of the American people,” Saracino said about both Republicans and Democrats.
Alexis, a 20-year-old college student in Florida, also expressed frustration with both parties in Washington.
“They’ve made a bunch of promises that haven’t been fulfilled, and you know why? It’s because people cannot talk to each other these days. Congress is so divided,” she said.

Alexis, an independent who voted for Harris in 2024, isn’t sure whom she’ll support in the Florida Senate race. She said more could get done “when we start allowing younger candidates who are more open-minded to vouching for the American people as a whole, rather than their own specific party.”

Essen Zali, a 46-year-old IT consultant from Texas, voted for Joe Biden in 2020 but backed Trump in 2024 after he became frustrated with Biden during the conflict in Gaza. Now, the Iran war has again left him frustrated.
“He went two steps forward with the whole war thing, and now we are all over the place,” he said. On top of that, Zali said, Trump seems focused on the wrong things.

“All the construction work that was going on in Washington, that was not ever required. All the beautifications and everything, that’s secondary. The tariff war without a reason,” Zali said. “It seems like he is burning all the ships.”
Connor Woodring, a 22-year-old independent from Colorado, also supported Trump in 2024. He was another voter who felt disdain for both parties.

“They’re one on the same side of the same coin, basically. Republicans are the warmongering side of it. Democrats are the side that try to pull at your heartstrings,” he said. “Either way, they’re going to vote and do the same thing they’ve done for the last 50 years, so it doesn’t matter which side you vote in.”
Woodring is a registered independent and doesn’t like any candidates in his area. His preference is to vote for someone not in either major party.
But, he said, “there’s a lot that can happen between now and November.”

title: U.S. pressures European allies to release diesel reserves as Trump considers export ban
summary: The Trump administration asked European allies to release diesel from their emergency stockpiles to increase global supplies and tamp down on soaring prices.
story: The Trump administration has asked several European allies to release diesel fuel from their national emergency stockpiles in an effort to increase global supplies and tamp down on soaring prices.
The average U.S. price of diesel has soared by 70% since the war with Iran began, hitting $6.38 per gallon Thursday, according to AAA.
Less than five weeks before the U.S. midterm elections, Republicans are eager for any way to lower domestic fuel prices.
U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright appeared confident this week that Europe would agree to tap its diesel reserves.

“You will hear announcements from our friends in Europe about new diesel supplies that’ll come to the market that’ll meaningfully push diesel prices down,” he told reporters Wednesday at an event with President Donald Trump in the Oval Office.
But U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer stopped well short of suggesting the European release was a done deal.
“I spoke with my French counterpart” about a diesel release, he said Thursday, calling it a “very good conversation.”
“I let him know that this is an idea that we’ve had in the U.S.,” he told Bloomberg Television. “We’d love to have a collaborative response to this.”

The United States is hosting G20 trade ministers in Milwaukee this week, where Greer said he planned to meet his European Union counterpart. Also in Milwaukee are trade ministers from China, India, the United Kingdom and other countries affected by tight global diesel supplies.
The message coming from Europe on Thursday was also a cautious one.
The E.U. is “in very close contact with our member states on this ongoing issue,” European Commission energy spokesperson Anna-Kaisa Itkonen told reporters at a media briefing in Brussels.
“We are also having high-level contacts ongoing with the U.S. administration,” she said.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

The majority of Europe’s emergency diesel reserves are stored in Germany and France. Both American and European oil refineries have been running at near full capacity for months, churning out as much diesel fuel as possible.

While the Iran war is responsible for the lion’s share of price increases in crude oil and unleaded gasoline around the world, the price of diesel has been outpacing both of them since July, albeit for a different reason.
Russia has traditionally been a major exporter of diesel, but that stopped this summer after Ukrainian drone strikes destroyed Russian refineries.
On July 8, Russia banned the export of diesel in order to preserve its domestic supply. On Wednesday, the Kremlin extended that ban until the end of October.

“We’re tight on diesel because we’ve lost diesel exports from Russia,” Wright said at the White House. “We’ve lost diesel, some diesel exports from the Middle East, although we’re restoring those. And we’ve lost diesel exports from China.”
“That’s a lot of interruptions,” he said.

But whether Europe will tap its emergency reserves of diesel to increase global supply is complicated by the fact that the Trump administration is actively considering a move that is effectively the opposite of what it is asking Europe to do.
On Wednesday, the president mused about imposing a ban on exports of U.S. diesel.
“I’m thinking about it,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “I speak to Chris and Doug about it a lot,” he said, referring to Wright and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum.
“They sort of think ... it’ll help diesel, but it might raise the price of other things,” he said.
An export ban on U.S. diesel would hit European countries particularly hard.
It would also land at a moment when average U.S. prices for unleaded gas remain almost 50% higher than they were on Feb. 28, the day the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran.

title: For the same ticket on StubHub, different prices for different people
summary: NBC News volunteers saw eight different prices for the exact same Harry Styles ticket on StubHub. The company said it’s running random price experiments.
story: The same seat at an upcoming Harry Styles concert at Madison Square Garden could cost $455. Or it could cost $517.
The difference comes from the fees that ticket broker StubHub adds. But how much those fees are — and why they can vary — is unclear.

NBC News gathered nine volunteers to check the same StubHub ticket at the same time for Styles’ Oct. 30 concert. They saw eight different prices. The ticket’s base price, set by the seller, was the same for everybody.
The big differences came from the fees StubHub added. One person was charged $72 in fees, while another was charged nearly twice as much, $134.

When the volunteers looked up the same ticket using incognito mode in Google’s Chrome web browser, a private session that doesn’t use cookies, saved logins or site storage, the price discrepancy declined to $19 between the highest- and lowest-priced ticket. When they checked on StubHub’s phone app without being logged in, almost everybody saw the same price, with the exception of just one person who would have been charged $3 more.

The days of a single, transparent price tag are fading. In the digital era, prices can change by the minute, without warning or explanation. Companies can run price experiments, in which shoppers are given a range of prices at random to determine the optimal price for profitability. Some companies use surveillance or personalized pricing, in which they charge individualized prices based on a customer’s data.

StubHub, one of the largest online ticket resale platforms, has recently faced scrutiny over its business practices, including advertising ticket prices without clearly disclosing mandatory fees, leading to a $10 million Federal Trade Commission settlement, and listing “ghost tickets” from a seller who didn’t actually have them.
The company said it does not use personal information in setting prices but confirmed that ticket prices can vary.

In a statement, StubHub said it “regularly runs randomized tests on pricing — a standard e-commerce practice across retail and marketplace platforms. The fee variations observed in your experiment reflect that testing, not personalization based on individual user data.” The company also said that differences in incognito mode were due to the “natural randomness of a small sample, not a signal that cookie or browsing data drives fee differences.”

Lindsay Owens, author of the new book “Gouged: The End of a Fair Price — and What That Means for Your Wallet,” said price experiments are a way for companies to maximize profit by helping to identify the upper limits of what customers are willing to pay. Even if it is random, it’s still unfair, she said.

“It’s not the resale ticket holder who’s getting that money,” Owens told NBC News. “It’s StubHub, who’s just charging some parents more, some ticket holders more, concertgoers more, just to see their favorite show.”
Owens said it was notable that without access to users’ data trails, the company appeared to have a harder time determining what to charge users.

Mark Tremblay, an economics professor at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, noted that if the price experiments are random, consumers could take advantage of this by checking multiple ways. “As a consumer, you should shop around on different mediums,” he said.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

It’s not just StubHub, Owens said: More and more companies are charging different consumers different prices for the same products. Last year, Owens’ think tank, Groundwork Collaborative, and Consumer Reports found that some Instacart shoppers were shown different prices for the same grocery items. The company said it was price testing and later ended the program.

Companies also have the technology to go a step further, using personal data to determine what a customer is willing to pay and tailor prices to each individual, a practice called surveillance or personalized pricing.

There is no federal ban on personalized pricing, but some states have passed laws regulating the practice. In August, the FTC proposed a policy that would require companies to disclose their use of personalized pricing.

Bob Hedges, a digital fellow at the MIT Initiative on the Digital Economy, said new technology, more powerful algorithms and the explosion of online shopping have made it easier than ever for companies to do this. “Even five years ago, the compute power and real-time processing was not adequate to support some of the real-time pricing algorithms in place today,” he noted.

As companies increasingly use sophisticated algorithms to calculate and change prices in an instant, it’s becoming harder for consumers to know when the price they’re seeing is based on their personal data.
To find out what companies are thinking, Owens said look to their patents. She pointed to DoorDash as an example.

The delivery platform has filed a patent for technology that it says predicts how hungry users are based on things like “a low battery” and “fast scrolling,” suggesting you could be “searching urgently for something to order.”
In a statement, DoorDash said the patent was “never used and has been withdrawn” and was meant to “help people find support if they were struggling on the app.”

The company acknowledged that customers may receive “personalized promotions” for the same order based on “past orders and favorite stores” but said that this practice does not amount to “surveillance pricing.”

title: Mike Tomlin is a Super Bowl-winning coach. His real passion might have been ‘Minecraft.’
summary: As the coach of one of the NFL’s most successful franchises, the Pittsburgh Steelers, for nearly two decades, Mike Tomlin was charged with building championship-caliber teams.
story: As the coach of one of the NFL’s most successful franchises, the Pittsburgh Steelers, for nearly two decades, Mike Tomlin was charged with building championship-caliber teams.
In his free time, Tomlin was building something different: an elaborate cityscape in the video game “Minecraft.”

On his YouTube channel on Wednesday, Tomlin revealed part of that map, which he said he had been working on for more than 12 years. Within four hours, the episode had been viewed more than 334,000 times. By the next morning, that total had doubled.
“I’ve always had an interest in architecture and so forth,” Tomlin said in the video, which has amassed over 900,000 views. “And so I started building this creative city.”
Tomlin may have been perfecting the map for more than a decade, but his hobby had only become public three weeks earlier.

The 54-year-old stepped down as the Steelers’ coach in January after 19 consecutive winning seasons, which included two Super Bowl victories. As his debut season as a broadcaster for NBC’s “Sunday Night Football” began last month, Tomlin revealed in an interview with Craig Melvin that his passions, in fact, ranged beyond football.
Watching his then-young children spend hours playing “Minecraft” had inspired him to see what all the fuss was about. As they became teenagers and went off to college, their interest waned.
Not Tomlin’s, though.
“More than anything, it was therapeutic for me,” Tomlin said. “So, mindless entertainment. I’m not a big TV watcher. It allowed me to detach from the realities and the pressures of life.”

With the Steelers, Tomlin was known for unique sayings referred to as “Tomlinisms.” In 2020, he famously wouldn’t allow Covid restrictions to be used as a hardship, saying, “We do not care.” So it stunned some football fans last month to hear that what Tomlin privately did care so much for was a video game that is immensely popular with elementary-age kids.
Since its creation in 2009, “Minecraft” has become the bestselling game of all time, with more than 300 million copies sold, Microsoft said in 2024, and has since spawned a popular movie.

An open-world “sandbox” game, “Minecraft” allows users to build whatever their creativity desires using a variety of materials, from different types of stone and wood to beyond. Some players build fantasy worlds where building physics don’t apply.

Players often build in multiple maps. Tomlin stuck to just one, however, preferring to build what appears to be a midsize city centered around bodies of water and with a dense urban core that includes sports stadiums, high-rises and a PNC Bank. The map showed hills and wooded suburbs.
In other words, not all that dissimilar to … Pittsburgh.

Narrating his tour with a matter-of-fact delivery not out of place from his past weekly news conferences, Tomlin used verbiage a real estate developer would approve of while saying that his map all began by creating a bay. Then he built a boutique hotel, complete with an executive spa, therapy rooms and an “appropriate number of public restrooms.” Showing off a glass ceiling over the hotel’s conference room, Tomlin called his design philosophy “lighting-conscious.”
Mike Tomlin says he's been working on a city in 'Minecraft'

Some commenters online questioned how much time Tomlin had spent building while also working in the NFL, an industry known for its workaholic culture. Former Steelers running back Le’Veon Bell wrote, “we were tryna win super bowls and coach T was on minecraft building cities 😭.”
More so, the reaction tended to center on Tomlin’s dedication to realism.

“Never thought I’d watch Mike Tomlin discuss lighting and basement speakeasies,” one YouTube commenter said. On a Reddit thread devoted to Tomlin’s build, one person wrote, “When Mike Tomlin first mentioned this whole thing, I was NOT expecting such an impressive city!”

Tomlin built buildings by themes, intentionally placing them next to rivers, bays and lakes he carved out of the map. His designs are intricate; residential buildings included different floor plans for the penthouse than the lower floors. Kitchens featured islands. Bathrooms featured plants. Bedrooms included paintings. The living spaces in one high-rise, which was down the street from buildings named “CVS” and “7-Eleven,” wrapped around a central aquarium. Nearby were stadiums for professional soccer and baseball.

At some point, Tomlin acknowledged becoming “obsessed with rooftop penthouses” with great views. That focus then spilled over into designing spaces for indoor and outdoor entertainment, balconies, home offices, and his-and-hers bathroom concepts.
“Find someone who loves you like Coach Tomlin loves a Jack & Jill bathroom,” another YouTube commenter said.

It was one of many jokes sparked by Tomlin’s “Minecraft” devotion. Yet, perhaps it shouldn’t have been all that surprising. In “Minecraft,” Tomlin seems to have found similarities to the mixture of creativity and discipline required in the world of the NFL. Coaches’ lives abide by a rigid structure of practices, games and the offseason calendar. They conceive exotic play designs and defensive coverages, then put them into practice by obsessing over details and precision.

“Football is an emotional game played by high-energy men who are really emotional,” Tomlin said in 2022. “They need to hear a steady voice. They need to hear consistency in messaging in belief, and so it’s my job to exemplify that.”

Tomlin was praised as a coach for his never-too-high, never-too-low personality. The kind of person whose idea of winding down after a long day in the spotlight might include ensuring his “Minecraft” map had a “certain density,” as he said. When Tomlin dropped his son Dino off at college, he said he was inspired to re-create the look of off-campus housing into his own city.
“Bro I used to come home sometimes and my PlayStation would just be gone,” one of Tomlin’s sons, Mason, posted on X. “And I wasn’t in trouble.”
At one point during Tomlin’s tour, he focused on a tall, beige building labeled “Trump Tower.”
“Not an endorsement,” a chyron said on the video. “This build is (circa) 2015… We didn’t think he would win. Twice.”
Its penthouse had an “unbelievable open floor plan,” Tomlin said approvingly.
He promised his roughly 76,000 YouTube subscribers more episodes.
“I’ll give you a tour of this aquarium at some point,” he said. “It’s crazy.”
