title: Christa Pike is in critical condition after a failed execution in Tennessee, her lawyers say
summary: As harrowing details emerge from Tennessee’s failed execution of Christa Pike, who survived despite her lawyers saying she was administered two doses of a lethal drug, scrutiny is falling on how the procedure was carried out.
story: As harrowing details emerge from Tennessee’s failed execution of Christa Pike, who survived despite her lawyers saying she was administered two doses of a lethal drug, scrutiny is falling on how the procedure was carried out.

Nearly 24 hours after Pike was set to be put to death for a murder she committed when she was 18, her lawyers said Thursday afternoon that she was still alive. Her prognosis was unclear, lawyer Randall Spivey said, but she remained in critical condition and was receiving “lifesaving medical care.” Neither he nor another lawyer, Stephen Ferrell, who spoke with reporters, said they had seen her in the hospital.
“I’m haunted by last night,” said Spivey, who was there during the execution attempt.
Spivey said he counted at least seven needles used in Pike’s left arm alone, “one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her arm after an unsuccessful attempt.”

He added that Pike’s right arm had turned purple after the second round of the drug pentobarbital, a sedative used in Tennessee’s execution protocol, was dispensed. Pike’s lawyers said they also learned of “blistering and burning around the sites of the injection.”

The description sheds additional light on what occurred inside of the execution chamber as the execution team attempted to put Pike, 50, to death. After the curtain to the chamber was opened at 7:26 p.m., a media witness said Pike complained that “my arm feels like it’s about to burst open.”
Other media witnesses said Pike moaned that one spot was “really throbbing” and was kicking so often she knocked a sheet that was laid on her.
She continued to make snoring sounds, groan and move after the drugs were presumed to have taken effect, the witnesses said.
Five minutes after the second dose, “it was clear that Miss Pike was still breathing,” Spivey said.

He said he did not see any lifesaving care provided to Pike when he was able to witness the events unfold, but there was a time before the witnesses were led out when no one could see what was happening. Medical care was administered in an ambulance that was called at 8:50 p.m. to the prison in Nashville where executions are held.
“Last night was not just inefficient; it was cruel and it was torturous,” Spivey said.

Medical experts told NBC News that Pike’s injuries could be consistent with the drug failing to go directly into her bloodstream but ending up in surrounding tissue because of incorrect insertion or leaking.

If that happened, it would mean less of the drug getting into her circulatory system, keeping her breathing and moving rather than becoming deeply comatose before death, said Dr. Jonathan Groner, an emeritus professor of clinical surgery at the Ohio State University College of Medicine.
Burning around the injection site could also be evidence of the drug not getting properly injected into a vein, he added.
“I’ve seen partial thickness burns look red or purple,” Groner said.

Ferrell said he thinks a “number of factors” could explain the execution failure, but said that based on what medical experts told their team about Pike’s difficult veins, it seems like the intravenous line may have infiltrated.

This occurs when a misplaced needle deposits the medication into the arm instead of the bloodstream. That, he said, would be consistent with Pike’s complaints that her arm was hurting during the process, and that it felt like it was “about to explode.”
Where is Christa Pike now?

Spivey described venous issues that Pike has had throughout her life, noting problems with typical blood draws. It’s part of the reason she feared this method of execution, and why she requested a different method, the lawyers said.
“I do know that that really was her biggest fear,” Ferrell said. “It was not a fear of dying. It was a fear of a prolonged, painful, traumatic death, and that’s what happened minus the death.”
Spivey said he was given an emergency number for the Tennessee Supreme Court to call if something went wrong with the execution, but that when he called it, it went to voicemail.
Pike’s attorneys have since appealed her execution. Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee has stayed Pike’s execution until a third-party investigation uncovers what happened Wednesday.
“This is a tragedy. There is no one that wanted what happened last night to happen. It shouldn’t have happened,” Lee said at a news conference Thursday morning.
He declined to give details on Pike’s condition and said he would be hiring a team to look into the circumstances surrounding the failure.
“I do hope he cares, because this is as a citizen of Tennessee, this is something that was done in all of our names,” Spivey said of Lee.

It’s the second time an execution did not go as planned in Tennessee this year. Tony Carruthers, convicted in three 1994 killings, was granted a one-year reprieve after executioners in May couldn’t find a vein for a backup IV.
Many questions remain in Pike’s case: Was she in pain when this was occurring? Will she remember what happened? Will there be long-term damage? Ferrell said he does not have the answers.

“We may never know what all she was suffering through, either because she can’t remember it, she can’t tell it, or it overwhelms her in such a way that, you know, sometimes pain and suffering affects people that way,” he added.

Pike’s conviction stems from a 1995 murder case. Pike, along with two other teenage accomplices, worked together to torture, slash and fatally beat Colleen Slemmer, Knoxville police said at the time. Pike was convicted in Slemmer’s death and sentenced to death; she was on death row for decades.
A number of last-minute efforts to stop the execution were unsuccessful. Pike was set to be the first woman Tennessee has executed in more than 200 years.

title: Amber Guyger, ex-police officer, granted parole after Botham Jean murder conviction
summary: Former Dallas police officer Amber Guyger was granted parole just under seven years after she was convicted of murdering neighbor Botham Jean in a 2018 shooting.
story: A former Dallas police officer was granted parole on Thursday just under seven years after she was convicted of murdering her neighbor in a 2018 shooting.
Amber Guyger, 38, was granted parole by the Texas Board of Pardons and Paroles, the board said in a statement. In 2019, Guyger was convicted of murdering 26-year-old Black man Botham Jean.

Guyger told authorities that she shot Jean after mistakenly walking into his apartment, believing it to be her own, according to officials. She told authorities she believed Jean was an intruder. Jean was eating ice cream in his living room and not armed, according to authorities.
The former police officer was sentenced to 10 years in prison for the crime. Prosecutors asked jurors to sentence Guyger to at least 28 years.

The Texas board said that Guyger was granted parole because she did not have a documented pattern of violent arrests, she “maintained a satisfactory institutional adjustment” and completed programs “that should enhance chances to obtain and maintain full-time stable employment” during her imprisonment.

Guyger initially became eligible for parole on September 29, 2024. Her initial review occurred on October 10, 2024, and resulted in a parole denial with her next review being scheduled on or about October 2026.
During her trial, questions were raised about the role race may have played in the killing.
Prosecutors revealed racist text messages the former police officer sent, unrelated to Jean or his killing.
One of the texts was about the Martin Luther King Jr. parade in Dallas in 2018.
“When does this end lol,” an officer wrote to Guyger.
“When MLK is dead … oh wait …,” she joked.
Two days before Guyger killed Jean, she texted someone who had just adopted a German Shepherd.
The dog’s owner wrote that the dog “may be racist.”
Guyger replied: “It’s okay ... I’m the same.”
Prosecutors said that Jean was watching television and eating a bowl of vanilla ice cream in his living room just before 10 p.m. when Guyger burst inside and shot him.
Guyger testified that she used her electronic key fob to open Jean’s door and that she immediately drew her service weapon once she was inside.
The prosecution said the trajectory of the bullet showed that Jean was either getting up from his couch or cowering when Guyger fired at him.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
A lawyer for Jean’s family, Lee Merritt, said in a statement to NBC News Dallas-Fort Worth that the family was “disappointed by the decision.”

“A 10-year sentence was already a fraction of what was lost,” Merritt said. “Releasing Ms. Guyger after seven years makes that loss feel even smaller in the eyes of the system. It is not. The family still lives with this loss every day.”
Jean’s family said in a statement on Thursday that they are requesting privacy at this time.
“To all of the many well-wishers who have continued to say Botham’s name and carry his memory, they wish to give their thanks for the continuing support,” the family said in a statement.
Jean’s brother, Brandt Jean, said he forgave Guyger during her sentencing in 2019.

“I personally want the best for you,” he said at the time. “I wasn’t even going to say this before my family, but I don’t even want you to go to jail. I want the best for you, because I know that’s exactly what Botham would want you to do — to give your life to Christ.”
The Dallas Police Department said in a statement that it had “no role in this decision.”

“The Dallas Police Department understands this decision may bring renewed attention and emotion surrounding the tragic death of Botham Jean,” the department said. “Our thoughts remain with the Jean family and all those impacted by his loss.”

Jean grew up in Saint Lucia before coming to the United States to go to Harding University in Arkansas, which he graduated from in 2016. He was working as an accountant for one of the most prestigious accounting firms in the world, PricewaterhouseCoopers, in Dallas when he was killed.
He would have turned 35-years-old on Tuesday.

title: Diddy placed in solitary following NBC News report on his VIP prison life
summary: Sean “Diddy” Combs has been placed in solitary confinement following an NBC News report on his VIP lifestyle inside prison.
story: Sean “Diddy” Combs has been placed in solitary confinement following an NBC News report on his VIP lifestyle inside prison, according to a source with knowledge of the matter.

The disgraced hip hop mogul arrived at the Fort Dix federal prison in New Jersey in October after he was sentenced to 50 months behind bars for transporting people across state lines for sexual encounters.

Since then, he has spent thousands of dollars a month to bring his high-end lifestyle to the low-security prison, NBC News reported Tuesday in a story based on interviews with four men who spent time in the same unit as Combs.

They said he had no trouble acquiring contraband items such as cellphones and premium liquor, including Hennessy. He also pays several inmates who cook special meals for him, clean the toilet and shower areas before he uses them, do his laundry, make his bed and even give him Chinese-style massages.
“This is not some normal s--- you see in jail. This is some rich s---,” one of the sources said. “It looks crazy, but again, it’s Diddy.”
NBC News also obtained photos and videos inside the prison, which includes footage of Combs appearing to use a contraband cellphone.
Diddy appears to use cellphone in prison
After the report was published, Combs was removed from his dormitory-style quarters and placed in a special housing unit, better known as solitary confinement or the SHU, according to the source.
A Bureau of Prisons spokesperson would neither confirm nor deny that Combs was moved.

“For privacy, safety, and security reasons, we do not comment on the conditions of confinement for any incarcerated individual, including quarters assignment or whether a particular individual is the subject of allegations, investigations, or sanctions,” the spokesperson said.
TMZ was first to report that the Bad Boy Records founder was moved to solitary.
Federal prisons often transfer inmates to the special housing unit when they are the subjects of an investigation, experts say.
“We’d put people in the SHU while we were gathering evidence,” said Vito Maraviglia, a retired special investigator for the Bureau of Prisons who worked at Fort Dix in the late 1990s.

Maraviglia said the New Jersey prison is known as one of the cushiest in the federal prison system. It has segmented housing areas that are more difficult to monitor than at other facilities, making it easier for inmates to hide and use contraband items like cellphones.
“A high-profile guy like that, with all that money, I’m surprised they put him at a place like Fort Dix,” Maraviglia said.

Inmates placed in the SHU are locked in a cell with one other person for at least 23 hours a day, according to two men who spent time at Fort Dix. Inmates are allowed a book or two and a wind-up radio, the sources said, and they must wear an orange jumpsuit instead of the regular khaki uniform or grey sweatpants and shirts.
Meals are delivered in trays but commissary access is restricted, and they are permitted to shower only a few days a week. The sources said they must otherwise wash up in a sink.
“It’s nasty down there,” one of the sources said.
It isn’t Combs’ first time in solitary confinement at Fort Dix. Last summer, he was placed in the special housing unit after he got into a fight with another inmate.
He was later kicked out of a drug treatment program at the prison but continued paying inmates to do a range of services for him, NBC News reported Tuesday.

The story prompted responses from people as varied as Combs’ longtime nemesis 50 Cent and the prominent attorney Gloria Allred, who represents a woman suing him for allegedly raping her more than 20 years ago. (Combs has denied the allegations, and the case is ongoing.)

“These serious allegations against Mr. Combs cry out for an immediate federal investigation and appropriate federal action including a prosecution if the allegations of having and using a cell phone while incarcerated can be proven beyond a reasonable doubt,” Allred said in a statement.
Other famous people have also received perks in prison, including Martha Stewart and Harvey Weinstein.

Combs’ trial last year centered on drug-fueled orgies he organized called “freak offs.” They involved male sex workers and his former girlfriends – including the singer Cassie – who filed a lawsuit against Combs alleging years of physical and sexual abuse. (The case was settled, with Combs denying any wrongdoing.)
The trial ended in a split verdict, with a New York jury finding him not guilty on the more serious charges of sex trafficking and racketeering charges that could have put him in prison for life.

title: Phil Mickelson sought treatment for addiction and family trauma, spokesperson says
summary: Golf legend Phil Mickelson checked himself into a treatment facility earlier this year to address family trauma and addiction, his spokesperson confirmed to NBC News Thursday.
story: Golf legend Phil Mickelson checked himself into a treatment facility earlier this year to address family trauma and addiction, his spokesperson confirmed to NBC News Thursday.

Mickelson, 56, is no longer at the facility, and it is not clear when he entered treatment or for how long. His representative did not give further details about the nature of his stay at the unnamed facility and declined to answer additional questions.
The announcement comes amid a turbulent year for the six-time major champion.
For Subscribers
In April, Mickelson said he would step away from competition for an extended period while his family navigated “a personal health matter.”

Mickelson, who is married and has three children, was reportedly barred from his longtime Southern California golf club, The Farms Golf Club, after being accused of making “nonconsensual and inappropriate physical contact” with a female club employee. The allegations were first reported by Golf Digest, citing multiple sources.
For Subscribers

At the time, a representative for Mickelson described the encounter as a “misunderstanding.” Mickelson’s attorney, Tom Locke, said in a statement: “There is a great deal of misinformation circulating and, while Phil’s full attention is devoted to a private family health matter, he has retained defamation counsel and is determined to hold accountable any publication or individual trafficking in speculation or false rumors.”

Mickelson is far from the first professional athlete to seek treatment for addiction. Olympic champion Michael Phelps went to rehab in 2014 after a DUI arrest. This spring, golf champion Tiger Woods said he was seeking treatment for substance abuse after his vehicle rolled over in Florida and he was charged with driving under the influence in March.
Mickelson has won 45 PGA Tour events, including six majors.

title: Patriots tight end Eli Raridon and wife announce death of newborn son
summary: New England Patriots tight end Eli Raridon and his wife, Anna Raridon, announced the death of their newborn son, who they said in a social media post never went home after he was born.
story: New England Patriots tight end Eli Raridon and his wife, Anna Raridon, announced the death of their newborn son, who they said in a social media post never went home after he was born.
Their son, Peter James Raridon, was born on September 11th, according to an Instagram post on Wednesday from the couple sharing the news.

In the caption of the post, the couple said they learned at their 20-week anatomy scan that their son was diagnosed with anencephaly, which the couple described as “a fatal condition in which he would not survive outside the womb.”

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, anencephaly is a condition in which a child is born missing parts of their brain and skull. The condition is fatal and there is no current cure or treatment.

“While we are absolutely devastated that we were unable to bring our baby boy home, I am grateful to have loved him deeply, kept him safe, and had been his home for the past 9 months before he was called back to Heaven,” the couple wrote in the Instagram post.

“Though his time with us was brief, his life still precious, his purpose still meaningful, and he will forever be a part of our story,” the post added. “I have loved you every second of your life & will miss you every second of mine. What a sweet sweet reunion ours will be.”
For Subscribers
Eli and Anna Raridon were married on May 25, 2025, and announced on March 31 that they were expecting.
For Subscribers
“half me, half you— fearfully & wonderfully made, thank you Jesus!!! baby Raridon arriving this fall,” the caption of the announcement post said.
Eli Raridon was drafted to the New England Patriots in the third round of the 2026 draft. He previously played college football at Notre Dame University.

title: Rick Ross charged with battery after alleged attack on girlfriend
summary: Rapper Rick Ross was arrested Thursday after he was accused of beating his girlfriend at his Miami Beach home, according to authorities.
story: Rapper Rick Ross was arrested Thursday after he was accused of beating his girlfriend at his Miami Beach home, according to authorities.

Ross, whose legal name is William Leonard Roberts II, was charged with felony battery by strangulation and misdemeanor battery in connection with a domestic violence incident at his home on Miami Beach’s exclusive Star Island, according to a statement and affidavit from the Miami Beach Police Department.
Police said the accuser reported that Ross, 50, struck her multiple times during an altercation on Aug. 28 and restricted her breathing by twisting the collar of her hoodie.
The woman, whom police did not name, reported the incident to police on Tuesday. Ross turned himself in Thursday morning. He has pleaded not guilty to the charges.
An attorney for Ross did not immediately return a request for comment.
The woman provided detectives with a sworn statement and photographs documenting her injuries, police said. A criminal affidavit identifies the woman as Ross’ girlfriend at the time of the incident.
On the morning of Aug. 28, Ross was “enraged” that his girlfriend was tagged in an Instagram photo, accused her of lying to him and slapped her across the face, the affidavit says.
Later that morning, according to the police record, Ross accused her of having a romantic relationship with someone she said she was “merely friends with.”

The woman told police that Ross then struck her in the chest several times and choked her “to the point she could not breathe by grabbing the collar of the hoodie she was wearing and twisting it,” the affidavit said.
Ross then grabbed her by her ponytail and slammed her against a wall, the affidavit says.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

She told police she escaped the residence, returned and waited until Ross left before retrieving her belongings, according to the affidavit. The two dated for about a year, and lived together at the Star Island home at the time of the incident, the affidavit says.
Ross is best known for his breakout single “Hustlin’,” released in 2006, as well as “Aston Martin Music” and “Stay Schemin.” He’s received nine Grammy nominations.
The rapper’s bond was set at $5,000 for the battery by strangulation charge and $1,000 for the battery charge, according to online jail records.
“I’m totally innocent of these fabricated allegations made against me,” Ross said, leaving the jailhouse “I repeat: I’m totally innocent of these fabricated allegations made against me.”
Ross said he would be traveling to Dubai on Friday and in Paris on Saturday.

If you or someone you know is facing domestic violence, call the National Domestic Violence hotline for help at (800) 799-SAFE (7233), or go to www.thehotline.org for more. States often have domestic violence hotlines as well.

title: Fiona Lowe, daughter of Chad Lowe and Kim Painter, dies at 13
summary: Fiona Lowe, the daughter of actor Chad Lowe and producer Kim Painter, has died, the family announced.
story: Fiona Lowe, the daughter of actor Chad Lowe and producer Kim Painter, has died, the family announced.
She was 13.
“We are deeply heartbroken by the loss of our beloved Fiona,” the Lowe family said in a statement posted Wednesday to the Instagram stories of her sister, Mabel Lowe.
The family remembered Fiona as “a loving young girl who was smart, creative, and loved to dance.”
The statement added: “She was adored by her sisters and she was deeply loved by her parents. In fact, she was the light of our lives.”

“Her passing is devastating for our entire family and we ask for prayers and privacy at this time,” the family statement said. “If you or someone you know is struggling with mental health, please reach out to the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by calling or texting 988.”
Fiona Lowe’s cause of death was not announced. People was the first outlet to obtain the family statement.
Her grandfather, Chuck Lowe, said Wednesday on Instagram: “Rest in peace sweet Fiona.”
Born on Nov. 16, 2012, Fiona Lowe was the second of Chad Lowe and Kim Painter’s three daughters.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Chad Lowe, an Emmy winning actor with television roles on “Life Goes On” and “ER” who is the brother of actor Rob Lowe, often posted photos of his children on his Instagram page. That included shots of the whole family, pictures of the three girls together and video clips that show the family enjoying their travels and day to day lives.
One of his most recent posts of Fiona Lowe featured her on her 13th birthday.
“Celebrating Fiona officially becoming a teen today!!” Chad Lowe wrote in the caption. “Keep dancing through life FiBear! Love you soooo much!!”

If you or someone you know is in crisis, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline or chat live at 988lifeline.org. You can also visit SpeakingOfSuicide.com/resources for additional support.

title: Trump says he’d consider issuing pardons to administration officials before he leaves office
summary: President Donald Trump said in a new interview that he’s considering pre-emptively pardoning members of his administration before the end of his second term.
story: President Donald Trump said in a new interview that he’s considering pre-emptively pardoning members of his administration before the end of his second term.
“Yeah, sure I’d do that,” he said in an interview this week with Time magazine, which published a transcript of the conversation Thursday.
Asked to further elaborate, Trump referenced how President Joe Biden pre-emptively pardoned a slew of people who worked in his administration at the end of his presidency.

“It was a disappointment to a lot of Republicans,” Trump said. “Sleepy Joe gave pardons to everybody. He gave them to Fauci. He gave them to this. But you mean I’m not allowed to give them, but Sleepy Joe’s allowed to give them?”

Biden had done so in an effort to protect people that Trump had threatened during the 2024 presidential campaign, including former Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Mark Milley; Dr. Anthony Fauci; and lawmakers and staffers of the House committee that investigated the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol.
In April, The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump had repeatedly promised his top administration officials pardons before he leaves office, citing people who had heard his comments.

“I’ll pardon everyone who has come within 200 feet of the Oval,” Trump said in a meeting, according to the report, which also said that he had told advisers last year that he would host a news conference and announce mass pardons before he leaves office.
In Time’s interview, Trump was asked how he is preparing for the scenario of Republicans losing the House majority in the midterm elections.
“They’ll probably go after me and I’ll go after them,” Trump said.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Democrats have said that if they win back control of the House, their top priority would be focused on healthcare, including reversing Medicaid cuts implemented under Trump and extending Obamacare tax credits that Congress didn’t approve a continuation of when they expired last year.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who could become the next speaker of the House, recently said that a House Democratic majority would conduct aggressive oversight of the Trump administration and “certainly will fight to hold the crooks accountable.”

The House has the power to impeach officials and to hold them in contempt of Congress, but doesn’t have the power to bring criminal charges. The House is already slated after Election Day to vote on a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, though that was introduced by fierce Trump critic Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky.

On the first day in office last year, Trump had issued pardons and commutations to roughly 1,500 defendants who were charged in the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol. Since then, he has issued about 170 pardons and commutations to other individuals convicted of crimes, according to a list compiled by the Justice Department.

On the last day of Trump’s first term in office, he granted clemency to 143 people, including his former chief strategist and longtime ally Steve Bannon, who had been indicted on wire fraud and money laundering conspiracy charges but had not yet faced a trial.

title: RFK Jr. to roll out $10 million challenge to encourage Presidential Fitness Test in schools
summary: Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. plans to announce a nationwide competition for schools aimed at expanding participation in the Presidential Fitness Test.
story: Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. plans to announce a new nationwide competition for schools aimed at expanding participation in the Presidential Fitness Test, which President Donald Trump revived last year.

The challenge will offer $7 million in prizes to schools, districts and youth organizations that demonstrate effective ways to implement the test, the Health and Human Services Department told NBC News. Another $3 million in awards and vouchers will be available for fitness or sports equipment.

Trump signed an executive order last year to bring the test back to schools. But only 161 schools on U.S. military installations are required to do so, so the administration has looked for ways to boost participation.
Starting Thursday, organizations can apply for the cash prizes on a new federal website, Fitness.gov. Entries can be submitted until February, then winners are expected to be announced in the spring.

The fitness test is a lengthy tradition in public elementary, middle and high schools that measures children’s physical health based on their performance in various cardiovascular and strength exercises. Children compete to win awards by hitting certain benchmarks for their age and sex, such as running a mile in under 10 minutes. The exercises for the revived test under the Trump administration include a one-mile run, curl-ups, planks, pushups, pullups and shuttle runs.

The test aligns with a broader interest in fitness among several top Trump administration officials. Kennedy, who often shares his own workout videos on social media, has pledged to reverse what he describes as an “epidemic” of chronic disease in children in part by lowering obesity rates through exercise. And Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has tightened fitness standards for military troops. The Defense Department posted a video last year of Kennedy and Hegseth challenging each other to a pushup and pullup competition.
Trump has also promised “a golden age for American sports” as the 2028 Summer Olympics approach.

A variation of the same Presidential Fitness Test was implemented in public schools from 1956 until the 2012-13 school year, when the Obama administration replaced it with the Presidential Youth Fitness Program, which focused on individual health and aimed to minimize comparisons between children.
Kennedy has criticized that change, arguing that competition is good for children.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

“If we’re going to be competitive internationally, we need to be competitive with each other. We need to teach people how to win and how to lose and how to process victory and defeat,” he said at the signing of Trump’s executive order last year.

Kennedy’s uncle John F. Kennedy made a similar argument shortly after he was elected president in 1960. Kennedy has often pointed to the era of his uncle’s presidency as a time when American children were healthier, but the reality is complicated. While kids were less sedentary in the 1960s, their life expectancy is higher today, and while rates of some chronic diseases are rising among children, the trend is sometimes attributable to improvements in screening and detection. Increases in childhood obesity and Type 2 diabetes, however, are strongly associated with diets heavy in processed food and sedentary lifestyles.

Experts widely agree that young people should be more active. The federal government recommends that children ages 6 to 17 get at least an hour of moderate or vigorous physical activity each day. Only 20% to 28% of kids meet that goal, according to the Physical Activity Alliance, an advocacy group that promotes physical fitness.

However, some researchers who study physical activity among children worry that dividing kids into winners and losers the way the Presidential Fitness Test does could discourage them from engaging in fitness. The test also rewards certain types of athletic ability, they say, when there are other ways to be physically active.

Russell Pate, a professor of exercise science at the University of South Carolina, said the test is not an indicator of overall health. Many schools already use a program called FitnessGram to holistically assess a child’s physical health rather than their athletic skills, he said. Most kids will also find it difficult to meet the benchmarks for the Presidential Fitness Award, he added.
“It’s based on high-level performance in all the test items, and we know from long, hard experience that only a very small percentage of kids realistically can achieve that,” he said.

title: Judge bars U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro from charging ex-Olympian in Reflecting Pool case
summary: A D.C. Superior Court judge has permanently banned Jeanine Pirro’s office from bringing charges against a former Olympic canoeist over damage to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.
story: WASHINGTON — A Superior Court judge in the District of Columbia has permanently banned U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro’s office from bringing charges against a former Olympic canoeist over damage to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

Judge Todd Edelman entered an order on Thursday that dismissed the case with prejudice. Edelman cited the “exceptional circumstances” of the case and said the government’s “own representations make plain” that bringing another indictment against David “Davey” Hearn “is theoretical at best, and more likely, is simply fanciful.”

Trump, Edelman wrote, “has criticized the decision of the Office of the United States Attorney to drop the case in the most vituperative terms; demanded that the government reinstitute the prosecution, in part because of Mr. Hearn’s political activity and the identity of one of his attorneys; and publicly entertained the possibility of firing the United States Attorney as a result of the dismissal.”

Hearn, Edelman wrote, “faces the unique possibility that the government will revive this case — one that it has already announced to be meritless — based on political pressure brought by the President of the United States upon his subordinate officers.” The government “has no right to retain the ability to compound the errors it has already made, or even to threaten to do so, at Mr. Hearn’s expense,” Edelman wrote.
Trump had lashed out at Hearn over political donations and because one of his lawyers, Norm Eisen, has been a longtime Trump critic involved in many legal battles against the administration.

Eisen and Hearn’s other attorneys — Mary Dohrmann, Steve Levin and Michael Bromwich — said in a joint statement that the decision “is a victory for the rule of law and for an innocent American seeking justice” and said the case never should have been brought in the first place.

“This was a miscarriage of justice, and what happened to Mr. Hearn is an outrage that should shock every American,” they wrote. “This administration chose to pursue an unjust prosecution against Mr. Hearn. It should not get repeated chances to wield the power of criminal prosecution against someone who should never have been prosecuted. Today’s decision protects Mr. Hearn from that threat, allowing him to move forward with his life as he deserves.”
Pirro’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Attorneys for Hearn and the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia sparred in court last month over whether Hearn’s Reflecting Pool case should be dismissed with prejudice, meaning prosecutors would be barred from bringing another case against him. At the center of much of the discussion: Donald Trump’s pressure campaign on Pirro’s office and his decision to link his desire for prosecution to the political beliefs of Hearn and one of his attorneys, Norm Eisen.
Pirro’s office dropped the case in late July after evidence showed the area was already damaged, and Hearn’s team moved to ban the office from bringing another case in August.
At an unrelated press conference last month, Pirro declined to answer several questions from reporters about her handling of the Reflecting Pool case.

Pirro’s office wanted to maintain its ability to bring a theoretical case, even though its own evidence — that the section of the Reflecting Pool that Hearn allegedly touched was already damaged, and they can’t prove more than $1,000 in damage — would make bringing another felony case impossible.
“What future prosecution could even occur?” Edelman asked at the hearing.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
“That I don’t know,” said Michael Spence, a career official in the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia.
“Give me an example of one possible thing that could happen” to change the fundamentally flawed case, the judge asked. “Even theoretically, what could there be?”
Spence conceded he had no satisfactory answer. He added that the U.S. Attorney’s Office had no investigation going into Hearn “as of this second” but said that could change.

Edelman noted that it was going to be pretty difficult to find a case with similar circumstances to Hearn’s case, and asked Spence how he was supposed to look at Trump’s statements calling for a prosecution that Pirro’s office admits was meritless. The president’s statements, Spence said, “speak for themselves.”

Steve Levin, an attorney for Hearn, said prosecutors “had no case” and that the government abused its prosecutorial discretion by rushing to indict Hearn to please the president, misleading a grand jury along the way.

“That’s where the bad faith comes into play,” Levin said. How is Hearn supposed to trust the grand jury process, Levin asked, given that the case got through before? “There’s no confidence that Mr. Hearn has that the grand jury will do the right thing” if another case was presented,” he said.
Pirro’s office, Levin argued, is trying to keep a “discredited felony accusation on life support,” and doing so served no public interest.
“There is nothing that can save the case they dismissed,” Levin said. “The government has basically acknowledged there is nothing that can revive this case.”
But Spence said the grand jury process would still give Hearn protection from a bad faith prosecution.
“The government did act in good faith in this case,” Spence argued.

title: Alix Earle Says the Last Book She Read Was Dr. Seuss. Jenna Has a Reading Syllabus for Her
summary: Alix Earle says she has never read a book, so Jenna Bush Hager is here to help.
story: Alix Earle says she has never read a book, so Jenna Bush Hager is here to help.

The creator of the Read with Jenna book club broke out a reading list for the social media star on TODAY Oct. 1 after Earle, 25, told Interview magazine that she’s “never read a book,” except for “maybe Dr. Seuss.” The revelation sparked backlash and shocked Jenna.
“Alix, you’ve been on the show,” Jenna said on TODAY. “We know that you’re smart, so you know what we want to do, we want to give you a little syllabus.”
Earle reacted to her comment going viral on her Instagram story by reposting a tweet about it, adding the caption, “This is sending me,” per EW.
Before Jenna broke out her reading recommendations for Earle, she and Sheinelle talked about the benefits of curling up wth a book.

“With social media, you have to use your mind quickly,” Jenna said. “When you sit in a book and you’re there for a while it uses a different part of our brain, which is a part that we used a lot back in the day and has been sort of combated with the rise of short videos.
“Reading fiction brings about — and we know this — the rise of empathy,” she continued. “Because you’re sitting in the shoes of somebody else.”
With that said, she offered the following books for Earle.
“Come here, sit on our show, and we can teach you how to be a great reader,” Jenna said.
‘The Baby-Sitter’s Club’
Jenna first recommended the classic children’s book series by Ann M. Martin.
“We know you’re an entrepreneur,” Jenna said. “She started her own brand. This talks about females getting together, starting a club, empowering each other. Let’s start here, Alix.”
‘Are You There God? It’s Me, Margaret’
Judy Blume’s iconic 1970 novel about sixth-grader Margaret Simon has been a rite-of-passage read for generations of kids.
“Alix, if you haven’t learned about sex, this might hit the ticket,” Jenna joked.
‘Of Mice and Men’
The 1937 novella by John Steinbeck about the Depression-era experiences of George Milton and Lennie Small is a staple of scholastic reading lists.
“If you didn’t get assigned this in eighth grade, I want to talk to your English teacher,” Jenna said.
‘Pachinko’
A more contemporary classic, the 2017 novel by Min Jin Lee follows the saga of multiple generations of a Korean family who move to Japan.
“I love this author so much,” Jenna said before showing off the weighty tome. “This is a bigger one, so that’s why you start with these (other books).”
Jenna wasn’t done, and she included a syllabus with seven more books:

title: Leigh Bardugo Reflects on Backlash to ‘Ninth House,’ Her First Novel Written For Adults
summary: Leigh Bardugo looked back at the uproar over content warnings in Ninth House and whether she thinks trigger warnings are necessary.
story: Leigh Bardugo is looking back at a conversation-starting chapter of her career.

The author rose to fame with her sprawling Grishaverse YA novels, set in a magical world. In 2019, she made her adult debut with “Ninth House,” the first book in a trilogy that unfolds among the secret societies of Yale.

At the time of its publication, a graphic assault scene in “Ninth House” sparked a discussion about content warnings. Some readers said they were shocked and disturbed by the scene and that there should have been a warning before reading.
On an episode of Jenna Bush Hager’s “Open Book with Jenna” out Oct. 1, Bardugo said the uproar is “still surprising” to her, “given some of the things that are popular now.”
“There was nothing in this book that really deviated from what you would find in any horror novel or urban fantasy novel, but it was a departure from what I had written for teens,” she said.
Bardugo said while there’s “an argument to be made” for content warnings, she noted that calls for them tend to be loudest for books written by women who previously wrote books for kids.
“I think there’s a very puritanical streak that runs through all this,” she said.
She also said if content warnings are expected, they need to be in every book, “and I’m not interested in being the test case.”

“I believe that things belong on different shelves,” she said. “That where we shelve a book is all about expectations. And if you are coming to a young adult shelf, you would never find ‘Ninth House’ there.”
Bardugo said her first impulse was to be defensive over the backlash to her book’s content. “I didn’t write this for shock value,” she remembered thinking.
Then, she realized the outrage was proof the book was working.

“You should be troubled by this. If you’re reading about an assault on the page. You shouldn’t just be able to skim right past it. It should hit you. It should hit you like a ton of bricks. And if I did that, maybe I did something right,” she said.
Ultimately, she said, the book “found the people it needed to find.” If she had changed or softened its contents, “it would not have found those people.”
Plus, she said, books are an excellent place to raise difficult and uncomfortable topics, “because you’re safe when you’re doing it.”

“(Books) can lead to conversation. They can lead to difficult thoughts that we have about things we’ve been through, things that we’re going through with other people, things that our friends have been through, that maybe we don’t know how to speak to them about. That kind of connection exists in these places of discomfort,” she says.
The final installment of Bardugo’s “Ninth House” series, called “Dead Beat,” came out Sept. 15, wrapping up Alex Stern’s voyage through the magical portals of Yale University.

title: Amanda Peet Reveals First ‘Weird’ Sign of Breast Cancer. It Wasn’t a Lump
summary: Amanda Peet had an early breast cancer warning sign six months before she was diagnosed. She reveals the skin symptom that she calls “weird.” It wasn’t a lump.
story: Amanda Peet was diagnosed with breast cancer last fall, but she had an early warning sign that something was wrong six months earlier.
The actor revealed the “weird” symptom during an interview with TODAY on Thursday, Oct. 1.

“I was in my closet, I was probably putting something on and I felt a weird — it just didn’t feel like normal skin, but it wasn’t the frozen pea that everybody talks about,” Peet, 54, told Savannah Guthrie, referring to what a breast cancer lump can feel like.
“I went and I even got an MRI and then they sent me away. So I thought I had a clean bill of health, but they were actually watching it.”

Six months later, on the Friday before Labor Day in 2025, the actor thought she was going in for a routine scan, when her doctor spotted something concerning on her ultrasound, Peet wrote in an essay for The New Yorker.

She knew something was wrong because her physician, who was usually very chatty, went silent. The doctor then performed a biopsy and told her she would walk the sample over to Cedars-Sinai and hand-deliver it on a Friday night, another concerning clue.
Peet said she’ll never forget the moment when she received her breast cancer diagnosis in a call soon after.

While lumps are the most common breast cancer symptom, skin changes like dents, swelling and redness can also be a warning sign. Skin that appears pitted, like the skin of an orange, is among breast cancer symptom a doctor monitors in herself.

Once diagnosed, Peet recalled having to deal with a “slow drip of information” about the treatment options, genetic information and hormone receptor status. “If you’re an anxious person, it’s your basic nightmare,” she noted.
The actor was diagnosed with hormone-receptor-positive and HER2-negative lobular breast cancer and underwent a lumpectomy and radiation.

Lobular breast cancer accounts for 15% of all new breast cancer diagnoses, according to the National Cancer Institute. Tumors don’t usually form in lumps, making them hard to detect, especially in women with dense breast tissue, it notes. Peet has dense breasts and was told she needed extra monitoring. She’d  been seeing a breast surgeon every six months for checkups, she wrote in her essay.
Her cancer was caught early, at Stage 1. “I think about how lucky I was in so many ways,” she said.
Peet previously told Hoda Kotb that she has great health insurance, lots of support from her friends and family and a nanny.
“There were a lot of people around to take care of me, but not everybody has that,” she said. “So I’ve also been giving that a lot of thought.”

title: Where Is Thomas Randolph from ‘The Widower’ Now?
summary: Where is Thomas Randolph from The Widower now? What did he do? Where is he serving time?
story: This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is in crisis, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. You can also text HOME to 741741 or visit SpeakingOfSuicide.com/resources for additional resources.
Out of Thomas Randolph’s six marriages, four of his wives are dead — three of them under mysterious circumstances.

The new Netflix documentary from Library Films and NBC News Studios, “The Widower: ‘Til Death Do Us Part,” chronicles the investigation into Randolph as it unfolded in real time through the lens of veteran Dateline producer and investigative journalist Dan Slepian, who was embedded with detectives. The story includes chilling background on his early marriages, stunning legal twists, and the push for justice by those left in the wreckage of his wake.
Randolph also shares his side of everything in the documentary through interviews with Slepian, who has followed all the twists and turns of Randolph’s story for 18 years.
“This guy was the most unusual murder defendant I’ve ever covered,” Slepian tells TODAY.com. “He’s a self-described narcissist who makes menace sound like charm, and charm sound like a warning.”

Here’s what to know about Randolph and his story in “The Widower,” which began streaming on Sept. 30. Also, for more on the case, tune into Allegedly, a weekly video podcast on Netflix hosted by NBC News’ Ellison Barber for a one-on-one conversation with Dan Slepian about his two-decade odyssey with Thomas Randolph.
Who Is Thomas Randolph?
Randolph, 71, earned the nickname “the widower” after four of his six wives died.
Two of them died via gunshot wounds. The death of his wife Beckie in 1986 was ruled a suicide by authorities, and the death of his wife Sharon in 2008 was found to be a homicide by police.

Another one of his wives died from cancer years after she divorced him, while his fifth wife died from a medical procedure that her family says in the documentary was orchestrated to take her life. Randolph was not charged with any crimes in connection with her death.
His two living ex-wives and the families of three of his other former wives describe a man who owned multiple firearms and was always taking out life insurance policies on his brides.
In the documentary, he repeatedly denies any wrongdoing in the deaths of any of his former wives or any involvement in murder-for-hire plots to collect life insurance money.
Randolph did get charged in the deaths of two of his wives and faced a potential sentence of the death penalty in both cases.
He was acquitted by a jury on a first-degree murder charge of his third wife, Beckie Gault, in 1988 — two years after her death.

He was convicted in 2017 by a Las Vegas jury on two counts of murder with a deadly weapon and a count of conspiracy to commit murder in the deaths of his sixth wife, Sharon Causse, and handyman Mike Miller. His conviction was overturned by an appeals court in 2020, and then he was convicted a second time by a Las Vegas jury in a retrial in 2023.

The documentary offers a striking visual of how long the ordeal lasted. Colleen Beyer, the daughter of Randolph’s sixth wife, was pregnant with her own daughter when Slepian began filming with her. By the time Randolph was convicted by a jury for the second time in 2023, Beyer’s daughter, Katie, was 15 years old.
Randolph’s first marriage was in 1975, and his most recent marriage came in 2007. He has lived in Utah, Nevada and Indiana during his various marriages, and they all had a common thread.
“One theme that is consistent is that he did not have a wife he did not get insurance money on,” Slepian said.

In addition, three different men claim in the documentary that Randolph approached them about murder-for-hire plots involving Randolph’s first, second and fourth wives. They all say they turned him down. The family of a fourth man, whom a jury convicted Randolph of killing, also said he was asked the same thing by Randolph in relation to Randolph’s sixth wife, Sharon Causse.

Randolph describes himself as “cocky” in two separate video interviews included in the documentary, including one with Las Vegas Metro Police detectives following the death of his wife Sharon in 2008.
The aunt of one of his late wives describes him as “an arrogant smartass” in an interview in the documentary.
Retired Las Vegas Metro Police detective Dean O’Kelley says in the documentary that Randolph also had a thorough knowledge of the legal system.
“He knew how the system worked, there’s no question about that,” Kelley says. “And like everything else he did, he knew how to manipulate things, too.”
“He continued using his charisma and legal knowledge that he developed over decades to play the system like his game,” Slepian tells TODAY.com.
One of his former wives also describes his love of firearms, which he confirms during the taped 2008 interview with the Las Vegas detectives.
“I got so many f------- bullets it’s scary,” Randolph says in the interview. “I could start a small war on a third country.”

He also liked to live extravagantly. Slepian says in the documentary that Randolph bought a Porsche and a hot tub with the money from life insurance policies he took out on his wife, Beckie, whose death in 1986 was ruled a suicide.
Randolph enjoys appearing on camera, frequently agreeing to interviews with Slepian.
“This is a guy who was remarkably comfortable about being filmed,” Slepian tells TODAY.com. “Most suspects become guarded, but he saw it as oxygen. He seemed to become more of himself.”
What Happened to Thomas Randolph?
Randolph faced murder trials in 1988, 2017 and 2023 in connection to the deaths of two of his former wives.

He first stood trial in the death of his second wife, Beckie Gault, which was ruled a suicide by the Clearfield Police Department in Utah in 1986. Investigators found her dead in her bed in their home with a gunshot to her head and a suicide note, Slepian says in the documentary.

Randolph was pulled over by police on the night of her death for driving erratically with a bottle of vodka in his car and spent the night in jail. He said he then came home to find Beckie dead from suicide.

Two years later, Randolph was charged with murder after his former friend, Eric Tarantino, told police he had been groomed by Randolph to kill Beckie and had refused, O’Kelley says in the documentary, citing the prosecutors in the case.
Prosecutors argued during the trial that Randolph intentionally got himself arrested after killing Beckie in order to have an alibi.

A Utah jury acquitted Randolph on the murder charge, but he was not initially set free. Randolph served about 18 months in prison for witness tampering, according to Slepian. Tarantino says in the documentary that Randolph tried to hire an inmate in jail to kill Tarantino, but it turned out to be an undercover agent, resulting in the tampering charge.
After being released, Randolph then sued the prosecutors for charging him with murder, received a settlement and had his record expunged, Slepian says in the documentary.

In 2008, Randolph called 911 from his Las Vegas home to report that his sixth wife, Sharon, had been shot by an intruder during a robbery attempt. He said that he shot and killed the alleged intruder, a man named Mike Miller, whom Randolph had previously hired as a handyman.
Sharon Randolph died from her injuries on the night she was shot.
O’Kelley, who was the lead detective on the case, says in the documentary that he didn’t believe the physical evidence corroborated Randolph’s version of the events.
In a scene captured on camera by Las Vegas Metropolitan Police, Randolph invites detectives into his home and reenacts what he says happened that night and how he shot Miller.
O’Kelley and a fellow detective present prosecutors with evidence they believe shows that Randolph hired Miller to kill his wife, then double-crossed him and killed Miller after Randolph shot Sharon.

However, prosecutors did not believe they had enough evidence to charge Randolph until eight months later in January 2009, when a warrant was issued for his arrest. The documentary shows police handcuffing and dragging a shirtless Randolph out of a home where he was living with his mother. He was charged with the murders of his wife and Miller.

It took 8½ years before Randolph stood trial. A jury initially convicted him in 2017 on two counts of murder with a deadly weapon and a count of conspiracy to commit murder, and he was sentenced to the death penalty.

However, the Nevada Supreme Court overturned the guilty verdict in 2020. The court ruled that the jury should not have been allowed to hear “prior-bad-act evidence” about Randolph’s previous trial in 1988 on the murder charge involving the death of his wife Beckie, according to NBC affiliate KSNV.

After winning his appeal, Randolph earned another trial in Clark County, Nevada, in 2023 and was convicted a second time by a jury. His most recent appeal was denied by the Nevada Supreme Court in September 2026.
Where Is Thomas Randolph Now?
Randolph was sentenced to 60 years to life in prison in April 2024 after being convicted by a jury for a second time for the murder of his wife, Sharon, and Mike Miller in 2008.
He appealed his second conviction, but the Nevada State Supreme Court announced on Sep. 2 that it was denying him a third trial.
Slepian tells TODAY.com that even though Randolph is in prison for the remainder of his life, he still reaches out to him to talk.
“He just called me two days ago,” Slepian said. “He sees me potentially as an opportunity to continue to have a bullhorn of some sort. He’s 71 years old, still talking my ear off.”

title: ‘East of Eden’ Ending: Joseph Zada Unpacks that Charged Scene and the True Meaning of Timshel
summary: What happens at the end of East of Eden? What does timshel mean? Here’s what to know.
story: Warning: This post contains spoilers for Netflix’s “East of Eden.”
Joseph Zada lights up when asked about the ending of “East of Eden,” Netflix’s seven-episode adaptation landing on the platform Oct. 1.
“It was ridiculous,” Zada tells TODAY.com of his co-star Christopher Abbott’s performance, awe in his eyes.
Zada’s character, Cal, is the cast out son of Abbott’s Adam Trask. Growing up, Cal always came second to the favored son, Aron (Joe Anders).

In the final scene, which takes place after Adam has a stroke, Cal and Adam have a charged interaction that encapsulates the story’s themes of forgiveness, redemption and choice. Incredibly, the interaction consists of just one, weighty word: “Timshel.”

“I was like, ‘Dude, like, you should not be able to act like that.’ It’s ridiculous. He was using half of his mouth and one of his eyes to act, and then he would say that line. It would be like the most like impactful full word of all time,” Zada says.
Zoe Kazan wrote and directed the series adaptation of the sprawling, multigenerational epic, over 70 years after her grandfather Elia Kazan directed his own adaptation of John Steinbeck’s 1952 book.
Here’s what to know about how her version of it ends.
What Happens at the End of ‘East of Eden’?
A loose retelling of Cain and Abel, “East of Eden” is the story of how two families came to live in California’s Salinas Valley, starting in the Civil War era and through World War I.

Cal, one of Adam’s two sons, grapples throughout the book with feeling immoral. His brother, Aron, is the apparent favorite — the “good” one. As Cal learns the truth about his mother, Cathy (played by Florence Pugh), he worries he inherited her badness.
His inner turmoil worsens when his actions inadvertently lead to his brother Aron’s death while serving in Europe in WWI. His father has a stroke after hearing the news.
Lee (Hoon Lee), Adam Trask’s housekeeper, urges him to forgive Cal and release him from guilt. All Adam says is one word, but it’s enough.
What Is ‘Timshel’?
Adam tells Cal one word at the end of the series and the book: timshel.

“Timshel” is a Hebrew word that appears during the Cain and Abel story in Genesis 4:7, at a time when God is speaking to Cain about overcoming sin or evil. In different versions of the Bible, the word has been translated a few ways — that man “must” or “shall.” But Steinbeck revisits another potential meaning of the Hebrew word: “thou mayest.”
The character Lee explains it in a conversation with Adam Trask and Samuel Hamilton in “East of Eden.”

“The American Standard translation orders men to triumph over sin, and you can calls in ignorance. The King James translation makes a promise in ‘Thou shalt,’ meaning that men will surely triumph over sin. But the Hebrew word, the word timshel — ‘Thou mayest’ — that gives a choice,” Lee says.
“It might be the most important word in the world. That says the way is open. That throws it right back on a man. For if ‘Thou mayest’— it is also true that ‘Thou mayest not.’ Don’t you see?”
That’s the choice Adam gives his son on his deathbed — he can still choose to be good.

“The whole book is about intergenerational trauma and the way that people believe that they’re sometimes fated to what their parents were like or what the environments that they grown up in,” Zada says.
For Zada, the word liberates his character from his family’s past.
“You can choose your own path, regardless of what you’ve been through and the choices that you’ve made already,” he explains. “You can change, and you don’t have to be like your predecessors.”

title: It’s Beginning to Sound A Lot Like Christmas, Spotify Data Shows
summary: Spotify says the trend of people listening to holiday music earlier and earlier each year has continued in 2026.
story: This Oct. 1, some people are listening to their favorite Christmas songs.

There are already 36.2 million average daily holiday streams on Spotify, according to data from the digital streamer, suggesting that for some, getting in the spirit of the winter holidays is starting earlier this year.
Nearly 100,000 holiday playlists were created by Spotify users in September, while its Christmas Hits playlist rose to No. 64 on playlist charts back on Sept. 25.
Spotify also released its five most streamed holiday tracks so far this season:
“Merry Christmas, Please Don’t Call” by Bleachers
“Merry Christmas, i miss you” by Alex Crichton
“Snowman” by Sia
“Last Christmas” by Wham!
“All I Want For Christmas Is You” by Mariah Carey

Listening to holiday music before the season officially gets underway is not new. Spotify says the phenomenon has started to take place earlier and earlier over the last five years. The streamer says in 2025, the first noticeable jump in listening to holiday music occurred Oct. 22, a week earlier than it did in 2021.

Hearing holiday music in October is just one part of early recognition of the holidays, known as “Christmas creep.” Stores sell holiday merchandise long before Christmas, or even Halloween. People and retailers may also put up decorations earlier than is typical and, yes, play music before there’s even a chill in the air.

In August, Cracker Barrel announced holiday items were already in stock, Best Buy said holiday savings would begin in October and the United States Post Office kicked off its annual gift donation program, Operation Santa, on Sept. 14.
Retail expert Trae Bodge said retailers try to capitalize early after the summer season ended on Labor Day.
“Now that Labor Day is over, it’s kind of slow, and so for retailers to have buzzy decor in the windows and sales and excitement, it kind of makes sense,” she told Emilie Ikeda on TODAY Sept. 16.

title: Witney Carson Reacts to Speculation She Wants to Be Voted Off ‘DWTS’ Amid Pregnancy
summary: “Dancing With the Stars” pro Witney Carson and partner Guillermo Rodriguez have been in the bottom three since the Season 35 premiere.
story: “Dancing With the Stars” pro Witney Carson and partner Guillermo Rodriguez have been in the bottom three since the Season 35 premiere.
Carson, who is currently pregnant with her third child, a boy, and  Rodriguez may have received the lowest scores week after week, but they have definitely secured the popular vote.
After the Sept. 29 “DWTS” episode, which saw them receive a 15 out of 30, their highest scores so far, Carson reacted to speculation that she’s ready to be eliminated.

“I do feel like I need to address some rumors going around or some opinions, speculations, whatever you want to call it,” Carson said in her TikTok video. “Every week, Guillermo and I have been put in the bottom three, which doesn’t necessarily mean all those couples have the lowest votes, but it does mean that you don’t get to celebrate that you’re safe. You only get to hear who’s going home.”

She said that when the cameras pan to her reaction after the eliminated couple is announced, it’s her being “genuinely sad for the people going home.” Then there’s “excitement” that she gets to continue in the competition.
“Those two emotions are existing at once,” she continued. “But my first initial reaction is sad for whoever’s going home, and then obviously we celebrate, and they don’t really show that bit.”

“Yes, I am very happy that we’re continuing on,” Carson said. “... I am truly so grateful to continue on in this competition week after week with Guillermo because he really deserves it. He is genuinely a kind person. He genuinely wants to get better. He never gives up.”
She shared how anytime she is resting, Rodriguez continues to practice and that he is so dedicated.

“What you see on Tuesdays is his very best,” the dancer explained. “There’s a lot to say about someone who may not have the skills, but is willing to learn and put in the work. That’s an amazing thing.”
She also addressed people who are “concerned” about her and her baby’s health.
“I know how far to push my body and the baby’s health has always been my No. 1 priority,” she said.
Carson previously shared the same sentiments in her chat with TODAY.com.

“As much as I want to dance and want to do all of it, I really have to be careful to make sure that I don’t overdo it,” she said ahead of the Sept. 15 “DWTS” premiere. “It’s perfectly safe to do all the things and I’m really not taking this any differently than I would any other season as far as mentally and physically.”
She stressed that she loves to dance and compete, but she and husband Carson McAllister were also ready to grow their family. The couple share boys Kevin, 5, and Jet, 3.

“I don’t feel like people necessarily have to lose parts of themselves to keep growing their family. That’s kind of my mantra,” she told TODAY.com. “I’m gonna stay true to what I love and continue on my career and continue to grow my family. It’s a big blessing to be able to do both.”

title: Who Were Thomas Randolph’s 6 Wives in ‘The Widower’ and What Happened to Them?
summary: What happened to Thomas Randoph’s six wives?  Here are all six of his wives and what happened next.
story: The lives of multiple women and their families were irrevocably changed when they ran into Thomas Randolph.

The new Netflix documentary from Library Films and NBC News Studios, “The Widower: ‘Til Death Do Us Part,” details the story of a Las Vegas man who has been married six times, and four of his wives have died. The film is directed by Chris Smith, who executive produced the pandemic-era sensation “Tiger King” for Netflix, and begins streaming on Sept. 30.

In 2023, Randolph, now 71, was convicted by a Las Vegas jury for a second time on charges of murdering his sixth wife, Sharon, and a handyman, Mike Miller, whom prosecutors said he double-crossed after hiring Miller to kill his wife.
He had his initial conviction in 2017 overturned by the Nevada Supreme Court in 2020 and then was convicted again after a second trial in 2023.

The new documentary from Library Films and NBC News Studios explores a 20-year odyssey involving Randolph, as well as one family’s efforts to bring him to justice. “Dateline” producer and veteran investigative journalist Dan Slepian, who appears in the documentary, was embedded with detectives and frequently interviewed Randolph over the years.
In the documentary, Randolph repeatedly denies any wrongdoing in the deaths of any of his past wives or any involvement in murder-for-hire plots to collect life insurance money.

The film begins with Randolph’s 911 call informing police that his  wife, Sharon, had been shot at their Las Vegas home in 2008. That moment triggers an investigation into Sharon’s death that mushrooms into a deep dive by detectives into Randolph’s chilling past, with Slepian there to film it all.
Here’s what to know about Randolph’s six wives, what happened to each of them, and what connected their experiences with Randolph.
“Eventually, each family came to the conclusion that he was dangerous, horrible, manipulative and ruined their lives,” Slepian tells TODAY.com.

For more on Thomas Randolph and his six marriages, tune into Allegedly, a weekly video podcast on Netflix hosted by NBC News’ Ellison Barber. This week’s episode features a one-on-one conversation with Slepian about his experience following the Randolph case for nearly two decades.
Kathryn Thomas
Married August 1975
Randolph’s first wife, Kathryn, is one of his two former spouses who are still alive.
Now living in Carnation, Washington, she shares in the documentary that many of the chilling behaviors that surfaced in Randolph’s future relationships were evident early.
She said she met Randolph through mutual friends when she was a senior in high school and married him when she was 18 and he was 20. The former couple have two children together.

“He was a very charming and witty person and very intelligent, and I fell for that at first,” she says in the film. “He got really scary, not physically but psychologically. He liked to control you, (and) didn’t want you to have any friends.”
Thomas said she left him when he started seeing other women and doing drugs, recalling that his face “went red” when she told him she had enough.
She also shared two recurrent themes throughout Randolph’s marriages. He had taken out a life insurance policy on her, and he owned several guns.
“He really scared me at that point,” she says.
“You know, there’s always been a lot of insurance on every wife I’ve ever had, and I’ve had a bunch of them,” Randolph says in an audio clip in the documentary.
After she divorced Randolph, she married one of his former friends, a man named Steve Thomas. He says in the film that he was approached by Randolph to see if he would kill someone for money.
“Looking back, I firmly believe she was the target,” Steve Thomas says about his wife.

“This is the first time we know that Tom Randolph tried to groom someone to commit murder,” Dean O’Kelley, the lead detective in the Las Vegas case involving Randolph’s sixth wife, says in the documentary.
Beckie Gault
Married April 1983
Randolph began a relationship with Beckie Gault while he was still with Kathy Thomas. He ended up marrying Gault a day after he divorced his first wife, Slepian says in the documentary.

Rosealie Allred, an aunt of Beckie Gault, says in the film that her niece was getting ready to leave Randolph and move in with Allred when she was found dead in their Utah home in 1986. Investigators ruled it a suicide after finding a gun in her hand and a suicide note, Slepian says in the documentary.

On the night of her death, Randolph was pulled over by police for driving erratically, and a bottle of vodka was found in the vehicle, Slepian says in the documentary. He spent the night in jail and said when he returned home, he found his wife dead in their bed and called 911.
“I’d been in jail for about four hours before my wife killed herself,” Randolph says in audio of a conversation with Slepian in the documentary. “So, I didn’t do this s---.”
O’Kelley, who investigated Randolph’s past after his sixth wife’s death, says in the documentary that Randolph cashed in on insurance policies from Gault’s death worth close to $500,000.

Two years after she died, Randolph was arrested on a charge of first-degree murder after a former handyman, Eric Tarantino, told authorities Randolph tried to hire him to kill Beckie, and he refused, O’Kelley says in the documentary, citing the prosecutors in the case.
Randolph was acquitted by a jury in Utah on the murder charge, which is shown in the film.

He pleaded guilty to felony tampering with a witness for trying to hire a man to kill Tarantino while Randolph was in prison, and the inmate turned out to be an undercover cop, Slepian says in the documentary. He served about 18 months in prison.
Leona Stapleton
Married March 1994
Randolph met his third wife, Leona, in Utah, and then the two moved together to Indiana, Slepian says in the documentary.
They got divorced, and then years later, she died from cancer.
Gayna Allmon
Married October 1995

Barely a year after his previous marriage ended, Randolph married Gayna Almon, who is one of two of Randolph’s ex-wives who is still alive. She says in the documentary that she met him through a personals ad in the newspaper.
“He brought flowers and the next thing I know I’m stupid enough to marry him,” she says.

After Randolph was involved in a shooting at a local bar, police in Edinburgh, Indiana, informed her about the death of Randolph’s second wife, Beckie, Slepian says in the documentary. The police asked if he had taken an insurance policy out on her, and she said he had.
“I had no knowledge of any of that,” she says in the documentary about his past. “I was totally shocked.”

One night, a bullet went through the floor right near where she was sitting while Randolph said he was cleaning his firearms, O’Kelley says in the documentary. She says she waited until he went to work and then left him for good.

A former associate of Randolph’s named Glenn Morrison appears in the film and says Randolph offered him to make “some quick money” by shooting Allmon and making it look like a robbery. Morrison said he declined.
Randolph denies repeatedly in the documentary that he ever asked anyone to commit a murder-for-hire.
No investigation was ever done, and Randolph was never charged with any crimes in connection to his fourth wife.
Frances Randolph
Married August 1997
Randolph met his fifth wife while he was still with his fourth wife, and then convinced Frances to leave her husband to marry him, Slepian says in the documentary.

Carolyn Austin, the sister of Frances Randolph, says in the film that Frances had a heart condition that needed to be addressed before she was older, and Randolph encouraged her to get the procedure done.
She went to a doctor who was selected by Randolph, according to Austin. While recovering from surgery, Frances took a turn for the worse and died, O’Kelley says in the documentary.
Her death was never declared a murder, and Randolph insists to this day it was due to medical malpractice, Slepian says in the film.
Randolph collected money from life insurance policies on Frances and also received a settlement from a wrongful death lawsuit against the hospital, according to Slepian.

In a chilling aftermath, Austin found a VHS video that Randolph had his late wife make, which she shows in the documentary. The tape serves as a video will in which Frances declares her wishes to have Randolph inherit everything from her.
“I’m making this tape so people will know what I want when I pass away,” Frances says in the video.
“One of the moments that stand out the most to me is the video will that we saw on that VHS tape,” Slepian tells TODAY.com. “You can hear him coaching her.”
Sharon Causse
Married March 2007
Randolph moved from Utah to Las Vegas when he married Sharon Causse 10 years after his previous marriage.
Three months into their marriage, Causse made a will leaving almost everything to Randolph, and he took out three life insurance policies for about $350,000, Slepian says in the documentary.

The two were married for barely more than a year when Randolph called 911 in May 2008 to report that his wife had been shot by an intruder. Randolph said he shot and killed the man in self defense, according to audio of the 911 call in the documentary.
The alleged intruder was a man Randolph knew named Mike Miller, who had worked for him as a handyman, which he tells the 911 operator.
Prosecutors declined to charge Randolph with any crime at the time.

Causse’s daughter, Colleen Beyer, describes in the film that she was fearful of Randolph after she informed him that he would not be inheriting Sharon’s possessions after Beyer was named the administrator of her mother’s will. When she had the locks changed on her home, Randolph showed up to confront her but was stopped at the door by O’Kelley, according to footage in the documentary.

Eight months after his sixth wife’s death, Randolph was charged with two counts of murder with a deadly weapon and a count of conspiracy to commit murder in the deaths of his wife and Miller. However, it took 8½ years for him to stand trial, as he is shown in the film repeatedly hiring new lawyers to delay the case.
A jury initially convicted him in 2017 on two counts of murder with a deadly weapon and a count of conspiracy to commit murder, and he was sentenced to the death penalty.

However, the Nevada Supreme Court overturned the guilty verdict in 2020. The court ruled that the jury should not have been allowed to hear “prior-bad-act evidence” about Randolph’s previous trial in 1988 on the murder charge involving the death of his wife Beckie, according to NBC affiliate KSNV.

After winning his appeal, Randolph faced another trial in Clark County, Nevada, in 2023 and was convicted a second time by a jury on charges of murder and conspiracy to commit murder. His most recent appeal was denied by the Nevada Supreme Court in September 2026.

Beyer testified at both Las Vegas trials in the hopes of seeing justice for her mother. The ordeal lasted so long that her daughter, who she was pregnant with when Slepian began filming with her, was 15 years old by the time Randolph was convicted by a jury for the second time.

title: Craig Melvin Is Nominated In People’s Sexiest Man Alive Poll. How to Vote
summary: Craig Melvin is nominated in the “hotter than your cup of coffee in the morning” category in People’s Sexiest Man Alive Readers’ Choice Poll.
story: People’s Sexiest Man Alive Readers’ Choice poll is back, and TODAY’s very own Craig Melvin is among the contenders.

The co-anchor is among the nominees featured in the “hotter than your cup of coffee in the morning” category for morning show personalities, going up against Michael Strahan, Gio Benitez and Vladimir Duthiers.
The TODAY team celebrated the news Sept. 30 with cups of coffee.
“Am I being punk’d right now?” Craig said of his nomination.
“Let’s vote!” Jenna Bush Hager said.
“Vote early and often,” Savannah Guthrie chimed in.
“Try to stuff the ballot,” Carson Daly said.
Voting in the survey runs through Oct. 12. The results will be available starting Oct. 20. Readers can vote in the poll here.
Other Readers’ Choice poll categories for 2026 include “sexiest fake hockey player,” “sexiest cat dad” and “sexiest period drama dreamboat.”

This isn’t the first time Craig has appeared in the magazine’s Readers’ Choice poll. In 2023, he was nominated for sexiest morning show host. That same year, Al Roker was also up for sexiest grandpa. Mark Consuelos ultimately took home the morning show host award, while Pierce Brosnan won sexiest grandpa.

title: ‘Dancing With the Stars’ Yacht Rock Night Ends With Emotional and Tearful Elimination
summary: It was Yacht Rock Night on “Dancing With the Stars” and the 13 remaining couples delivered heart-pounding routines.
story: It was Yacht Rock Night on “Dancing With the Stars” and the 13 remaining couples delivered heart-pounding routines.

Last week, three celebrities — Amber Glenn, Ezra Frech and Jenna Dewan — led the leaderboard, while Giada De Laurentiis and partner Alan Bersten were eliminated.
The troupe, along with eliminated pros Hailey Bills and Adele Zaikman, opened Tuesday’s episode as co-host Alfonso Ribeiro and Julianne Hough explained the theme of the night.
Derek Hough, Carrie Ann Inaba and Bruno Tonioli dished out the hard and constructive criticism, praising celebs for their weekly improvement.
